The Dean's daughter Sabine matches Pennie in age. Country childhood, kindness to the poor, and family scrapes fill the sequel.
21232-the-hawthorns-a-story-about-childr:
An old pear tree grows close to the nursery window at Easney Vicarage. Ivy hugs its trunk, its blossom is white each spring, and its pears drop with a soft splosh. Amy Walton opens her story of the Hawthorn children under that tree. Four of them, Penelope, Ambrose, Nancy, and David, are schoolroom children when the tale begins.

Walton wrote the book for girls of about eleven or twelve, in a late Victorian country setting. Daily life at the vicarage, lessons, games, and small troubles make the plot rather than great events. Its sequel, Penelope and the Others, continues the same family's story at Easney.
21293-brownsmith-s-boy-a-romance-in-a-ga:
George Manville Fenn sets this romance in a market garden around 1835, where fruit and vegetables are raised for daily trips to London market. Grant Dennison lives with his mother in a house overlooking the garden. After her death, old Brownsmith takes the boy in to learn the gardener's skills.

Another boy, Shock, sleeps rough around the garden, living on snails, hedgehogs, and rabbits, and teases Grant at every chance. Fenn, a keen naturalist, teaches real market gardening inside the story. Lessons run from sowing to the night cart ride to market with old Ike and the horse Basket. Danger and near disaster season the lessons, as Fenn readers expected.
2136-the-tale-of-balen:
Algernon Charles Swinburne retells an Arthurian tale in verse, dedicated to his mother in March 1896 and published that year by Chatto and Windus. Balen, the knight of the two swords, moves through a world of hawthorn time and bright spring. Swinburne took Balen from Malory, where the knight bears two swords to his doom.

Swinburne's lines are musical and dense, full of colour and fate, as Balen's story runs toward its tragic end. The poem suits readers of Victorian Arthurian verse who enjoy sound and image as much as plot. The 1896 edition, dedicated to his mother, shows Swinburne late in life returning to Arthurian verse.
21565-the-queen-s-matrimonial-ladder-a-n:
William Hone attacks King George the Fourth in The Queen's Matrimonial Ladder, a satire of 1820. Fourteen step scenes, with verses and cuts by Cruikshank, climb the ladder of Queen Caroline's wrongs. The pamphlet and its toy sold together for one shilling.

Hone, who wrote The Political House That Jack Built, reached a twenty-first edition with this piece. The king's bid to shed his wife, bag of charges and all, is mocked scene by scene. A line from Measure for Measure fronts the work. The piece shows how cheap print and bold pictures could shake a throne in Regency London.
21741-the-island-queen:
An open boat drifts on a calm Southern Ocean at the start of this Ballantyne tale of fire and water. An albatross circles the silent craft, puzzled by its stillness. In the boat, a young girl lies faint while a man struggles up to scan her face with fear. How they came there is the story's first question.

Ballantyne calls the tale the story of a queen dethroned by fire and water. Shipwreck, island life, and rule among castaways follow from that drifting boat. The sea gives and takes in his usual measure. It is a South Seas adventure built on survival, with a girl's fate at the heart of the storm and the calm.
21777-the-years-between:
Poems written across the years of the Great War make up Rudyard Kipling's The Years Between, first published in 1919. The title names the span between the old peace and whatever would follow the war. Contents range from The Declaration of London and For All We Have and Are to Epitaphs and The Female of the Species. A dedication to seven watchmen opens the book.

Kipling writes of France, of Lord Roberts, of Irish Guards, of Mesopotamia, and of sons who would not come home. Some poems scold Parliament and the public; others grieve in a few hard lines. The voice is the famous one, turned to wartime Britain. Few books show so plainly what those years asked of, and took from, his generation.
21838-which-or-between-two-women:
Two women love one man in Which? Or, Between Two Women, a French novel by Ernest Daudet in Laura E. Kendall's English translation. The tale opens with a gypsy mother fleeing with her child and dying at the Château de Chamondrin. The friendless little one is taken in and raised there. From that start, the publisher promises, stirring incidents crowd every chapter.

Paris and the country share the scene, and part of the action passes in the Conciergerie, the grim prison of the Revolution. History and fiction are woven close in this double love story. Daudet, brother of Alphonse, was among France's most read novelists. The romance keeps its grip by heart and event in equal measure, page after page.
21850-a-little-norsk-or-ol-pap-s-flaxen:
A Norwegian child grows up on the hard northern plains in Hamlin Garland's A Little Norsk, also called Ol' Pap's Flaxen, published in 1892. The book opens with a poem of the prairie winter: a cabin cowering in the blast, snow hissing like wolves across the plain. Against that cold, Garland sets the tale of a flaxen-haired girl and the old man who raises her.

Her adoptive parents, her first trip in a blizzard, and the life of a settler's cabin fill the early chapters. Garland had won fame with Main Traveled Roads for his true pictures of farm life. This shorter tale brings the same honesty to a child's story. The plains are beautiful and pitiless in his telling, and both shape the girl.
21930-salthaven:
A ship-owner's son comes home to the firm in W. W. Jacobs's Salthaven, a novel of 1908. Mr. John Vyner tells his chief clerk Hartley that young Robert will join the firm next week. Robert has had three years at Cambridge and two studying business methods round the world. Hartley must give up his room, for a time, Vyner says, with kindly condescension. The general office is cheerful, too, he suggests.

Jacobs builds his comedy on such small demotions and the hopes tied to them. Salthaven port life, clerks, sailors, and courtship fill the chapters. His touch is lighter than the satire it hides. The novel shows Jacobs stretching his Thames-side world into a full social comedy, where a room with a door can decide a man's worth.
22096-stories-the-iroquois-tell-their-ch:
Mabel Powers collected Stories the Iroquois Tell Their Children in 1917. Powers lived near the Iroquois and learned their tales from tribal storytellers. She pictures the winter fire, where the children cry "Heh" and crowd close. The storyteller then begins, and ends each tale with "Na ho" — it is the end.

The stories tell of the Little People, of trees, flowers, birds, and animals. They explain how things came to be and how children should behave. Powers wrote them down in simple English for young readers. Her book keeps a place among the gentler records of Iroquois oral tradition made in the early twentieth century.
22156-the-boy-with-the-u-s-weather-men:
Francis Rolt-Wheeler put his boy hero with the United States Weather Bureau in The Boy with the U.S. Weather Men, issued in 1917. Rolt-Wheeler's U.S. Service series sent boys inside real government work. This volume opens in a storm: Ross looks down at his Airedale, soaked to a seal's likeness, tugging at his trouser leg. The boy is every bit as wet as the dog.

From that drenching the story follows forecasting, storm warnings, and mountain observatories. Weather men read instruments, telegraph warnings, and save ships and harvests by minutes. Rolt-Wheeler packs in real science between adventures. His series made civil servants into heroes for boy readers.
22175-stories-from-the-ballads-told-to-t:
Mary MacGregor retold Stories from the Ballads Told to the Children, with pictures by Katharine Cameron. MacGregor found the tales in old books of song. She promises children songs of love and hate, of joy and sorrow. When they are older, she hopes, they will seek the same old books themselves.

Her prose turns famous ballads into clear stories for young readers. Carterhaugh's lone plain, where Tam Lin waited, sets one scene. Others tell of Robin Hood's world, fairy queens, and true lovers parted by feud. The book belongs to a series that carried Britain's classics to the nursery, and its ballads carry blood, magic, and music in softened form.
2234-sketches-in-lavender-blue-and-green:
Jerome K. Jerome gathers short sketches and stories under colors that hint at their moods, from gentle humor to quiet melancholy. Sketches in Lavender, Blue and Green ranges across London life, holidays, friendships, and small human follies, each piece brief and polished. Jerome's easy voice ties the varied contents together.

Some sketches laugh at modern manners, others pause over loss or kindness, and all show his gift for finding meaning in ordinary scenes. The collection is best read a piece at a time, like a stroll through a familiar town. It offers a charming sample of Jerome beyond his famous comic novels.
22372-a-labrador-doctor-the-autobiograph:
A Labrador Doctor is the autobiography of Wilfred Thomason Grenfell, published in 1919. Grenfell served as a medical missionary in Labrador. He admits he long resisted pressure from friends to write his life.

Living alongside his own autobiography felt risky to him. It calls, he says, for confessions from its author. In God's eyes, the only alternative is a book of lies. That blunt honesty frames everything that follows in the memoir. Readers get a doctor's years among fishing folk in a harsh north. The book made Labrador's needs known to a wide world of readers.
22728-the-foundations-of-the-origin-of-s:
Charles Darwin wrote the two essays gathered here in 1842 and 1844, the first drafts of his theory of evolution. The catalog record gives no year for this edition. Long before On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859, Darwin sketched his ideas in private, testing them against the evidence of breeding and geology.

The contents of the 1844 essay show the theory already formed. Variation, its causes, and its hereditary tendency come first. Then come selection, the crossing of breeds, and the descent of domestic races from wild stocks. Darwin weighs the limits of variation and sums up what domestication proves. His son Francis later published these foundations so readers could watch the great argument grow. Few books let us see a world-changing idea at the drafting stage so plainly.
22888-under-the-window-pictures-rhymes-f:
Kate Greenaway fills Under the Window with pictures and rhymes for children. One verse sends three tabbies out with their cats to tea. Each cat takes a favorite seat, calls politely for milk, and settles down purring. A riddle closes the verse, asking young readers to count up the cats' lives.

Greenaway's children wear the quaint dress that made her books famous across England and America. Short poems, games, and everyday scenes fill the pages, all carried by her drawings. The book first charmed Victorian nurseries and never really left them. Modern readers meet it as a landmark of children's publishing, gentle in tone and exact in dress, manners, and small pleasures.
22896-little-stories-for-little-children:
Plain lessons wear story dress in Little Stories for Little Children. One day a poor girl came to Ann, asking for bread, since she had eaten none all day. Ann had no bread to give. Instead she handed over the sixpence her mother had given her, telling the girl to buy bread with it.

Short tales like Ann's fill the little book, each built to teach kindness, honesty, or obedience without a long sermon. The language stays simple enough for new readers sounding out words. Such books were the first rung of the reading ladder in their day. They still show how early children's publishing worked, a story, a virtue, and a page a small reader could finish alone.
22922-the-posy-ring-a-book-of-verse-for-:
Editors Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Archibald Smith gather children's verse in The Posy Ring, published in 1903. Its acknowledgments thank publishers for reprint rights, naming poems like Baby Corn, Susan Hartley Swett's The Blue Jay, and John B. Tabb's Fern Song, A Bunch of Roses, and The Child at Bethlehem.

A posy ring was a ring carrying a verse inside the band, and the editors chose the name for a circle of poems. The anthology mixes nursery rhymes, nature verse, and short lyrics meant for reading aloud at home and school. Many selections became standards of the American classroom. The book preserves the taste of its moment, when a good anthology was a family's poetry shelf in one volume.
23189-the-lily-of-leyden:
The Lily of Leyden is a work of historical fiction set in the Dutch town of Leyden. High above the town rises an ancient tower, commonly linked by local belief to Hengist and to the Saxon crossing from Holland into Britain. Few spots nearby stand anywhere near as high.

Mynheer Van der Werf and a young woman named Jaqueline climb the mound to that tower. They mount a flight of winding steps to the battlements at the top. From there the whole district opens below them. Readers get Dutch history, old legend, and a wide view joined in one scene.
23347-mental-efficiency-and-other-hints-:
Arnold Bennett put together this set of short advice essays for men and women who want to use their minds and their days better. Issued in nineteen eleven, the book sits beside his well known guide to living on a full day, and it keeps the same plain, direct tone.

Bennett writes on the mind as a tool, on taste in books, on work habits, and on how small daily choices shape a life. Two short plays and lighter pieces sit beside the essays, so counsel and fun share the same covers. Readers get usable hints, not grand theory: how to pay heed, how to read well, and how to make spare hours count.
23594-a-picture-book-for-little-children:
Kimber and Conrad of Philadelphia printed this early picture book for little children. It opens with letters: small Roman, italic, Roman capitals, italic capitals, and double letters, each set out for a beginner to learn. Merritt printed the book, whose plain type and clear forms suit a child first meeting print.

Pictures follow, each with a short caption. They show a walk in the garden, strawberries on little vines, an old woman in trouble, a glass that shows no self, and a child told to obey its mother. The Swedes church, a farmer's fruit not to be robbed, and a tree bare for now complete the captions. The book teaches letters, manners, and looking, all in one small volume. Collectors and parents will enjoy its old fashioned charm, a primer where pictures and morals share each page.
23671-the-strange-little-girl-a-story-fo:
V. M. wrote this children's story for the Aryan Theosophical Press at Point Loma, California, where it appeared in 1911 under Katherine Tingley's copyright. Its heroine is Princess Eline, who lives with the king's children in a beautiful palace where they want for nothing and never dream that others might be less happy.

Yet stories of a world beyond the palace garden stay with Eline, and she gazes toward the purple forests and golden-edged clouds, wondering what lies there. The tale follows her curiosity outward, into a wider world very different from palace life, and it reads as a gentle fable about sympathy and the wish to know how others live.
23941-country-walks-of-a-naturalist-with:
The Reverend W. Houghton, rector of Preston on the Wild Moors in Shropshire, published Country Walks of a Naturalist with His Children in a second edition in 1870. His preface states his aim: less to hand young people facts than to get them learning for themselves, by making good use of their eyes.

Country walks, Houghton argues, are full of interest and instruction for all who look. His book is illustrated with eight colored plates and numerous wood engravings, including copies of Gould's drawings of British birds and drawings of sticklebacks. Words that puzzle young brains are kept few, for readers of nine or ten, with a little help from parents or teachers.
24258-the-ruba-iya-t-of-a-persian-kitten:
Oliver Herford wrote this illustrated verse parody, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1906, with copyright in 1904. It takes the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam and retells it through a kitten, in quatrains that keep the old pattern while turning every image feline. The Golden Cat puts the Mouse of Darkness to flight with a paw of light, which means, in plain speech, the dawn is bright.

Later verses chase the early bird and the early worm, and watch the mouse make merry among larder shelves. They puzzle over an inverted bowl of sky-blue delf on the pantry shelf, and toss a ball that always returns. Readers get a witty, gentle spoof of a famous poem, told by a kitten for cat lovers.
24271-children-s-rhymes-children-s-games:
Robert Ford, author of Thistledown and editor of Ballads of Bairnhood, gathered this collection of Scottish children's lore, published at Paisley in 1904 in a second edition. It brings together children's rhymes, games, songs, and stories, much of it from Ford's own memory and much gathered with patient industry from wide and varied sources. Ford calls it the first sincere effort to collect in ample fashion the natural literature of Scotland's children.

Early pages comment, with texts, on the nursery rhymes, puerile yet regularly fascinating, whose vitality has puzzled ages. Auld rhymes and auld chimes, runs the proverb, make us think on auld times. Readers get a treasury of Scots childhood, rhymes, games, and tales, for bairns and big folk alike.
24304-american-lutheranism-volume-2-the-:
F. Bente wrote this church history, published by Concordia Publishing House in St. Louis in 1919. It is volume two of American Lutheranism, treating the United Lutheran Church, formed from the General Synod, the General Council, and the United Synod in the South. Bente planned four volumes, with volume one on early Lutheranism in America, though the planned third and fourth volumes never appeared in print.

The volume's chief object is to record the facts of the theological attitude of the various Lutheran bodies in America, with only such comment as seemed necessary. Quotations from the Lutheran Observer and other English periodicals often come through retranslations from German papers. Readers get a careful, documentary history of American Lutheran union.
24361-teddy-her-book-a-story-of-sweet-si:
Anna Chapin Ray wrote this story of sweet sixteen, published by Little, Brown, and Company in Boston in 1901, copyrighted in 1898, with pictures by Vesper L. George. Its verse epigraph praises spring's hands, full of rosy flowers and unopened buds, and life's hands, full of buds, coming on singing with radiant eyes across youth's golden gate. Pictures show Theodora's face, rosy with blushes, and Theodora flying across the road.

The story opens with the five McAlisters gathered in the dining-room on a rainy night in late August. Servants are few, given the size of the household circle and its income, so division of labor rules the house. Old Susan clears the table, brings the lamp, and retires to the kitchen, leaving the young people alone. Hope darns stockings, Hubert sits near with little Allyn on his knee. Readers get a girl's sixteenth year, at home.
24373-mornings-in-the-college-chapel-sho:
Francis Greenwood Peabody, Plummer Professor of Christian Morals at Harvard University, wrote these short addresses to young men on personal religion. They were published by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in Boston and New York in 1896. They are dedicated to his beloved colleagues, the preachers to the university. They honor the sacred memory of Phillips Brooks, of the first staff of preachers.

In Harvard's morning prayers, a service of only fifteen minutes, the preacher says a few plain words to explain or press home the Bible lesson read. An address of two or three minutes can offer just one wholesome thought for a young man's day. Peabody recalls that religion at Harvard ceased to be college discipline and became a natural, rational opportunity for youth. Readers get brief chapel talks, plain, earnest, and meant for mornings.
2441-the-burgess-animal-book-for-childre:
Thornton W. Burgess's Burgess Animal Book for Children introduces young readers to the wild creatures of the Green Meadow and the Smiling Pool. Through the stories of Peter Rabbit and his friends, Burgess teaches how animals live, what they eat, and how they survive the seasons. The book mixes gentle tales with real natural history.

Burgess wrote for children who knew the woods, and his animals behave like their real counterparts. The volume charmed generations and still serves as a first nature book. Young naturalists will enjoy its warmth and facts.
24485-a-floral-fantasy-in-an-old-english:
Walter Crane set forth this short book in verses and coloured designs, published by Harper and Brothers in 1899. In an old English garden, flowers take human names and disport themselves as squires and dames. The dreamer follows them past formal knots, clipped thickets, and smooth greensward.

Rosamond's Bower, with its peacock hedges of yew, hides its flower unless the visitor holds the key of the wicket. As Time whets his scythe, the four seasons pass in pageant. Crane's verses and designs work together as a decorative fancy, charming readers who love gardens, old English craft, and the art of the book itself.
24496-making-a-rock-garden:
Published as one of the House and Garden Making Books, this short handbook shows the home-maker how to build a rock garden. It belongs to a series of little illustrated volumes that aimed to make country and suburban home features plain to amateurs. Sister volumes covered rose gardens, lawns, tennis courts, fireplaces, paths, and poultry houses.

Text, pictures, and diagrams explain how to choose a site, place stones, prepare soil, and plant for year-round effect. The book is practical rather than grand, written for readers with a modest garden and a wish to try. Gardeners today will enjoy it as a clear, old-fashioned guide, and as a picture of how Americans gardened a century ago.
24519-the-story-of-rouen:
Theodore Andrea Cook wrote this history of Rouen, published in London in 1899 with pictures by Helen M. James and Jane E. Cook. Rouen, the old capital of Normandy on the Seine, holds a cathedral, abbey churches, and streets steeped in the story of Joan of Arc, who was tried and burned there.

Cook traces the city from its Roman and Norman roots through sieges, trade, and revolution, pausing at its buildings and its famous dead. The book belongs to a series of city stories for general readers. It gives a readable, well-illustrated introduction to one of France's most historic towns.
24524-the-young-maiden:
A. B. Muzzey wrote this conduct book for young women, first entered for copyright in 1840 and reprinted at Boston in 1848 in a tenth edition. Its chapters treat the capacities of woman, female influence, female education, home, society, love, single life, and marriage.

Muzzey, author of The Young Man's Friend, argues that a young woman's influence shapes families and the nation, and he advises her on study, company, and courtship. His counsels are earnest, religious, and very much of their age. The book remains a revealing record of what respectable America expected of its daughters in the 1840s.
2465-carmen:
Prosper Merimee's Carmen introduces the gypsy heroine whose love and freedom destroy the soldier Don Jose. The novella follows Jose from honest dragoon to smuggler and murderer, drawn by Carmen's beauty, wit, and refusal to be owned. Merimee's cool, detached narration makes the tragedy feel inevitable.

The story inspired Bizet's opera, which made Carmen immortal, but the original is darker and stranger. Its Spanish setting and its heroine's independence still fascinate. Readers will find a short, powerful classic. Merimee based his gypsy heroine partly on stories he heard in Spain.
24739-bidwell-s-travels-from-wall-street:
George Bidwell wrote this autobiography of his travels from Wall Street to London prison, fifteen years in solitude. Tried at the Old Bailey, he was sentenced for life for the million-pound forgery on the Bank of England. Freed a human wreck, he rose again to a national reputation as writer, speaker, and authority on social problems.

Bidwell claims his life's events surpass the imaginations of famous novelists, with thrilling scenes, hair-breadth escapes, and marvellous adventures. His story is not a record of crime, he insists, but proof of what the world of wrongdoing teaches. Readers get a sensational Victorian confession, dramatic and self-justifying.
24812-the-three-midshipmen:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote The Three Midshipmen about three boys, one English, one Scottish, and one Irish, who meet at a boarding school near London. Bullies and schoolboy trials teach them to stick together, and they carry that bond into the Navy. The tale follows them on to become lieutenants, commanders, and admirals.

Their postings cross in the Levant, Africa, and China, and they meet again under fire, often when boats' crews are mowed down around them. Kingston tells it straight for schoolboys, with pluck and loyalty to the fore. The book, long a library favorite, gives a rousing, old-style naval adventure for young readers.
24866-a-lieutenant-at-eighteen:
Oliver Optic published A Lieutenant at Eighteen in Boston in 1895, in his Blue and Gray on Land series. Dexter Lyon, called Deck, wins his bars at eighteen, raised from the ranks after every man in his company and nearly every officer asked for it, his own father alone excepted.

Deck serves under Captain Ripley and his father's squadron, and one picture shows Sergeant Fronklyn dragging the young lieutenant from a melee. Optic mixes camp talk, marches, and battles with a hero's rise through merit. Young readers get a brisk Civil War tale where courage, not birth, earns the shoulder straps.
24912-finger-plays-for-nursery-and-kinde:
Emilie Poulsson wrote Finger Plays for Nursery and Kindergarten, published in Boston in 1893, with music by Cornelia C. Roeske and pictures by L. J. Bridgman. The book follows Froebel's rule: what the child imitates, he begins to understand, whether birds in flight, fishes in water, or the work of farmer, miller, and baker.

Plays include Pat-a-cake, Here is the Church with its steeple, the squirrel in the hollow tree, and five little mice feasting on a pie while the wise old cat watches. Notes describe each hand shape in brackets, since the gestures matter as much as the words. The book remains a classic tool for nursery teachers and parents.
24948-finnish-legends-for-english-childr:
R. Eivind retells Finnish legends for English children in this 1893 volume from T. Fisher Unwin's Children's Library. Wainamoinen, the ancient singer and hero, stands at the center of the tales, and Aino's sad fate gives the collection its tenderest episode. The stories move between music, magic, and the hard bargains of the old northern world.

Lemminkainen's mother provides the most memorable quest, sending a bee to fetch the magic honey-balm from the seventh heaven to heal her son. The retelling keeps the wonder of the original songs while shaping them for young readers, who meet a Finland of singers, sorcerers, and grieving mothers. It serves as a gentle doorway into Finland's old song tradition.
25542-black-oxen:
Gertrude Atherton's 1923 novel Black Oxen takes its epigraph from Yeats. The epigraph pictures years as oxen driven on by God the herdsman. Time and its tread on human lives supply the novel's governing image.

The story opens with a failed playwright turned critic, weary of bad first nights. It moves to Clavering, Madame Zattiany, and Judge Trent. Trent guards a secret about the charming Madame Zattiany. At a mountain lodge, Clavering pleads with her to marry him, as her return to Europe looms. Pictures from the screen version front the book.
25555-fairy-tales-of-the-slav-peasants-a:
Emily J. Harding translates twenty fairy tales of Slav peasants and herdsmen from the French of Alexander Chodsko, with her own illustrations, in this 1896 London volume. Very few of the tales had appeared in English before, a point the publisher stresses.

The Plentiful Tablecloth supplies one front picture, and kinship with Eastern tales runs through the collection. Herdsmen, peasants, magic helpers, and household wonders fill stories meant first for young folk, with added interest for older readers tracing tale types across borders. The publisher notes the translation was carefully revised, with as little interference as possible.
25621-merry-words-for-merry-children:
A. Hoatson writes merry words for merry children in this picture book, published by W. Hagelberg in London and New York and printed in Berlin. Short verses face pictures throughout, in the bright style of Victorian children's gift books.

Jim's Dream opens the fun, with a boy fond of clowns who talks so much of them that one night he dreams he is one. He serves boiled slate pencils and rice to five fat geese, has two of them dance to his fiddle, and hears them call the meal wholesome rather than nice. Playful nonsense carries each verse.
25650-all-about-the-little-small-red-hen:
John B. Gruelle pictures this telling of the little small red hen, published in New York by Cupples and Leon as part of the All About series, priced at thirty-five cents a volume. The book dedicates itself to the nicest child in the whole world.

Companion volumes picture Peter Rabbit, the three bears, the three little pigs, Mother Goose, Cinderella, and Little Red Riding Hood, with Gruelle or Hartley and Kirby-Parrish as artists. The red hen tale itself teaches industry and sharing through a hen who plants, harvests, and bakes while her neighbours refuse to help.
25654-stories-of-king-arthur-s-knights-t:
Mary MacGregor retells stories of King Arthur's knights for children in this volume of the Told to the Children series, edited by Louey Chisholm, with pictures by Katharine Cameron. Jack in London and Dutton in New York published it, dedicated to Marie Winifred.

More than four hundred years ago, Sir Thomas Malory wrote many Welsh tales of Arthur's knights in English words. All stories here come from Malory's big book, except Geraint and Enid, itself an old Welsh tale of brave knights and fair ladies. Beside her stood her beautiful daughter fronts one tale.
25824-the-tale-of-rusty-wren:
Arthur Scott Bailey tells short tales of small wild folk for bedtime reading, with Rusty Wren at the heart of this volume. Rusty and his wife keep house in a snug nest, and much of the fun lies in their clashes with bigger, louder birds. Jasper Jay drums on their roof and screams abuse until the farm boy Johnnie Green hears the row and drives the bully off with a flung potato.

The book belongs to the Tuck-Me-In Tales, and its cast runs far past one wren, from Solomon Owl and Jolly Robin to Daddy Longlegs, Kiddie Katydid, and Betsy Butterfly. Each tale is brief, plain, and kind, with the small creatures outwitting bluster by sense and pluck. Pictures mark the best moments, such as the ant soldiers rushing Daddy Longlegs.
25933-english-as-she-is-wrote-showing-cu:
Printed by D. Appleton and Company in 1883, this companion to English as She is Spoke collects curious ways English gets written badly or oddly. Chapters show how she is wrote by the inaccurate, by advertisers and sign boards, for epitaphs, by correspondents, by the effusive, and by the untutored. A prefatory tale tells of a lawyer who won a verdict by claiming a man may spell a word two or three ways if he likes.

The humor lies in real specimens, from grand definitions to homely blunders. One scientific writer defines a sneeze through nasal membranes, the trifacial nerve, the Gasserian ganglion, and a chain of reflex acts ending in the expiratory muscles. The book invites readers to laugh at tangled prose, and to mind their own spelling, sense, and stops.
25950-the-complete-bachelor-manners-for-:
Written by the author of the As Seen by Him papers and printed by Appleton in 1896, this guide fills a gap the author found in etiquette books: the bachelor. For years, while running the query department of Vogue, he fielded letters from across America asking small points of manners from a New York standpoint. Chapters cover the bachelor in public, his dress, his toilet, care of clothes, calls, table manners, hosting, servants, sport, and travel.

Advice runs practical: greet your hostess at a dance, even briefly, shake no hands in the crush, and note that dance cards, common elsewhere, have faded in New York. At the Patriarchs' ball, chaperons sit together on a raised dais while their charges roam the rooms. The book is a crisp, amused manual for a young man about town.
25974-god-s-plan-with-men:
T. T. Martin, evangelist, sets out God's plan with men in this 1912 book from Revell. A verse preface prays that every line not inlaid with the Lord be blotted out, and that one worthy line be the glory of his work. Chapters move from sin and its punishment, with degrees in hell, through sins not excused, Christ as sin bearer, the new relation, and the sins of God's children. Rewards, degrees in heaven, and how to be saved follow.

Martin argues from Scripture throughout, quoting Romans that all have sinned and come short of God's glory, and Hebrews that apart from shedding of blood there is no remission. A man who keeps the law, he says, needs no Christ, but no man has kept it whole. The book is a plain evangelistic statement of justice, love, and faith.
25989-a-beautiful-alien:
Julia Magruder sets a romance of art, law, and a stranger's past in A Beautiful Alien, printed by Badger in 1901. It opens on a homeward steamer from Europe, where a man and a girl pace the deck for an hour under the eyes of fellow passengers. Behind them walks Albert Noel, artist by instinct and lawyer by trade, who paints for love and pleads for money, convention, or family wishes.

Noel finds Christine, the beautiful alien of the title, caught between a bright world of music and painting and a present life that cuts her off from it. Talk of foreign lands feels like recalling dreams, till Dallas enters in slovenly dress with a horrible pipe and Christine snaps back to reality. Later sittings in the studio pass in near silence. Magruder writes of beauty, duty, and a hidden past.
26010-valley-of-the-croen:
Lee Tarbell tells a pulp tale of a golden statue, flying disks, and sudden death in Valley of the Croen, from Amazing Stories, April 1949. A cross eyed stranger with a livid scar from cheekbone to jaw seeks Keele, a mining man, with a secret he would tell few. A tiny golden statue leaps like a lodestone toward its huge counterpart, pointing one way and leading to death in a valley where disks land.

Keele is later bound in a strong net of metal mesh, unable to move a muscle, while a metal disk swings before his nose and hides his companion's fate. A tall queen enters, eyes intent, and a light flashes in the disk, faster and faster, sending a beam of energy through his head. Tarbell writes of pulp wonders with pace and chill.
26181-stories-of-siegfried-told-to-the-c:
Mary MacGregor's volume, in the Told to the Children series edited by Louey Chisholm, retells the German hero tale for young readers. Its preface tells a boy named Denis that the story comes from the old poem called the Nibelungenlied. Pictures by Granville Fell show scenes such as Mimer the blacksmith spotting a bear.

Chapters follow Siegfried from Mimer's forge to the winning of a treasure, his journey to Worms, and his meeting with Kriemhild. Later tales cover his voyage to Isenland, his taming of Brunhild, a wedding feast, and his slaying at Worms. The book keeps the adventure clear and swift, while holding back the darkest turns for older readers.
26603-the-later-cave-men:
Katharine Elizabeth Dopp, lecturer in education at the University of Chicago, published this school book with Rand McNally in 1906. It is Book Three of her Industrial and Social History Series, subtitled The Age of the Chase, and it follows The Tree-Dwellers and The Early Cave-Men. Howard V. Brown drew its full-page and text pictures for primary grades.

The story follows cave children such as Fleetfoot and Chipper through cold days, frozen rivers, and reindeer hunts, showing how early people lived by the chase. Dopp wrote the series to give children practical activity in school, learning by doing what early workers did. Awe at work, hunger, and the hunt give young readers a plain picture of Stone Age life.
26735-stories-and-legends-of-travel-and-:
Grace Greenwood published these stories and legends of travel and history for children with John B. Alden at New York in 1885, entered in 1857 by Leander K. Lippincott. Greenwood dedicates the volume to Mary and Alice Seelye, in memory of a pleasant summer at the Water Cure at Cleveland, and dates her dedication Christmas 1857.

Sketches pair places with child heroes: London parks and gardens with Mabel Howard and her pet, St. Paul's Cathedral with Sir Philip Sidney, and Greenwich Hospital with little Robert and his noble friend. Hampton Court, Windsor Castle, and King James of Scotland follow, then Ireland: Grace O'Malley at Dublin and Howth, little Norah and the Blarney Stone, Kathleen of Killarney, and the Giant's Causeway. Greenwood opens by praising London's open parks against America's stunted public squares.
26796-no-sect-in-heaven:
A short poem published by H. Longstreth of Philadelphia in 1861, framed as a troubled dream. After an evening spent talking of sects, the dreamer stands beside a dark river and watches believers cross toward heaven, each carrying the badge of his own church. A Churchman clutches his gilt-edged Book of Common Prayer and his silk gown. A Quaker buttons his gray coat to the chin and pulls his broad-brimmed hat tight. Dr. Watts bears a bundle of psalms and hymns.

Every crossing ends the same way: gown, coat, hat, hymns, and Wesley's manuscripts all slip away into the flood, and the saints pass through alone. Even two saints who part over sprinkling against plunging, and a whole Presbyterian church divided over the old way and the new, enter together at last. In heaven, the poem insists, nobody asks about sect at all.
26883-the-sword-and-the-atopen:
Taylor H. Greenfield wrote this future-war tale. An eastern invading force, armed with the secret of gravitation, lifts metal transports off the sea and crosses the Pacific in five days. Held in check from summer to winter, the invaders reach the Mississippi, stayed only by the river and the severest winter in many generations. The narrator credits Dr. Rutledge's discovery and stratagem with freeing the country from the menace.

One surprise the invaders had not counted on was Dr. Mernick's transformer, which steps sunlight through grates into electricity and gives the defenders a sudden, limitless source of power. The narrator watches from General Sanford's observing helicopter, fifteen thousand feet up behind transparent clersite walls and an electric field screen, as a new weapon debuts on the Nebraska prairies. Physicists labor beside him to turn the enemy's invention into a boomerang.
26965-heroes-and-hunters-of-the-west-com:
Published at Philadelphia in 1860, this collection sketches the heroes and hunters of the American West, from Daniel Boone and Simon Kenton to George Rogers Clarke, Benjamin Logan, and Lewis Whetzel. Each chapter tells one life or one fight in short, plain prose.

Alongside the famous names sit sieges, escapes, and Indian fights, including the siege of Fort Henry, the murder of Cornstalk, and the massacre of Chicago. The book reads as a mid-1800s hall of frontier fame, praising courage and woodcraft while showing the violence of the border wars without softening it.
27001-jewish-children:
Jewish Children gathers stories by Shalom Aleichem, translated from the Yiddish by Hannah Berman and published by Knopf in 1922. The pieces recall a village childhood through festivals and small events: Passover in a village, Elijah the Prophet, greens for Shevuous, and the Tabernacle.

A child narrator named Busie, short for Esther-Liba, watches neighbors, teachers, and beadles, and learns pity for the living when boys kill small birds for sport. The stories mix humor and tenderness, giving English readers a window onto East European Jewish life before its world vanished.
27083-the-subjection-of-women:
John Stuart Mill's The Subjection of Women, published in London in 1869, states its object at once. He seeks to explain his long-held opinion that the law's ranking of one sex below the other is wrong in itself. Mill calls it a great hindrance to human improvement.

He argues it should give way to full equality, with no power or privilege on one side and no disability on the other. Mill admits the difficulty lies less in reason than in feeling, since opinions rooted in feeling gain stability from argument against them.
27176-more-beasts-for-worse-children:
H. Belloc's More Beasts for Worse Children, with pictures by B. T. B., published by Duckworth, follows his Bad Child's Book of Beasts for readers who deserve worse. The Python opens the book: it wants a doctor for its eyes and suffers the measles yearly.

An aunt in Yucatan kept a python for a pet, and the verses warn against music near its cage and advise severe chastisement in a rage. Later a missionary breakfasting by the Nile finds his egg contains something green, hungry, and horrible, in Belloc's cheerful, cautionary nonsense.
27336-three-women:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox, author of Poems of Passion and Maurine, published Three Women with W. B. Conkey in Chicago and New York in 1897. The book is a verse narrative that stages life itself as a theatre piece. A dull little station, a dreaming man, a bevy of girls passing by, a swift train, and a hot summer sun raise the curtain.

Wilcox calls the action a drama of passion, of sorrow, and of strife, and the linked lyrics and scenes follow love in its young, hopeful, and losing moods. Her direct, musical verse made her one of the most popular poets of her day. Readers get a compact, emotional story told almost entirely in song-like lines.
27424-cautionary-tales-for-children:
Hilaire Belloc wrote the verses of these Cautionary Tales for Children, with pictures by B. T. B., designed for the admonition of children between eight and fourteen years. First published by Eveleigh Nash in 1907, the tales warn, in cheerful and gruesome rhyme, against the small disobediences that lead to dreadful fates.

Jim is the dreadful example sampled here: told never to leave his nurse in a crowd, he slips his hand and runs away at the zoo. There a lion named Ponto springs with open jaws and eats him, beginning at his feet. The keeper, though very fat, almost runs to help. Belloc's mock-serious morals have delighted children and adults for generations.
27471-the-wall-between:
Sara Ware Bassett, author of The Taming of Zenas Henry and The Harbor Road, published this novel with Little, Brown in Boston in August 1920, with a frontispiece by Norman Price. Its motto, from Edward Rowland Sill, calls lives the miracles men call lives, and the story opens where the Howe and Webster farms adjoin on sun-flooded land.

Chapters titled A Modern Richelieu, The Episode of the Eggs, and A Clash of Wills trace a tangle between neighboring families. The Unraveling of the Mystery and Ellen's Vengeance follow, with Lucy, Ellen, Jane, and Melviny at its center. Blossoms of Martin's raising figure in the frontispiece. Bassett writes a warm New England tale of pride, love, and fences mended.
27595-eight-keys-to-eden:
Mark Clifton published this science-fiction novel with Doubleday in Garden City, New York, in 1960, in a first edition. Clifton's other novels listed in the volume include They'd Rather Be Right, written with Frank Riley, and The Forever Machine.

His shorter work ranges from novelettes such as Remembrance and Reflection and What Thin Partitions to stories such as The Conqueror Kenzie Report and Reward for Valour. A note states that all characters in the book are fictitious. Eight Keys to Eden stands as a late-1950s science-fiction novel from a working writer of the field.
2762-the-brethren:
H. Rider Haggard sets this crusading romance by the waters of Death Creek, where Sir Andrew D'Arcy and his brethren take their knightly vows. A letter of Saladin, a wine merchant, and a Christmas feast at Steeple carry the tale toward the Holy Land.

The banner of Saladin, the widow Masouda, and horses named Flame and others fill a story of chivalry, love, and war. Haggard writes with his usual vigor, and the Third Crusade gives him a grand stage. The novel offers a rousing tale of brotherhood sworn before God and tested by battle.
27622-the-story-of-my-first-novel-how-a-:
Mrs. Hungerford, Margaret Wolfe Hamilton, told the story of her first novel in The Ladies' Home Journal of Philadelphia in July 1890. She calls her first story the raven she sent out of her ark and never saw again.

Unlike the proverbial curse, it never came home to roost; it stayed where she had sent it. The only word she ever heard of it was a polite letter from an editor, offering it back for twopence halfpenny in stamps, or else consigning it to the waste-paper basket. She was only sixteen, and never sent the money, so her manuscript likely lit the heartless editor's fire. She has hated the words waste-paper ever since.
27684-anthony-lyveden:
Dornford Yates published Anthony Lyveden in 1921, opening with Major Anthony Lyveden, a decorated ex-officer down on his luck in London, who has just pawned his wristwatch for twenty-two shillings. A small white Sealyham dog attaches itself to him as he waits on a hot June day.

The novel follows Lyveden through a series of encounters that test his honor, humor, and resourcefulness in civilian life after the war. Yates mixes light comedy with adventure, and the book's many reprintings show how popular its hero became. Later chapters carry titles such as The Voice of the Turtle and The Golden Bowl.
27735-in-the-great-steep-s-garden:
Elizabeth Madox Roberts wrote these poems, with pictures by Kenneth Hartley, under the title In the Great Steep's Garden. The verses move among hill people, mountain winds, and Colorado wildflowers such as the columbine.

Roberts peoples the hills with pixies, gnomes, and the Maid of the Corn, and lets hill winds lay snatches of song on the poet's lips. Short, musical, and fanciful, the collection blends Kentucky mountain feeling with a playful mythology of the high country. One poem asks whether a Pikes Peak pixie, a Cheyenne shee, or a gnome in a stone whispered its rhyme.
27921-the-love-of-frank-nineteen:
David C. Knight wrote The Love of Frank Nineteen, a science-fiction love story about the far-off day after tomorrow, introduced by an editor who praises the range of science fiction subjects. The narrator and his wife Min run a spotel, a space motel, out in the spacelanes.

Their place, the Io, handles rockets up to the new Marvin 990s, offers television and Terran gravity in every cabin, and serves Min's Earth cooking to spacemen tired of synthetic food. A robot's leg found during spring cleaning sets the story moving, and the tale mixes humor, romance, and space commerce.
28235-in-orchard-glen:
Marian Keith wrote In Orchard Glen, copyright 1918, as a Canadian novel of a farm girl and the First World War. Christina Lindsay, nineteen on the day the story opens, has already learned hard truths about herself, first at eleven while picking raspberries with her brother Sandy. Apple-blossom days, berry patches, and neighbours fill the early chapters.

War drums, calls to the colours, and a plighted ring then test Christina and her village, from Craig-Ellachie to the hills above Orchard Glen. Keith follows love, loss, and return with warmth. The novel offers a gentle, home-front view of Canada at war.
28271-seven-miles-to-arden:
Ruth Sawyer wrote Seven Miles to Arden in 1916 as a children's novel of a road, a spring, and a lad waiting for Rosalind. Sawyer, author of The Primrose Ring, opens with a song to himself. It tells of a road at daybreak, thrushes by a holy spring, and a climb to purpling heather, where a roadside fire waits at night. Harper and Brothers published the book.

Chapters follow the way of it, twin oaks rustling in the wind, and a journey of seven miles to Arden, Shakespeare's forest of love and exile. Sawyer writes with lyrical warmth for young readers. The book offers a gentle, musical tale of friendship and first love.
28338-the-education-of-children:
The Education of Children, printed from a 1550 text, pairs Richard Sherry's treatise of schemes and tropes with Erasmus's declamation that children should be brought up gently in learning from infancy. Sherry, a Londoner, gathered his figures from the best grammarians and orators, for better understanding of good authors. Erasmus, in Latin first, argues for virtue and learning together.

The e-text, from scans at the Bibliotheque nationale de France, unpacks old letters and notes differences between two copies. Pilcrows mark paragraphs added by the transcriber. The volume offers a direct look at Tudor ideas on teaching children well and kindly.
28665-sea-garden:
H. D., the poet Hilda Doolittle, published this collection of short poems in London in 1916. Sea Garden gathers her early Imagist verse, much of it first printed in Poetry, The Egoist, and The Little Review. The poems are brief and sharp, built from single images: a harsh sea rose, a sheltered garden, a cliff temple, and gods of the shore.

Classical figures appear often, but the book's force comes from its close looking at wind, sand, salt, and light. H. D. strips each poem to a few hard lines, letting the image carry the feeling instead of explaining it. Sea Garden stands as a key early statement of Imagism, and it still rewards readers who like poetry that is spare, exact, and tied to the natural world.
28933-one-out-of-ten:
J. Anthony Ferlaine wrote this short science fiction story about a television quiz show and a strange contestant. The narrator, quiz master Smiling Jim Parsons, introduces Parlor Quiz to the camera while the announcer Don Phillips watches. The first contestant is a middle-aged woman in a faded print dress and old-style shoes, screened by staff before the show.

The magazine's introduction jokes that quiz prizes now rival a raid on Fort Knox, and asks readers to hear out this astounding science fantasy documentary first. The story plays on the quiz craze of its day, with a contestant whose eyes look strange and whose origins may not be earthly. Readers get a short, sly tale of television, fame, and visitors who play the game too well.
28960-the-backwoodsmen:
Charles G. D. Roberts wrote this 1909 book of backwoods stories, The Backwoodsmen, published by Macmillan in New York. The chapters bring the vagrants of the barren, MacPhairrson's happy family, and life on Big Lonely, then move from buck to bear and back, into the deep of the snow. Later tales follow the gentling of Red McWha, Melindy and the lynxes, Mrs. Gammit's pig, and the blackwater pot.

Roberts, author of The Kindred of the Wild, writes of lumbermen, trappers, and wild beasts with a naturalist's eye and a storyteller's pace. A frontispiece shows Red McWha's big form shooting past. Readers get a strong collection of Canadian wilderness tales, where men and animals meet in cold, danger, and rough humor.
28972-the-works-of-louis-becke-a-linked-:
David Widger edited this linked index to the works of Louis Becke, who lived from 1855 to 1913. The index lists Yorke the Adventurer, John Corwell, Sailor, Poisonous Fish of the Pacific Islands, and the Colonial Mortuary Bard, with Reo the Fisherman, Old Mary, and Martin of Nitendi. Later entries bring the Call of the South, the Ebbing of the Tide, and tales of the South Seas.

Becke, an Australian trader and writer, knew the Pacific islands from working life, and his stories carry that knowledge into fiction. The index gives every volume and chapter, from Tom Gerrard and the River of Dreams to Bully Hayes and the gallant Jack Renton. Readers get a guide to a once-popular storyteller of the South Seas, whose sea tales mixed adventure with island custom.
29018-critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote this third volume of Critical Miscellanies, with essay nine on The Expansion of England, published by Macmillan in 1904. The essay's contents run from politics and history and the eighteenth century through Mr. Green and his History of the English People to the secession of the American colonies. Later sections treat the mechanical and industrial development of England, the moral of Seeley's book, and organization in time of war.

Further sections cover Sir Henry Parkes on Australia, proposals for an imperial customs union, fair trade against free trade, and colonial representation in Parliament. Morley opens against two perversions: politics sunk to party struggle, and history aimed only at literary display. Readers get a Victorian statesman's review of empire, thoughtful and liberal in temper.
29155-blake-s-burden:
Harold Bindloss published this novel in London in 1917 with Ward, Lock and Company. The transcriber's note warns that the book's plot closely follows Bindloss's The Intriguers, though the text, paragraphing, and chapter structure differ widely. This version runs to thirty-two chapters against the other's twenty-four.

Chapters open with the Blake affair, Millicent renewing an acquaintance, and the cousins, then move to the prairie, the muskeg, and a cure. Harding grows confidential, then suspicious, and Mrs. Chudleigh gathers information and finds a clue. Readers get a Bindloss intrigue novel of the Canadian west, with secrets, suspicion, and a burden carried across wild country.
29415-soldiers-of-the-queen:
Harold Avery's 1898 boys' book, printed by Thomas Nelson and Sons in London, Edinburgh, and New York, follows Valentine and his sisters through school, pranks, and at last real soldiering. Chapters run from tin soldiers and an ugly duckling to the court of Queen Mab, an unlucky picnic, a robbery at Brenlands, and the sound of the drum. The Queen's shilling, active service, under fire, and battle close the tale.

Avery writes for boys who thrilled to the empire's drums: school loyalty first, then courage under fire. The book's values are frankly of its age, with pluck prized above all. Young readers and students of Victorian boys' fiction will find a brisk, period-perfect adventure from classroom scrapes to the battlefield.
2950-the-midnight-queen:
May Agnes Fleming wrote The Midnight Queen as a sensational romance of sorcery, courts, and hidden identity. Chapters promise a sorceress, a dead bride, a court page, a stranger, a dwarf and a ruin, a masked ball, and the earl's barge, before the midnight queen herself takes the stage. Leoline, an execution, a dungeon, and a plague pit follow in the chapter list. The plot turns on blushes and secrets.

A friend tells Sir Norman that a lady blushes to the roots of her hair at his name and cannot look her confidant in the face. Sir Norman blushes just as deeply and denies knowing her. Fleming's melodrama moves fast through love, revenge, and revelation, and it appeals to readers who enjoy Victorian sensation fiction at full tilt.
29612-treatise-on-the-diseases-of-women:
Dedicated to the women of the world, this treatise on the diseases of women bears the name of Lydia E. Pinkham, whose medicine company of Lynn, Massachusetts, copyrighted the book in 1901 and 1904. Its opening chapter declares that a woman best understands a woman, and that personal experience is a perfect teacher. After suffering, it says, one is ready to sympathize with those going through the same trials.

The book lists Pinkham's remedies beside its advice: vegetable compound in liquid, lozenge, and pill form, liver pills, blood purifier, and sanative wash, all sold by druggists. Its mix of counsel and sales talk marks an era of patent medicine. Students of women's health history will find a revealing, if dated, source.
29662-the-moon-is-green:
Fritz Leiber's short tale opens with Effie at a window, gazing at a green moon in terrified rapture. Her husband's voice chops through her mood, and her heart jumps like a startled cat, though her body shows no tremor. Dear God, she thinks, he must not see it, for it is so lovely, and he always destroys beauty. I am just looking at the Moon, she says listlessly. It is green.

Leiber's tag line gives the bargain: anyone wishing to escape death could do so for one simple price, the denial of life. A face, faunlike and pleading, draws away from the window's glow into the dark. Fans of Leiber will enjoy a strange, beautiful tale of marriage, moonlight, and a price too high.
29717-the-finding-of-haldgren:
Charles Willard Diffin printed this complete novelette in Astounding Stories in April 1932. It opens in 1974, at a great hall where the aged president of the Federation Aeronautique Internationale speaks to a world audience by radio and television. He has seen flight grow from the first flights at Kittyhawk to a vast new age of air and space travel.

Then a pinpoint of light calls for help from the craggy desolation of the moon. Chet Ballard answers that old call, and the tale follows the search for Haldgren, lost out there. Beasts, pits, and hard falls fill the rescue scenes. Diffin keeps the science plain and the peril close, in a brisk tale of one man's answer to a cry from the moon.
29750-zen:
Jerome Bixby's short tale follows E.T.I. Team 17, twenty-nine people assigned to the asteroids, four years and a quarter out of Terra and on schedule at Vesta. Its tag line warns that because the aliens were so likable, intelligent, and adaptable, they were vastly dangerous. On an asteroid, the narrator says, it is hard to keep one's eyes on the ground, for the sky is a vast ebony sphere heaped with silver clouds of stars.

Spaceships carry no portholes, flying by instruments, so an asteroid sky is one of the few places to truly see the stars. The team meets a likable people whose very charm threatens them. Fans of Bixby will enjoy a tense, thoughtful tale of first contact and quiet peril.
29766-audrey-craven:
May Sinclair published Audrey Craven in New York in 1906, in an author's edition from Henry Holt and Company. Its epigraph reads Made subject to vanity. Everybody knew, the first chapter says, that Miss Audrey Craven was the original of Laura, heroine of Langley Wyndham's masterpiece. She first caught the novelist's eye at Oxford, at a dinner given by her guardian, the Dean of St. Benedict's.

The dinner honored the new Master of Lazarus in name, but served in truth for Audrey's entertainment in the bewildering art of life. Thunder-weather hung over the city, and the Dean's mixed party of Oxonians and celebrities buzzed around her. Wyndham and his friend Percival Knowles, the critic, watch her closely. Sinclair's novel follows a young woman made into a heroine, and what that costs.
29980-the-cock-the-mouse-and-the-little-:
Felicite Lefevre retold The Cock, the Mouse and the Little Red Hen as an old tale, with twenty-four pictures by Tony Sarg, printed in Philadelphia by Macrae, Smith and Company. Lefevre dedicates the book to her nieces Cecilia Garry and Nelly Melville and to her little friend Harford Lury, with her love.

A pretty little house stood on a hill, once upon a time. A cock, a mouse, and a little red hen lived in it, behind a single little green door and four little windows fitted with green shutters. On another hill close by stood another little house, very ugly, with a door that would not shut, two broken windows, and all the paint off the shutters.
29982-culture-and-cooking-or-art-in-the-:
Catherine Owen wrote Culture and Cooking, or Art in the Kitchen, printed in New York, London, and Paris in 1881 by Cassell, Petter, Galpin and Company. A Brillat Savarin epigraph fronts it: the Creator, obliging man to eat to live, invites him by appetite and rewards him by pleasure. Owen's preface insists the book is not a cookery book and makes no attempt to replace a good one. It fills the gap between the reader and the household oracle instead.

 The latest and best of all, Owen notes, is a lady famous both for novels and for books on household economy. Her example proves Owen's thesis, set forth somewhat tediously, she admits: cooking and cultivation are by no means antagonistic. Seventeen chapters develop the art of the kitchen.
30000-the-bird-book-illustrating-in-natu:
Chester A. Reed wrote The Bird Book, printed in Garden City, New York, in 1915, with Doubleday, Page and Company. Its copyright, held by Charles K. Reed, is dated 1914. The subtitle promises more than seven hundred North American birds pictured in natural colors, with several hundred photographs of their nests and eggs. A topography of a bird and plates of the passenger pigeon, male, female, and young, open the visual feast.

The contents order the birds by kind: diving birds, with grebes, loons, auks, murres, and puffins, then long-winged swimmers, with skuas and jaegers. A barn owl plate shows the book's color work at its best. Page numbers are kept for reference, and picture notes sit at the end of each page. The book is a handsome, practical guide for bird watchers and nest hunters.
30220-evangelists-of-art-picture-sermons:
Rev. James Patrick, of the Couper United Free Church at Burntisland, teaches children through great pictures in eight picture-sermons. Longfellow's lines on Albrecht Dürer, the evangelist of art, open the book, and each chapter pairs a painting with a lesson. Holman Hunt shows Christ in the temple, Paton shows Luther at Erfürt, and Leighton shows Hercules wrestling death for the body of Alcestis.

Later sermons treat Watts on Orpheus and Eurydice and the rider on the white horse. Ward covers the last sleep of Argyll, Orchardson covers Wishart giving the sacrament before martyrdom, and Paton covers the man with the muck-rake. Jennings and Graham published the Cincinnati volume in 1903, printed at Edinburgh. The book suits families who want art, story, and moral teaching in one short volume.
30272-very-short-stories-and-verses-for-:
Mrs. W. K. Clifford offers short stories and verses for children, published in London by Walter Scott in 1886, with illustrations by Edith Campbell. Clifford, author of Anyhow Stories, notes in her preface that the stories, except the first, are reprinted from two books, Children Busy and Under Mother's Wing. There they were signed with her initials, while some verses appear for the time.

Master Willie opens. Swinging, a wooden doll, watching, the light on the hills, writing a book, a rabbit, a sandy cat, and a way to the sun follow. Moonlight, a poor little doll, violets, a fiddler, a broken horse, and a rainbow-maker follow. Over the porridge, a-coming down the street, a proud boy, seeking violets, Tommy's stockings, midsummer-night, a little maid, war, and peace follow. A little brother, a kite, and a tinker's marriage carry the world onward.
30418-traditional-nursery-songs-of-engla:
Felix Summerly edits Traditional Nursery Songs of England, with pictures by eminent modern artists, published in London in 1843. The front illustration shows the king in the parlor counting money and the queen in the kitchen eating bread and honey. The maid hangs clothes in the garden, until a blackbird pecks off her nose.

Summerly defends nursery songs against a lady who calls them trash, unworthy of utterance or remembrance and below the dignity of serious modern thought. He answers with humor, noting her loud talk during songs and her uncut copy of Wordsworth. The collection preserves classic rhymes in a handsome, illustrated home treasury for children.
30420-the-poets-lincoln-tributes-in-vers:
Osborn H. Oldroyd selects tributes in verse to the martyred President Lincoln, published in Washington in 1915 at the house where Lincoln died. Oldroyd, author of a book on Lincoln's assassination and editor of the Words of Lincoln, adds many portraits and illustrations of events in Lincoln's life.

An introduction by Marion Mills Miller treats the poetic spirit of Lincoln, and contents open with Lincoln's own poems, including My Childhood's Home I See Again. William Knox's Oh, Why Should the Spirit of Mortal Be Proud follows. The collection gathers poets' praise, grief, and memory into a memorial volume for readers and students.
30540-the-gates-between:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps writes The Gates Between, published in London, New York, and Melbourne in 1887, following her earlier Gates Ajar and Gypsy Breynton. Its epigraph quotes Revelation: write the things thou hast seen, the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter.

Narrator Esmerald Thorne warns that the story perplexed her as much as it may perplex readers, and offers no explanations at the start. She claims no special training as a writer, only the qualities of a faithful reporter. On 25 November in a year given as 187-, Thorne falls upon the event whose history she must tell, opening a tale of life beyond death.
30555-little-meg-s-children:
Hesba Stretton writes Little Meg's Children, published in London in 1905 by the Religious Tract Society, with a frontispiece by Harold Copping. Stretton, author of Jessica's First Prayer and Alone in London, opens with a chapter titled Motherless, set in London's East End near the docks, more than a mile from St. Paul's.

Later chapters follow Little Meg as a mourner, on cleaning day, treating her children, meeting a neighbor, spending her last money, and facing disappointment. Her red frock goes to pawn, friends come in need, and she works as a charwoman. Stretton tells a tender tale of poor children, duty, and faith, ending with father, farewell, and the end of trouble.
30723-fathers-and-children:
Ivan Turgenev wrote this Russian novel in Constance Garnett's translation, held here in the Harvard Classics Shelf of Fiction, edited by William Allan Neilson and published in 1917. A biographical note and critical pieces by writers such as Émile Melchior, Vicomte de Vogüé, and William Dean Howells open the volume. Its list of characters centers on Nikolai Petrovitch Kirsanov, his brother Pavel, and Nikolai's son Arkady.

Arkady brings home his friend Yevgeny Bazarov, a bold young man whose new ideas clash with the older Kirsanovs' ways. The novel follows that clash through country houses, love, and talk, as fathers and sons test each other's values. Turgenev's tale remains a classic study of a generation gap, and Garnett's plain English keeps its debates and feelings close at hand.
3074-the-burgess-bird-book-for-children:
Thornton Burgess wrote The Burgess Bird Book for Children to introduce little children to the birds they are most likely to meet. Dedicated to the children and birds of America, the book hopes to strengthen bonds of love and friendship between them. Booksellers urged it, feeling the lack of a simple medium for introducing little children to bird life. Burgess stresses it supplements, rather than competes with, fuller bird books.

The stories follow Peter Rabbit's neighbors and Farmer Brown's boy, who catches Blacksnake diving headfirst into a hole after eggs and strikes him with a switch. Each chapter teaches one bird's looks, song, and habits through story. The book remains a gentle classic of nature study for young children.
30767-new-apples-in-the-garden:
Kris Neville wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in July 1963, about problems that can be foreseen yet still defeat a programmed machine. Eddie Hibbs, an assistant underground supervisor, reports for work and is at once called out on an emergency, the third morning in a row. A section of distribution cable has blown in West Los Angeles, and Eddie climbs down a manhole with the nearby foreman of the maintenance crew.

Deep pull marks scar the lead sheath above the blow, and the cable came from a job on the East Side. Eddie judges a couple of hundred feet to be bad, worth about fifteen thousand dollars, and orders it cut back and spliced, with two men needed for a week. Neville builds his tale from workaday detail, showing how a routine fault can point to a larger, stranger problem underneath the city.
30800-nature-myths-and-stories-for-littl:
Flora J. Cooke, of the Cook County Normal School in Chicago, wrote this book of nature myths for small children. A revised edition came from A. Flanagan in 1895. Cooke felt a real need for stories built on good literature but still within a child's grasp. She hoped her tales would help primary teachers who lacked a press of their own. Her preface says myths are often fine truths dressed in fancy.

The stories give trees, flowers, clouds, and wind their own voices, so that a child can hear nature speak in tale form. Cooke argues that such tales, though thousands of years old, stay as true as in the days of Homer, and that they open sources of joy no power can take away. Teachers and parents will find a gentle, old-fashioned book for reading aloud and for first lessons in nature.
30845-the-boys-and-i-a-child-s-story-for:
Mrs. Molesworth wrote this child's story for children, published by E. P. Dutton in New York and W. and R. Chambers in London and Edinburgh, with pictures by Lewis Baumer. Its twelve chapters run from Our First Sorrow and Real and Play through three little travellers and the air-garden. They continue with a new trouble, trying to be good, toast for tea, and wanted a stamp.

Later chapters bring Miss Goldy-Hair, Tom's sore throat, a tea-party, and the white dove, with a frontispiece in which a voice asks a young man about a house to be sold. Molesworth writes in a child's voice, with small sorrows, games, and wonders at the center. Young readers will find a gentle, old-fashioned book about brothers, sisters, and the small adventures of home life.
30881-two-little-women:
Carolyn Wells wrote this 1915 girls' book for Grosset and Dunlap in New York, with pictures by E. C. Caswell. Wells, author of the Patty and Marjorie books, gives here a summer story of two little women, Dotty Rose and Dolly Fayre, whose names head the second chapter. The book opens on Summit Avenue.

Twenty chapters follow the girl next door, new rooms, a birthday morning, a double party, roller skating, two big brothers, and Crosstrees Camp. Dolly's escape, hidden treasure, a thrilling experience, and a tall phantom follow. Later chapters bring a luncheon, a cake contest, a walk in the woods, Surfwood, a doll overboard, and spending prize money. It is a warm, old-fashioned summer tale for young readers.
30910-the-queen-against-owen:
Allen Upward, author of The Prince of Balkistan, wrote The Queen Against Owen, held here in a new edition from Chatto and Windus in London in 1895. The press opinions printed at the front call it an unmistakable success and intensely dramatic, with high quality, vivid glimpses of life, and clever characterization. The Athenaeum calls it a realistic representation of a criminal trial.

Sporting Life praises narrative after narrative, somewhat in the manner of Wilkie Collins. Successive narratives pull the reader forward while keeping the crime unexplained until almost the final pages. Upward dedicates the book to Clement Harley Downs, in slight acknowledgment of his kind services. It is a powerful, original courtroom mystery, told through successive narratives that keep the crime hidden until near the close.
31131-boys-book-of-indian-warriors-and-h:
Edwin L. Sabin's 1918 book, published by George W. Jacobs in Philadelphia, retells the lives of Native warriors and heroic women for boy readers, with Chief Joseph as frontispiece. Chapters run from Piskaret the Adirondack champion and Opechancanoah through King Philip, the Squaw Sachem of Pocasset, Pontiac's bloody belt, Logan, Cornstalk, and Little Turtle.

Later chapters take up Tecumseh, the Red Sticks at Horseshoe Bend, and Black Hawk. They also cover Sacagawea as the bird-woman guide, Four Bears the Mandan, and the Pierced Noses' long trail in search of the Book of Heaven. Written in Sabin's stirring style, the volume honors Native courage while reflecting the storytelling of its time.
31195-english-caricaturists-and-graphic-:
Graham Everitt's history of English caricaturists and graphic humorists of the nineteenth century was praised by the press as a treatise worthy of its great subject. It traces comic drawing from its early masters to its Victorian stars. Its pages take in Seymour, whose suicide in 1836 Thackeray witnessed in London, and Cruikshank, whose genius a professor blamed for sterility. They also cover John Leech, waited on at Whitby by a deputation from the town's institute.

Appendices add such curiosities as a pirated Philadelphia edition of Charles Lever's Harry Lorrequer. Entertaining and learned, Everitt's volume doubles as a history of caricature and a gallery of the age's sharpest eyes.
3135-my-summer-in-a-garden:
Warner writes his garden papers as letters and notes through one summer. Weeds, weather, neighbors, and the small wars of the beds supply his matter. An introductory letter to Mr Fields jokes about introductions. It calls one a pilaster put on a building for looks, usually very flat. Calvin, a Study of Character, joins the garden pieces in this volume.

Calvin is Warner's cat, observed with the same affectionate irony as the beans and the bugs. The book made Warner's name, because readers recognized their own summers in it. A summer of beans, bugs, and one cat turns out to contain a whole philosophy of work and talk.
31456-the-upward-path-a-reader-for-color:
The Upward Path, a reader for colored children, was compiled by Myron T. Pritchard, principal of the Everett School in Boston, and Mary White Ovington, chairman of the board of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It carries an introduction by Robert R. Moton, principal of Tuskegee Institute, and was published by Harcourt, Brace and Howe with copyright in 1920. The book gathers readings chosen to educate and encourage Black children.

Its selections mix stories, poems, and biographical sketches, including notes on figures such as Joseph S. Cotter Jr. and George W. Ellis. The aim, in the compilers' view, was to give young readers models of achievement and a sense of their own history. As a document, it shows how Black educators and their allies built school reading for a segregated age, with pride and purpose.
31468-the-battle-of-franklin-tennessee-n:
Captain John K. Shellenberger's The Battle of Franklin, Tennessee, November 30, 1864, was privately printed at Cleveland in 1916 in only 125 copies. It is a statement of the erroneous claims made by General Schofield and an exposition of the blunder which opened the battle. Shellenberger writes as a participant. Facts about Franklin, he says, always drew his greedy interest, and he gave far more research to this battle than to any other in which he was engaged.

His presence in the midst of the limited area where the fighting raged let him observe its leading features himself, and he fills gaps in observation with research. The result is a veteran's corrective history, arguing a precise point about how the battle began. Readers of Civil War history will find a short, argumentative, firsthand study, valuable for its detail and its candor about sources.
3154-the-surprising-adventures-of-baron-:
Rudolph Erich Raspe gives the world its great liar-hero in this book of tall tales. Baron Munchausen rides cannon balls, pulls himself from a bog by his own hair, and travels to the moon with perfect gravity. The introduction places the book among imaginary voyages, beside Utopia, Robinson Crusoe, and Gulliver, the three great types all created in England.

Munchausen belongs to the satirical type, turning traveler's wonders into open jest. Each adventure outdoes the last while keeping a straight face. The book has delighted children and mocked adult credulity for two centuries. It remains the model for every later tale in which the narrator's word is the whole joke.
31550-the-first-essay-on-the-political-r:
Dr. Alice Drysdale Vickery translated Condorcet's essay Sur l'admission des femmes au droit de Cité, on the admission of women to the rights of citizenship. It was published by the Garden City Press of Letchworth at twopence, with a preface and remarks by Vickery. Condorcet wrote the essay in 1789, and Vickery's preface notes that more than one hundred years have passed since, yet women's enfranchisement still lacks a fair settlement.

Condorcet's argument, that women hold the same natural rights as men and should share citizenship, appears here in English for a new generation of campaigners. Vickery's edition joins translation to advocacy, with her own remarks framing the old text for the suffrage struggle. Readers will find a short, foundational feminist text, still sharp after more than a century.
31795-yellow-cap-and-other-fairy-stories:
Julian Hawthorne's Yellow-Cap and Other Fairy Stories for Children was published in London by Longmans, Green in 1880. It opens its title tale before Julius Caesar landed at Dover, while the plans for Stonehenge were still under consideration. England then was inhabited by a civilized and prosperous people, renowned for affability to strangers, with no fogs, smoke, railways, or politics.

The village of Honeymead, a few miles outside London's walls, holds fifteen or twenty thatched cottages with vegetable gardens, beehives, hencoops, and cowsheds. Readers get a set of Victorian fairy tales, beginning with Yellow-Cap's golden pledge, golden dwarf, and talisman, written for children but with a sly adult wit.
319-the-ways-of-men:
Eliot Gregory, writing as An Idler, studies American society with a light, knowing pen. The Ways of Men, from the 1900 Scribner's edition, is dedicated to Edith Wharton, who praised the author. Its first chapter, Uncle Sam, traces pompous classical town names.

A cultured governor named embryo towns Utica, Syracuse, and Ithaca, and Gregory notes the comic gap between name and place. Later chapters tour manners, money, and travel in the Gilded Age. The Merrymount Press printing adds typographic charm. The book suits readers of Wharton and James. Gregory's idle essays pair with Wharton's novels of the same society.
32022-a-problem-in-greek-ethics-being-an:
John Addington Symonds's treatise on Greek love, privately printed in London in 1908 for the Areopagitica Society, is an inquiry into the phenomenon of sexual inversion in ancient Greece. It was written in 1873, while Symonds worked on his Studies of Greek Poets, and printed in only ten private copies in 1883. Symonds addresses it especially to medical psychologists and jurists, as a scholarly study.

The preface stresses that the work is independent of an earlier article on the same subject by M. H. E. Meier, published in 1837. Symonds learned of Meier's piece only after reading Sir Richard Burton's terminal essay to the Arabian Nights in 1886. He notes with interest that Meier agreed with his own theory, set out in Section X: that Greek love came from the north of Greece and had a Dorian character. Readers get a frank, historical study of a subject long kept out of open print.
32064-the-wine-ghosts-of-bremen:
Wilhelm Hauff's short tale, translated by E. Sadler and C. R. L.
