Fletcher and published by White and Allen in New York and London in 1889, comes in a limited edition of five hundred copies, this one numbered 485. Frank M. Gregory supplied the illustrations. Their captions hint at the tale's spirits: It Was the Devil as frontispiece, The Cellar of Bacchus, The Gentlemen of the Rhine, and To the Dance, to the Dance. 

A preface opens by recalling Carlyle's effort to bring Jean Paul Richter before English readers. It notes the differences of taste between English and German readers of that day. The tale itself belongs to Hauff's world of wine cellars, Rhine gentlemen, and dancing ghosts in Bremen. Readers get a short, atmospheric German fantasy in a handsome limited edition.
32137-the-men-of-the-moss-hags-being-a-h:
S. R. Crockett's romance, published by Macmillan in New York and London in 1895, presents itself as a history of adventure. It is taken from the papers of William Gordon of Earlston in Galloway, told over again by Crockett. He dedicated it to Andrew Lang, poet, romancer, and scholar. Crockett calls himself born of the hill-folk. His dedication honours men who fought bravely under the blue banner.

A prefatory note thanks his researchers. James Nicholson of Kirkcudbright examined local records on the period and persons. The Reverend John Anderson of Edinburgh University Library brought to light materials from the Earlstoun Papers and records of the United Societies, long thought lost. Letters from those papers appear in the book. Readers get a Scottish adventure romance with a documentary frame, where moss-hags, hill-folk, and old papers ground a tale of bravery.
32139-an-appeal-to-honour-and-justice-th:
Daniel Defoe's Appeal to Honour and Justice, Though It Be of His Worst Enemies, printed in London by J. Baker in 1715, is a true account of his conduct in public affairs. The British Library notes a first publication in 1715 and a reprint by D. A. Talboys at Oxford in 1841. Defoe fronts the pamphlet with Jeremiah's words: come and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words.

Defoe hopes that at last a calm middle voice may get a hearing. Hitherto, he writes, noise has been so great, and prejudices and passions so strong, that offering any argument or reason for his actions would have been in vain. Readers get a self-defence by one of England's first journalists, pleading moderation against enemies who would not listen.
3227-defenders-of-democracy-contribution:
The Gift Book Committee of the Militia of Mercy edited this wartime gift book. Its title names its cause: defenders of democracy, with contributions from representative men of the day. The volume belongs to the First World War years, when such books raised money and morale by gathering essays, addresses, and poems from public figures.

Readers get a chorus rather than a single voice: statesmen, soldiers, clergy, and writers speaking for the democratic cause in their own styles. The book now serves two purposes. It preserves wartime argument at its most earnest, and it shows how a nation at war asked its famous men to explain, in print, what the fighting was for.
32318-greek-women:
Mitchell Carroll's study, copyrighted in 1907 and 1908, examines the character and standing of women among the ancient Greeks. Carroll, professor of classical philology at George Washington University, argues that women's influence worked quietly yet shaped the character and fate of a people. Historians, he notes, often overlook that force even when it runs through literature, art, and religion.

Rather than stopping at dress, ornaments, and home surroundings, the book asks what Greek women were like and what place they held in society. It treats them as part of a wider civilisation famed for philosophy, poetry, oratory, and art. Readers get a survey that links daily life to the larger Greek achievement in thought and beauty.
32356-roman-women:
Alfred Brittain's study, volume two of Woman in All Ages and in All Countries, examines Roman women from legend through the empire. Published in Philadelphia in 1907, it opens with legendary Rome. One vivid example is Tullia, daughter of Servius, shown as a bad queen in contrast to a good one. An illustration after Hildebrand shows Tullia driving her chariot, by tradition, over her dead father's body after Lucius seizes the throne.

Brittain treats queens, wives, and common women side by side, asking how law, family, and public life shaped their roles. The book links household power to political power, showing women as instigators, supporters, and victims of Rome's great changes. It offers readers a broad survey of Roman social history told through women's lives.
32388-the-new-warden:
Mrs. David G. Ritchie's novel, first published in November 1918 and reprinted in March 1919, is set in Oxford at a moment of change. Its opening chapter, The Warden's Lodgings, looks back to the founders and benefactors who built the grey, sacred city. Then it turns to a new threat: an endless spread of red brick building pressing against Oxford's walls.

Fire and siege belonged to older dangers; the new age brings quiet, steady encroachment. Against that backdrop the story follows college life under a new warden, with tradition, learning, and town growth pulling in different directions. Ritchie writes with affection for Oxford's past and a sharp eye for its present pressures. The novel suits readers who enjoy academic settings, English social comedy, and portraits of institutions trying to hold their character.
32390-black-man-s-burden:
Mack Reynolds's novel, serialised in Analog in December 1961 and January 1962, opens in the Sahara, where a two-vehicle caravan reaches a small camp of Taitoq Tuareg in seven goat-leather tents. Moussa-ag-Amastan, headman of the clan, watches the strange dust pillars raised by air rotors with fear, half expecting spirits from the desert wastes. The visitors bring news of a wider Africa in turmoil.

Reynolds argues through his story that peace will not come while Africans see themselves mainly as warring tribesmen rather than as one people. The caravan's journey becomes a test of that idea, as clan loyalty, outside power, and hopes for unity collide. The book takes its title from Kipling's poem and turns that poem's burden back on its readers with a deliberately provocative question.
32418-oriental-women:
Edward B. Pollard's study, volume four of Woman in All Ages and in All Countries, examines oriental women, with marriage customs at its centre. An opening illustration after Cabanel shows Rebekah and Isaac's agent Eliezer, and Pollard calls their courtship one of the most romantic in ancient or modern story. Rebekah at the well and in her household, he writes, presents a unique picture of womanly grace and beauty.

Her courage in mounting a stranger's camel to travel to a far country for marriage stands out, even beside her gentleness. Pollard uses such scenes to show how courtship, wedding, and household life marked oriental societies. The volume offers readers a broad, illustrated survey of women's lives across the East, from biblical times through later eastern cultures.
32452-british-sports-for-the-amusement-o:
W. Belch's British Sports for the Amusement of Children, a sixpenny coloured children's book printed and sold in London at Newington Butts, presents country sports in short verses and pictures. Pheasant shooting opens the sequence, with the fowler taking aim in September, when birds are in full prime. Rabbit shooting follows, showing rabbits prancing without fear before a gunner's aim cuts their enjoyment short.

Badger baiting, horse racing, and other sports follow in the same pattern, each with a coloured illustration and a few rhymed lines. Belch sold the book alongside entertaining views, scenes from nature, birds, beasts, and an alphabet of nations, all at sixpence coloured. The little book offers a period picture of children's print, country life, and sports that modern readers will rightly view as cruel.
3256-books-and-bookmen:
Ian Maclaren opens this 1912 volume by defining his tribe. Books and bookmen cannot be separated, he says, any more than sheep and a shepherd. Yet he will speak of the bookman rather than his books, and he begins by clearing a confusion. A man is not a bookman merely because he owns many books, for he may be a bookseller or a collector of a different kind.

The essays that follow praise the reader who lives with books: the minister, the teacher, the friend who lends and talks. Maclaren, himself a beloved Scottish preacher-writer, writes with warmth about reading as a way of life. Books kept for company, not for show: Maclaren knows the difference at a glance, and teaches it by example.
32725-work-for-women:
George J. Manson answers practical questions for women seeking paid work, in this Putnam volume of 1883. His chapters grew from articles in the Christian Union in the winter of 1882-3, rewritten from new investigations. For each occupation he asks the same questions: can work be found, how long does training take, how many are in the trade, and what do they earn.

Chapters cover industrial designing, shorthand, telegraphy, feather curling, photography, professional nursing, proof-reading and bookbinding, the drama, book-agents, dress-making, millinery, and teaching. Manson notes one common obstacle: employers fear a trained woman will leave the trade to marry.
3303-prince-hagen:
Upton Sinclair mixes Norse myth with American money in this play. Gerald Isman, a poet, meets Mimi, a Nibelung, and Alberich, king of the Nibelungs, with Prince Hagen, his grandson, close behind. Mrs Isman and Hicks, a butler, hold the domestic side, while Mrs Bagley-Willis rules society. John Isman, a railroad magnate, Estelle, his daughter, and Plimpton, the coal baron, bring capital to the stage.

Rutherford, lord of steel, De Wiggleston Riggs, cotillon leader, and Lord Alderdyce complete the order. Myth and monopoly bargain together, and Hagen's ancient curse meets modern finance. Sinclair's fantasy argues, in comic form, that gold still rules men, whether it comes from the Rhine or from a railroad. The play is odd, ambitious, and unmistakably his.
33066-the-garden-of-eden:
Max Brand's Garden of Eden, copyrighted in 1922, opens with Ben Connor, a westerner in disguise. His broad shoulders are tailored to look fashionably slender and his deep chest is hidden by a stoop learned on Broadway between sunset and dawn. He wears spats, a glowing Scotch tweed, and a Panama hat, a city costume that fools no one for long.

Brand, a master of the western, uses Connor's disguise to set up a story of identity, romance, and frontier justice, where clothes, manners, and a quick hand all matter. The novel's title points to a place of innocence and temptation at once, and Brand keeps the action moving between town and open country. It remains a lively, well-plotted western for readers who enjoy a hero playing a part he cannot quite sustain.
33086-the-duchess-of-wrexe-her-decline-a:
Hugh Walpole's Duchess of Wrexe: Her Decline and Death, a romantic commentary published in New York in 1914, opens the Rising City sequence while standing complete and independent in itself. Walpole warns nervous readers that the book is grouped with two stories to follow under the heading of The Rising City. Connected in place, idea, and time with some shared characters, it is not a fragment waiting for a sequel. The duchess's story ends here.

The novel follows a powerful woman's decline and death in a rising city, where new wealth, new buildings, and old families collide. Walpole, author of Fortitude, writes with a keen eye for social climbing and for the pride that outlives power. It is a period novel of ambition and decay, and the first panel of a larger picture that Walpole promised to complete in the books that followed.
33265-woman-s-club-work-and-programs-or-:
Caroline French Benton's guide, copyrighted in 1913, offers first aid to club women, with work and programs for women's clubs. Benton, author of A Little Cook Book and Easy Entertaining, writes for women who ran clubs, planned meetings, and sought order in their busy civic lives. The book draws in part on articles that had appeared in the Woman's Home Companion.

Its chapters give practical help: how to plan a program, run a meeting, and keep a club lively through the year. The tone is clear and friendly, suited to club officers and members alike. For readers of women's history, the guide is a vivid record of the club movement at its height, when women built learning and friendship into organized civic life.
33273-lives-of-celebrated-women:
This volume of Lives of Celebrated Women, by the author of Peter Parley's Tales, gathers short lives of famous women for young readers. Published in Boston in 1844 and entered by S. G. Goodrich, it opens with Ferdinand and Isabella, the Spanish monarchs whose reign shaped a new age. Its preface promises lives that teach by example, in the plain, instructive style of the Peter Parley books.

The book suits readers who want history in brief, moral portraits, each life told as a lesson in courage, wisdom, or virtue. Its tone is earnest and old-fashioned, and its choice of subjects reflects the tastes of its time. For students of children's literature and women's history, it is a revealing window on how the 1840s taught girls about great women.
33423-a-man-in-the-open:
Roger Pocock's Man in the Open, copyrighted in 1912, follows a hero through Labrador, a happy ship, youth, an ordeal by torture, and a burning bush. Its second part moves to two ships at anchor, the Trevor accident, love, and a landlord, with further turns that test the man in the open air. Pocock, illustrated by M. Leone Bracker, writes of adventure in wild places.

The novel's appeal lies in its outdoor vigor, as its hero faces nature, foes, and his own heart in the far north and beyond. Its pace is brisk, its scenes vivid, and its tone hearty. For readers who enjoy adventure tales of the old school, A Man in the Open offers a lively story of a man proved by the open world.
33510-stories-for-helen:
Miss Eliza Leslie selected and revised four moral tales for young readers in this 1845 collection, drawn from her earlier Atlantic Tales. The advertisement states her hope plainly: that juvenile readers may find a little instruction blended with a little amusement. The stories are written for girls and set in homes, schools, and neighborhoods where small faults carry real consequences.

The opening tale follows Rosamond Evering, a girl who repeats everything she hears and exaggerates it, to her parents' distress. Further stories cover a boarding-school feast, a week of idleness, and Madeline Malcolm. Leslie's clear, direct prose makes the book a pleasant window onto nineteenth-century children's literature and its lessons in honesty, industry, and kindness.
33612-the-land-of-strong-men:
A. M. Chisholm writes a western novel of ranching, love, and conspiracy in this 1919 book, illustrated by Frank Tenney Johnson. Forty-seven chapters follow Angus from a deathbed and a lost-and-found beginning through assertions of himself, love and war, gains and losses, a hold-up, a race, a fight with a grizzly. Judge Riley, drunk and sober, the Frenches, old Sam Paul, Dorgan, and Faith Winton people the story.

Later chapters bring an auction, an unmasking, duplicate deeds, sudden death, outlaws, a trail, a red avenger, and a great show-down before peace. Chisholm balances ranch work, romance, and mystery, with cattle rounded up before heavy snows and driven to the ranch. Readers of classic westerns will enjoy its large cast, its action, and its strong, plain-spoken heroes.
33722-donalblane-of-darien:
J. Macdonald Oxley writes a boys' adventure of Scotland's Darien scheme in this 1902 Toronto book, illustrated by W. Rainey. The hero's unusual name promises a tale, and Oxley begins with a glance back to the close of the seventeenth century, when the remarkable Scotsman William Paterson rose to prominence in England. Twelve chapters follow Donalblane carrying his point, off to Darien, a rescue and retreat, across the Atlantic, a brush with buccaneers, and the founding of the city of Darien.

Later chapters add a successful embassy, perilous plight, the chase of the manatee, a midnight attack, and New York and home. Illustrations show a child placed on a chest, a liking for the sea, ravening swine, appalling eyes, and a harpoon raised in a bow. Oxley turns a tragic colonial venture into sturdy adventure for young readers.
33762-the-adventures-of-elizabeth-in-ru-:
The author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden recounts a walking tour of Rügen in this 1904 book, with a map of the island. Rügen, the biggest island Germany possesses, lies in the Baltic off Pomerania, and Elizabeth wished to walk around it that summer, though no one would walk with her. Walking, she argues, is the perfect way of moving if you want to see into the life of things, and the one way of freedom.

Eleven days of contents carry her from Miltzow to Lauterbach, Vilm, Göhren, Thiessow, Sellin, Binz, the Jagdschloss, the Granitz woods, Stubbenkammer, Glowe, Wiek, and Hiddensee, before she returns home. Driving binds a traveler to horses' legs, bicycling and motoring hurry past delicate wayside joys. The book is a witty, observant travel diary for walkers and lovers of the Baltic coast.
33787-rockhaven:
Charles Clark Munn writes a Maine coast romance in this 1902 Boston novel, illustrated by Frank T. Merrill. It is dedicated to all who despise hypocrisy, admire manly courage and womanly devotion, and respect simple faith. Forty-five chapters open on Rockhaven itself, introduce Winn Hardy, the Rockhaven Granite Company, Jess Hutton, and Mona Hutton. Forty-five chapters move through Sunday on Rockhaven, the hand of fate, a friendly hand, the Devil's Oven, and the parting of the ways.

Later chapters follow a matter of business, the growth of a bubble, a path of moonlight, fog, a cloud over Rockhaven, two rascals, the starting and progress of a corner, a climax. Munn balances coastal life, granite quarrying, speculation, and romance. Readers of regional fiction will enjoy its sea air and its moral steadiness.
33792-poems-of-emile-verhaeren:
Alma Strettell chose and turned into English these poems of Emile Verhaeren, published in London and New York in 1915. Verhaeren was born at Saint Amand, near Antwerp, in 1855, and grew up beside the Scheldt among flat Flemish fields, dykes, and marshes. His youth in that misty country left a lasting mark on his verse.

The poems range from village scenes, rain, snow, and bell-ringers to bright hours of love and joy. Strettell's notes present him as a leading voice of young Belgium, praised in France for lyric power. The book gives English readers a broad first path into a poet of landscape, feeling, and color.
33918-mr-punch-with-the-children:
J. A. Hammerton edited this volume of the Punch Library of Humour, gathering Mr. Punch with children in 175 pictures. Drawings by Phil May, George du Maurier, Charles Keene, John Leech, Gordon Browne, and other humorists show children at home, at play, and in mischief. Punch had run since 1841, and each library volume stands complete in itself.

The pictures favor the comic side of nursery life: tears, tantrums, and small triumphs, drawn with affection. Hammerton's set aimed to give the cream of national humor in handy form. The book still delights readers who love Victorian cartoon art.
33927-not-quite-eighteen:
Susan Coolidge, author of What Katy Did, published this set of short tales in Boston in 1894. The stories follow girls and young women who are not quite grown: a lucky bunny, a wilful girl, wolves at Saint Gervas, three little candles, and a pony that kept a store. Each tale turns on a small choice or a kind act.

Coolidge writes with warmth for young readers, praising courage, patience, and good humor without preaching at length. A blessing in disguise and a granted wish close the set. The book remains a gentle sample of the girls' stories that filled American shelves in the 1890s.
3398-my-first-visit-to-new-england-and-o:
William Dean Howells gathers New England memories in this volume from Literary Friends and Acquaintance. Its contents name a biographical sketch, my first visit to New England, and first impressions of literary New York. Long before he began the papers that make up the volume, Howells writes, he had meant to write of literary history in New England.

He meant to write it as he had known it in the lives of its great exemplars, during the twenty-five years he lived near them. The papers that follow keep that promise in part: visits, first meetings, and impressions, rather than a formal history. Readers get New England's literary age as one man lived it, neighbor to its makers and junior to most of them.
34025-ancient-rome-the-lives-of-great-me:
Mary Agnes Hamilton told the lives of great men of ancient Rome in this volume, published at Oxford in 1922 by the Clarendon Press. Lives run from Brutus and Tarquin, Lucretia, Mucius, and Cloelia through Regulus, Coriolanus, Pyrrhus, and Fabricius to Hamilcar, Hannibal, the Scipios, the Gracchi, Cato, Marius, Sulla, Pompeius, Crassus, Cicero, and Caesar.

Sections open with the people and city of Rome, then treat early heroes, great enemies, the Scipios, and the Gracchi. Hamilton writes for young readers in clear, lively prose. The book offers a classic introduction to Rome through its leading lives.
34107-the-curry-cook-s-assistant-or-curr:
Daniel Santiagoe's Curry Cook's Assistant, in its third London edition of 1889, teaches English cooks to make curries in their original style, as cooked in Ceylon and Madras. Santiagoe, son of a butler and fiddler of Colombo, had served at exhibitions at Liverpool and Glasgow.

The book opens with home-made curry powder, then gives plain receipts for beef, chicken, game, egg, and vegetable curries, with notes on heat, spice, and method. Its charm lies in its plain voice and its care for true flavour over show, a guide for cooks who want the dish as its makers knew it.
34135-a-book-lover-s-holidays-in-the-ope:
Theodore Roosevelt wrote this book of open-air holidays, published in New York in March 1916 by Charles Scribner's Sons, with pictures. A frontispiece from a painting by Theodore B. Pitman shows Roosevelt on the brink of the Grand Canyon. Roosevelt, author of Through the Brazilian Wilderness, African Game Trails, and The Rough Riders, turns here to reading and rambling outdoors.

The book joins a love of books with a love of the open, in the former president's vigorous voice. It serves readers who like nature writing with a literary bent. The volume offers Roosevelt at leisure, book in hand, under open sky.
3622-the-duke-s-children:
Anthony Trollope returns to the Palliser family in this novel, first serialized in 1879 and 1880 and published in book form in 1880. The book opens when the Duchess is dead, leaving the Duke of Omnium a widower with grown children. Lady Mary Palliser loves Francis Oliphant Tregear, a gentleman without fortune, while her brother Lord Gerald falls into further trouble.

The Duke must learn to be a father as well as a statesman, and his children must choose between duty, love, and money. Chapters follow meetings at Matching, a tavern called the Bobtailed Fox, and a major deposed from his place. The novel suits readers who have followed the Pallisers and want Trollope's late, tender view of family pride.
3655-the-parent-s-assistant-or-stories-f:
Maria Edgeworth writes stories for children in this collection, first framed by a preface addressed to parents. Edgeworth quotes Pope, that education forms the common mind just as the twig is bent, the tree's inclined. She argues that the grand difficulty in education is to ascertain facts about how children actually learn. Her stories test that idea in practice.

The tales follow children through small moral trials: truth telling, generosity, industry, and obedience, with consequences shown rather than preached. Edgeworth, a leading Irish educator, wrote for the nursery and the schoolroom alike. The book suits parents and teachers who want early children's fiction with a clear, humane purpose.
4065-side-lights-on-astronomy-and-kindre:
A popular astronomy book explains telescopes and kindred fields for general readers. A chapter on the Huyghenian eyepiece notes that a small telescope, used by hand as a spyglass, needs little support, but regular use demands a proper mounting.

Later chapters turn from instruments to stars, planets, and the wonders they reveal, in clear, patient prose. The book belongs to the age when amateur stargazing grew with cheap optics and public lectures. Readers curious about the night sky will find a friendly guide to how telescopes work and what they show.
4313-the-odd-women:
George Gissing gave this novel a title from the census term for women left unmarried by a shortage of men. Its contents open with the fold and the shepherd, a woman adrift, and an independent woman, then follow Monica's majority, a casual acquaintance, and a camp of the reserve. Weddings, discord, and the clank of chains follow.

The odd women here seek work, training, and a life beyond marriage, and Gissing treats their hopes with respect and doubt. Later chapters bring confession and counsel, retreat with honour, and a new beginning. The novel is a landmark of Victorian fiction about women's work, and it still speaks to readers today.
4360-vendetta-a-story-of-one-forgotten:
Marie Corelli wrote this novel of revenge and return under the subtitle A Story of One Forgotten. Its preface warns readers not to judge the tale before its end, and its thirty-seven chapters carry a hero through injury, exile, and a long-plotted reckoning. Corelli, already known for Ardath, Thelma, and A Romance of Two Worlds, writes in her high romantic manner.

The vendetta of the title is both a plot and a passion, pursued across years and countries. Corelli mixes Italian color, fierce feeling, and moral argument, as her heroes often do. Readers of Victorian sensation fiction will find the book's pleasures familiar: secrets, disguises, and a final settling of accounts.
4529-biographies-of-working-men:
Grant Allen published these seven short lives in 1884, choosing men who rose by work rather than by birth. His subjects are Thomas Telford, stonemason; George Stephenson, engine-man; John Gibson, sculptor; William Herschel, bandsman; Jean Francois Millet, painter; James Garfield, canal boy; and Thomas Edward, shoemaker. Allen drew his facts from standard lives of engineers, Stephensons, Gibson, Herschel, Millet, and Garfield.

Each life shows a craft learned by hand, long patience, and a chance seized at the right hour, from Telford's heather hills between England and Scotland to Garfield's canal work in America. The book is plain, encouraging biography, written for readers who like real examples of effort rewarded. It suits young readers and anyone who wants short, true stories of how skill and grit can carry a working man or woman far.
4644-the-adventures-of-mr-verdant-green:
Cuthbert Bede, a pen name, tells the adventures of Mr. Verdant Green in three parts, revised here to match the first editions of 1853, 1854, and 1857. The book follows a fresh, green young man to Oxford, where college jokes, tutors, and fellow students cure his dumps, in Swift's phrase from the frontispiece. Minor spelling changes between editions, such as shew for show, are noted in the editorial matter.

Verdant Green blunders through examinations, friendships, sports, and scrapes, learning town and gown manners as he goes. Bede writes with affectionate humour, and the book became a classic Oxford tale. Readers get a light, old-fashioned university comedy, full of period slang and student life, and a useful picture of Oxford in the middle of the nineteenth century.
4713-the-veiled-lady-and-other-men-and-w:
F. Hopkinson Smith gathers stories in The Veiled Lady and Other Men and Women, opening with a note to readers on the title. The collection is labelled The Veiled Lady as the easiest way out of a dilemma, he says. Yet the title may mislead. Beyond doubt these covers hold a charming Houri, to whom nightingales sing lullabies, and a beautiful Venetian whose love affairs upset a quarter.

Other figures include a common-sense, motherly nurse whose heart warmed toward a companion in an adjoining berth. They add a plucky New England girl with courage of her convictions, and a prim spinster whose only consolation was the boarder opposite. Rough sea-dogs with friendly feelings fill the book. Contents list Loretta of the shipyards, a coat of red lead, Miss Murdock special, and Captain Joe and the Susie Ann. Readers get warm, varied American stories, told with humour and heart.
473-stories-to-tell-to-children:
Sara Cone Bryant gathers fifty-three tales for telling aloud in this companion to her guide on storytelling. The Little Red Hen, the Gingerbread Man, the Boy Who Cried Wolf, the Elves and the Shoemaker, and David and Goliath sit beside lesser-known tales from many lands. Notes for the teller open the book.

Bryant shapes each tale for voice, not print, with short sentences and clear action. Stories suit school, home, and library hours. The volume remains a handy store for tellers who want tried tales that hold small listeners from first line to last.
4782-when-we-dead-awaken:
Henrik Ibsen's When We Dead Awaken, translated by William Archer, is Ibsen's late dramatic epilogue. Archer notes that from Pillars of Society to John Gabriel Borkman, Ibsen's plays followed at regular two-year intervals. Indignation over abuse heaped on Ghosts cut the gap to An Enemy of the People to a single year. Borkman appeared in 1896, and a successor was expected in 1898, but Christmas brought no rumour of a new play.

In a man over seventy, that breach seemed ominous. The new National Theatre in Christiania opened in September of the following year. Archer, meeting Ibsen for the last time, heard he was at work on a play he thought of calling a Dramatic Epilogue. Ibsen wrote it with such labour and passionate agitation that those around him were almost alarmed. Readers get Ibsen's final play, about an artist, a model, and lives that wake too late.
4984-the-hidden-children:
Three riders draw bridle in the middle of the Bedford Road in this Revolutionary War novel, facing a tavern shot to splinters. The sign dangles by one hinge. Buckshot mars the freshly painted house. Blue paper fills broken windows. A wanton fire has been set at the northeast corner. The misused house seems to watch them out of patched eyes.

The hidden children of the title move through this war-torn country, where loyalty, danger, and family secrets cross. The work arrives without a named author here. Readers get a romance of the American Revolution, atmospheric in its ruined taverns and roads, and centered on young people caught in a war larger than themselves.
4996-number-seventeen:
Number Seventeen opens outside a London theater in drizzle, where a red-faced commissionaire pockets sixpences summoning cabs for playgoers leaving Daly's latest musical comedy. All London, as the phrase goes, flocks to the show. Most of the crowd owns no motor cars and cannot afford taxicabs. So they hurry on foot toward tubes and omnibuses.

Into that ordinary crowd steps a mystery, centered on the title's number seventeen. The record carries no author byline. Readers get an Edwardian London thriller that begins with theater crowds and rain. Then it draws its hero into a puzzle where a number, a cab, and a stranger matter more than they first seem.
5007-the-poisoned-pen:
A reporter narrator hurries uptown from the Star office to find his friend packing in haste for Danbridge, and this mystery opens with a suitcase lying open on a bed. Clean laundry goes in without its wrapping paper, and five minutes is all the time allowed before the six o'clock train, because Danbridge is on everybody's lips.

The quiet Connecticut town is the scene of a notorious case, and the two men travel to investigate it. The author goes unnamed in the catalog record. Readers get a detective story in the newspaper tradition, where a journalist's nose for news drives the inquiry and a small town hides a large crime.
514-little-women:
Louisa May Alcott follows the four March sisters through Civil War years and beyond in this beloved novel. Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy live in modest Concord with their mother while their father serves as chaplain. Christmas without gifts, plays, picnics, and neighbor Laurie fill part one; weddings, work, and loss fill part two.

Alcott writes with warmth, humor, and plain moral sense, letting Jo's pen and Beth's music carry the heart. The book grew from Alcott's own family life, yet it speaks to any home. It endures as a classic of girlhood, where love, work, and pluck shape four very different lives.
5172-aladdin-o-brien:
Gouverneur Morris's novel follows Aladdin O'Brien, a boy who grows into a young man of charm, mischief, and restless ambition. The book opens with a Sunday-school walk that turns into a forbidden river outing with Margaret, and its three books trace Aladdin from childhood pranks toward love, work, and the wider world.

Morris writes with humour and sentiment, giving Aladdin a storyteller's gift and a habit of exaggerating his own exploits. The novel offers a light, nostalgic portrait of American boyhood and young manhood, in the manner of the popular romances of the early twentieth century.
5179-a-siren:
Thomas Adolphus Trollope's novel A Siren opens on Ash Wednesday morning in Ravenna, after the last night of carnival. It then turns back four months to show how its story began. Its books follow singers, a marchese, an impresario, and a young woman whose voice. Charm draws men into rivalry, as carnival glitter gives way to quieter consequences.

Trollope, brother of the more famous Anthony, sets the tale in the Papal States, among theatres, churches, and provincial society. The novel mixes romance with Italian local colour, and it will appeal to readers who enjoy nineteenth-century stories of art, ambition, and love in an old Italian city.
5269-driven-back-to-eden:
E. P. Roe's Driven Back to Eden, first serialised in St Nicholas magazine, tells a simple story written expressly for young people. Roe, doubting whether he could beguile honest little critics with words that did not tell an interesting story. Roe aimed to present an experience that might be verified in real life, avoiding all that was merely fanciful.

The tale follows a family driven back to a simpler, country life, finding in Eden a place of work, faith, and renewal. Readers get a gentle, moral story for the young, in the manner of nineteenth-century family fiction, where hardship teaches contentment and home becomes a garden again.
5591-the-nuts-a-christmas-story-for-my-c:
Georg Ebers wrote The Nuts as a Christmas story for his children and grandchildren, told by a wounded colonel nursed back to health in the family's house. The colonel may not walk long, and after pottering about, he rests in the comfortable old easy chair known as grandfather's chair. At twilight he lights the last of three pipes the doctor allows him daily, then signs to the children, who gladly obey, loving his stories.

The convalescent must not talk for more than half an hour, so his tales come in measured, cozy installments. Ebers frames the Christmas story as family listening. Readers get a warm holiday tale, told in a chair at twilight, for children gathered close.
5792-the-stories-mother-nature-told-her-:
The Stories Mother Nature Told Her Children gathers nature tales for young listeners, opening with a starfish on a summer journey. The little starfish has five fingers and five eyes, one at the end of each finger, and more tiny feet than can be counted, though without legs he cannot walk very fast. Later chapters visit Coraltown on Roncador Bank and a child called Little Sunshine.

Each story turns a creature or a season into a gentle lesson about growth, kindness, and the living world. Children meet sea, shore, and sky through personified guides who speak in friendly, clear prose. The book suits read-aloud families and early readers who enjoy Victorian nature stories, where wonder and moral teaching walk hand in hand.
5834-bimbi-stories-for-children:
Louise de la Ramee gathers children's stories in Bimbi, opening with The Nurnberg Stove, where August lives in a little town called Hall. Hall, the narrator notes, is a favorite name for towns in Austria and Germany, but this Hall holds August's particular story. Further contents include The Ambitious Rose Tree, Lampblack, The Child of Urbino, and Findelkind, each a fable of art, pride, or kindness.

Readers meet children, artists, and humble folk whose wishes meet magic, loss, and grace in turn. De la Ramee writes with sentiment and moral warmth, favoring beautiful objects and brave hearts over clever twists. The book suits families reading classic children's tales aloud, and readers who enjoy Victorian stories where feeling matters more than realism.
5835-the-story-hour-a-book-for-the-home-:
Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora Smith offer The Story Hour as a book for the home and kindergarten, opening with a Froebel epigraph. Ear and heart, Froebel says, open to the genuine storyteller as flowers open to spring sun and May rain, and the volume that follows puts that belief into practice. An introduction by Wiggin guides parents and teachers in telling stories well.

Here is a classic manual of storytelling, with tales chosen for young children and advice on voice, pacing, and attention. The book treats stories as education through delight, not as lessons in disguise. It suits teachers, parents, and students of early childhood education, and it preserves a Victorian approach to the kindergarten that still charms.
5890-games-for-hallow-e-en:
Mary Blain gathers party games in Games for Hallow-E'en, published in New York in 1912. Hallow-e'en is the last night of October, she explains. It is the eve or vigil of All-Hallow's or All Saints' Day. No holiday in all the year is so informal or so marked by fun for grown-ups and children alike. The games that follow suit that informal spirit, favoring laughter over ceremony.

You get a practical party book of old-fashioned Halloween amusements, from fortune games to active play. Blain writes plainly for hosts and hostesses planning an evening's fun. The book suits families, teachers, and Halloween enthusiasts curious about how the holiday was celebrated a century ago, and it offers games still playable today with little preparation.
5954-religious-reality-a-book-for-men:
A. E. J. Rawlinson writes for thoughtful men who want faith stated plainly, without jargon or convention. The Bishop of Lichfield, in his preface, says such readers do not fear theology, which he calls a reasoned account of religion. They want the Christian faith shown as reasonable, and the problem of evil faced honestly.

Rawlinson draws on wide contact with undergraduates, soldiers, and ordinary civil life. He links belief to real problems of living and to demands that are large, not easy. The book aims to give men a faith they can think with and act on, day by day.
6092-the-fair-haven:
Samuel Butler presents The Fair Haven as a work in defence of the miraculous element in Christ's ministry on earth. It is written by the late John Pickard Owen, with a memoir by William Bickersteth Owen and an introduction by R. A. Streatfeild. It argues against rationalistic impugners and certain orthodox defenders alike.

Chapters treat Strauss and the hallucination theory, the character and conversion of St. Paul, Paul's testimony, ill-judged methods of defence, and the Christ-ideal. Butler's defense, cast as another man's book, tests how miracles can be argued honestly. The volume closes with a conclusion and appendix.
6167-business-hints-for-men-and-women:
A. R. Calhoun offers Business Hints for Men and Women, opening with common sense farming: wealth, land and labor, money, sources of wealth, and the farmer as producer and seller, with business methods essential. Documents to understand follow, with deeds, abstracts of title, and parties to a deed.

Forms of deeds and mortgages, wills, letter writing, and bills, receipts, and accounts complete the manual. Calhoun explains how to make a will, handle administrators and debts, write business letters, and discount bills. The book gives plain, practical guidance for men and women handling money and property.
6467-letters-to-his-children:
Theodore Roosevelt's Letters to His Children, first published in 1919 and edited by Joseph Bucklin Bishop, gathers letters written over more than twenty years. A few went to friends or relatives about the children, but most went to the children themselves, from early childhood to maturity. Whenever Roosevelt was separated from them, in the Spanish War, on a hunting trip, or while they were at school, he sent messages of constant thought and love.

Long before they could read, he sent picture letters, crude drawings of his own fitted to childish imagination. A mid letter from the White House, November 15, 1903, tells Kermit about dogs Hector, Brier, and Sailor Boy. They lie around Seaman's house in excellent health, Sailor Boy and Brier affectionate, Hector kindly but uninterested. Roosevelt writes fatherhood in brief, warm notes, full of animals, games, and cheer.
6492-biographies-of-working-men:
Grant Allen tells the lives of seven men who rose from plain work to wide fame, from a stonemason to a canal boy who became a president. Telford, Stephenson, Gibson, Herschel, Millet, Garfield, and Thomas Edward each get a short, clear life story, drawn from longer books Allen names with care. The focus stays on work done well, day after day.

No life here turns on luck alone; each man learns a trade, keeps at it, and finds a way past want or doubt. Allen writes for readers who like plain facts and steady effort more than praise. Together, these lives form a kind of lesson in how skill, patience, and grit can lift a worker into history.
6595-advice-to-a-mother-on-the-managemen:
Pye Henry Chavasse, a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, writes plain medical advice for mothers on rearing children and on sudden illness and accidents. His preface notes that the book had reached a twelfth edition, with twenty thousand copies sold in under three years, and had been turned into French, German, Polish, and Tamil. It was widely known wherever English was spoken.

Chavasse speaks as a doctor and a friend, with clear rules for food, care, and first aid at the moment of need. His tone is firm but kind, and his advice aims at the home, not the clinic. Advice to a Mother remains a vivid record of how Victorian doctors taught mothers to keep children safe.
6755-canada-for-gentlemen:
James Seton Cockburn's letters from Canada, printed by his father to save the worn manuscript from many hands, form Canada for Gentlemen. The hope was that the letters might aid young emigrants, telling of troubles agencies seldom mention, with lessons often worth more than tales of uniform success. Names of friends are changed to fictions.

Cockburn writes home in a plain, personal voice, on land, work, and the hard first years. His letters feel private, not polished for print. Canada for Gentlemen is a frank, useful emigrant's record, valuable to readers of Canadian settlement history.
677-the-heroes-or-greek-fairy-tales-for-:
Charles Kingsley retold three Greek myths for young readers: the tales of Perseus, Jason and the Golden Fleece, and Theseus. He keeps the gods, monsters, and sea voyages of the old stories, but tells them in a plain, warm voice meant for children at home. Each hero faces a hard task and must show courage, patience, and care for others.

Perseus sets out against the Gorgon, Jason sails with the Argonauts in search of the fleece, and Theseus meets the Minotaur in the maze. Kingsley frames the myths as lessons in how to act well, not just as wonders. The book has lasted as a first door into Greek myth, because it keeps the adventure while making the old tales easy to follow.
681-creatures-that-once-were-men:
Maxim Gorky gathered stories of men who had fallen out of settled life in late Tsarist Russia: tramps, thieves, and drifters living on the edge of towns and ports. They were once workers, soldiers, or clerks, but drink, debt, or bad luck cut them loose. Gorky knew this world at first hand and wrote it without softening its dirt or its hunger.

The tales turn on small choices: a job refused, a coin stolen, a kindness given or withheld. Beneath the rough talk, the men still argue about God, freedom, and what a human life is worth. The book made Gorky's name as the voice of Russia's outcasts, and it still hits hard as a portrait of pride and ruin among people the world had passed by.
7006-bonnie-prince-charlie-a-tale-of-fon:
G A Henty sets Bonnie Prince Charlie at Fontenoy and Culloden, opening on a dull September evening in 1728. Apprentices have barred the shutters, supper stands in the long room over the shop, and Bailie Anderson, his wife, foreman John Gillespie, and two apprentices wait through a long grace. A knock sounds below, twice repeated, before the bailie finishes, and old Elspeth is sent to look through the grille.

These are not times, the bailie warns, to open to the first stranger who knocks. The knock proves the return of a prodigal, and the tale that follows carries a Scots lad from shop to battlefield, through the Jacobite rising to its end at Culloden. Henty writes for boys, with loyalty, daring, and defeat in full color.
7039-the-angel-adjutant-of-twice-born-me:
Minnie Carpenter tells of Staff Captain Kate Lee, the angel adjutant of Twice Born Men, with an introduction by General Bramwell Booth and a foreword by Commander Evangeline Booth. Booth calls the book an intimate and living picture of a woman whose fine character and ceaseless labor held singular charm and amazing fruitfulness. The Salvation Army, he notes, has been happy in its women officers.

Long denied public testimony and the chance to proclaim the Saviour's mission, women in the movement proved their worth. They stood as effective, acceptable, and successful as their brethren, as teachers and rulers in Christ's kingdom on earth. The book follows Kate Lee among the twice born, those remade by faith. It is a portrait of service, courage, and a life spent for others.
7045-marching-men:
Sherwood Anderson's Marching Men, dedicated to American workingmen, opens in Coal Creek, Pennsylvania, at Nance McGregor's bake shop. Uncle Charlie Wheeler stamps on the steps, laughs and whistles softly, and taps the showcase before the Reverend Minot Weeks. A boy fumbles wrapping his loaf, and Uncle Charlie waves at the pretty name Norman McGregor, vowing to change it to a name that will stick.

Norman, he says, is too soft and delicate for the boy. The novel that follows carries Norman McGregor from a coal town boyhood toward a vision of workingmen marching together, disciplined and purposeful. Anderson writes of labor, manhood, and the hunger for order in industrial America, in his plain and searching style.
7208-kathleen:
Christopher Morley's Kathleen opens at Merton College, Oxford, where Kenneth Forbes must finish the first chapter of a serial story before the Scorpions meet at eight. The literary society counts eight members, each to write a chapter in turn. Named on a grotesque undergraduate whim, it made Forbes, first operator for his fertile wit, spend the whole Christmas vacation on his opening.

On the first Sunday of term, while the rest of college dines in hall, Forbes sits at his desk driving his pen in desperation. Morley dedicates the book to the real Kathleen, with apologies, and the joke of a story written by committee gives the novel its light, teasing start. Oxford talk, youth, and invention set the tone.
7488-celtic-tales-told-to-the-children:
Louey Chisholm retells Celtic tales for children, with pictures by Katharine Cameron. She worked from several variants and retellings: Joyce's Old Celtic Romances, Cameron's Reliquae Celticae, O'Grady's pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne, Hyde's Three Sorrows of Story-telling, and Fiona Macleod's Laughter of Peterkin. The book is dedicated to Christopher, and its note explains its sources with unusual care.

The tales open in Erin, where none was greater than the great Concobar, whose fair realm poets sang and whose palace inspired the sweetest songs of Ireland. Heroes, kings, sorrows, and wonders follow, told in simple language for young listeners. Chisholm's collection remains a gentle doorway into Irish and Scottish legend, where the old stories keep their strangeness and their beauty.
7868-a-child-s-story-garden:
A Child's Story Garden, compiled by Elizabeth Heber for kindergarten and primary grades in Indianapolis schools, gathers tales chosen to build literary culture and high ideals through story. Contents include Siegfried the king's son, the song of the pine tree, a Christmas story, and myths of Arachne and Pan.

Other pieces bring the birds of Killingworth, the bell of Atri, the anxious leaf, how dimples came, and a proud little apple blossom. Grace Garfield's pictures accompany thanks to many authors and publishers. Mothers and teachers will find short, moral tales fit for reading aloud.
8152-henrik-ibsen:
Edmund Gosse wrote this biography of Henrik Ibsen, tracing his life from childhood and youth through early influences, Bergen from 1852 to 1857. The satires of 1857 to 1867, and the successive periods of his maturity to his last years. Later chapters assess his personal and intellectual characteristics, and the volume includes portraits, a drawing by Gustav Laerum, a facsimile of Ibsen's handwriting, and a bust from about 1865.

Gosse, who knew Ibsen's work intimately, wrote when analyses of the plays were already numerous in many languages, yet no full English life existed. His biography remains a classic introduction, clear and sympathetic, to the playwright of A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler. For theatre readers, it is the place to start on Ibsen the man.
8523-val-d-arno-ten-lectures-on-the-tusc:
John Ruskin gave these ten lectures on Tuscan art in the Val d'Arno, the valley of the Arno, tracing the art directly antecedent to the Florentine Renaissance. Lecture titles run from Nicholas the Pisan and John the Pisan through Shield and Apron, Parted Per Pale, and Pax Vobiscum. Marble Couchant, Marble Rampant, Franchise, The Tyrrhene Sea, and Fleur de Lys follow, with an appendix and plates.

Ruskin, the great Victorian art critic, argues that Tuscan sculpture and painting grew from faith and craft, not from sudden genius. Readers get Ruskin lecturing at his most detailed, on Pisano sculpture and the Arno valley's shores. The volume suits students of Italian art, and of Ruskin's moral criticism.
8531-tales-and-novels-volume-10-helen:
Maria Edgeworth's Helen fills volume 10 of her Tales and Novels in Ten Volumes, with engravings on steel, in the 1857 edition. The volume gives Helen in two parts, chapter by chapter, as Edgeworth's tale of a young woman's reputation, friendship, and truth-telling, in the society of her day.

Edgeworth, the Anglo-Irish novelist who influenced Scott and Austen's generation, wrote Helen late in her career. It shows her mature art: clear prose, social observation, and a heroine whose honesty is tested. Readers of classic Irish and English fiction get a substantial novel in a handsome collected edition. The volume suits those reading Edgeworth in sequence, or meeting Helen first.
8772-the-learned-women:
Moliere's Learned Women, Les Femmes Savantes, appears here in Charles Heron Wall's English prose translation, with short introductions and notes. First acted on March 11, 1692, with Moliere himself playing Chrysale, the comedy sets an honest bourgeois against his wife Philaminte and daughters Armande and Henriette. Ariste, Belise, the suitor Clitandre, the wit Trissotin, the learned Vadius, and servants Martine, Lepine, and Julien complete the cast, with a notary to settle matters.

Philaminte's academy of would-be learned ladies, and Trissotin's pretentious verse, are the satiric targets, while Henriette's plain wish to marry Clitandre drives the plot. Moliere mocks pedantry, especially when it invades the household and ruins good sense. Wall's prose keeps the comedy accessible to readers without French, and the notes explain its jokes. It remains a sharp, funny classic of the comedy of manners.
908-treatise-on-parents-and-children:
George Bernard Shaw wrote this treatise on the relations of parents and children, with essays on trailing clouds of glory, the child as father to the man, and what a child is. He tackles the sin of Nadab and Abihu, the making of monsters, small and large families, and children as nuisances, child fanciers, and childhood as a state of sin.

Shaw argues, with wit and provocation, that children are persons, not property, and that schools and homes often crush what they claim to nurture. His prose is brisk, combative, and full of paradox. The book is a bracing Shaw manifesto, and it still challenges readers who think children should be seen and not heard.
915-library-work-with-children:
Alice I. Hazeltine writes a practical guide to running a children's library, from book choice and storytelling to rooms, hours, and the training of staff. The book grew from real library work, not theory alone. Hazeltine worked at the New York Public Library, a leader in children's rooms.

Hazeltine argues that a children's room should welcome young readers and help them find books they love. Librarians and teachers will find here the methods of an early professional, still useful for anyone who serves young readers. Her guide, published in the early twentieth century, helped train a new profession.
918-sketches-of-young-gentlemen:
Charles Dickens, as Boz, sketched young gentlemen for the young ladies of Great Britain, Ireland, Wales, and the Channel Islands, to whom the volume is humbly dedicated. He parades the dandy, the bashful youth, the military aspirant, and other types, each with his dress, talk, and airs.

Dickens writes with satirical affection, catching the vanities and hopes of young men on the town. His sketches are short, vivid, and theatrical, full of London shops, balls, and lodgings. The volume pairs with his sketches of young couples, and it charms readers who enjoy social comedy in miniature.
926-ten-thousand-dreams-interpreted-or-w:
Gustavus Hindman Miller offers interpretations for ten thousand dreams, arranged so a reader can look up a symbol and find what it was said to mean. The book promises both scientific and practical readings of dreams. Miller's dream book, first published in the early twentieth century, sold widely.

Miller lists animals, places, people, and events, with short, plain meanings for each, in the style of popular dream books of his day. Modern readers will enjoy it as folklore and curiosity, not as a guide to the mind. Its alphabetical list lets a reader find a dream symbol in seconds, which explains its appeal.
9469-the-call-of-the-twentieth-century-a:
David Starr Jordan, head of Stanford University, gave young men this address in 1903, at the dawn of a new century. He speaks straight to boys on the edge of adult life, and to the men they will become in the 1920s and 1930s. His theme is plain: each youth holds his own future self in his hands. What he does now will shape that man's health, mind, and soul.

Jordan urges clean habits, hard study, honest work, and care for the body and the nerves. He warns that lust and waste can spoil a life before it starts. He also trusts that a trained mind can meet the new age with hope. A reader gets a frank, old-style pep talk, full of moral drive and faith in self-rule.
9475-the-lovels-of-arden:
Mary Elizabeth Braddon, famed for Lady Audley's Secret, wrote The Lovels of Arden as a sensation novel of love and rank. The tale follows Clarissa and her kin through Hale Castle, London rooms, and country houses, as love, pride, and plots collide. Chapters bear titles like Dangerous Ground, Smouldering Fires, and Clarissa's Elopement. Braddon, called queen of the circulating libraries, knew how to hold a reader.

Temptation, a fatal turn, and a fresh start shape the later acts, as Clarissa's fate hangs on choices made in haste. The prose moves fast, with sharp scenes and bold feeling. A reader gets a classic Victorian page-turner, rich in romance, scandal, and the social traps of its age.
9586-personal-poems-complete-volume-iv-o:
Volume four of Whittier's complete works gathers all his personal poems, verse to friends, heroes, and the dead. Early poems lament Charles B. Storrs and S. Oliver Torrey, salute Channing, Kossuth, and Wordsworth, and mark Ichabod and The Lost Occasion. The Cross honors a Quaker jailed for aiding runaways, while later pieces praise Sumner, Garibaldi, and Bryant. Each poem ties a name to a moral hour.

The volume spans Whittier's whole public life, from young reformer to honored elder. His voice stays plain and warm, even when the theme is loss. A reader gets a full gallery of a poet's friendships and causes, and a moving record of nineteenth-century America's conscience.
96-the-monster-men:
A scientist on a Borneo island grows men in vats, and one creation turns on him. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Monster Men opens with a man dissolving a body in nitric acid to hide a crime. Professor Maxon seeks to restore his daughter's lost lover by artificial means.

Number 13, the latest creation, gains a soul and a name through love and suffering. Treachery, a bull whip, and buried treasure drive the middle chapters. Virginia Maxon must judge man against monster. The novel blends horror, romance, and early science fiction. Burroughs asks whether a made man can claim a soul, a question later science fiction kept asking.
9660-the-first-blast-of-the-trumpet-agai:
John Knox wrote The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women in 1558, a fiery tract against rule by women. Edited here by Edward Arber in 1878, the book opens by rebuking godly preachers for their silence on what Knox calls an abominable empire. He names a traitress and bastard queen as its head, and summons prophets' examples. The preface sets the blast's hard tone.

Knox answers objections, admonishes readers, and declaims against female rule as contrary to God and nature. His prose burns with Reformation zeal. A reader gets a notorious Tudor polemic, vital for grasping Knox, Mary Tudor, and the age's fierce debate on queens.
a-child-s-story-garden: Elizabeth Heber compiles a child's story garden for mothers, teachers, and young pupils. Its stories include Siegfried the king's son, the myth of Arachne, the myth of Pan, the bell of Atri, and the anxious leaf. Teachers in Indianapolis schools had used these tales in kindergarten and primary grades. Heber chose them to build literary taste and to suggest high ideals through story.
a-christmas-mystery-the-story-of-three-w: William John Locke tells a Christmas mystery built around three wise men. The story opens with a dead man, an uncanny place, and a cry that it is fey. Its characters sense beating wings and a presence they cannot explain. Locke blends suspense, wonder, and the Christmas theme into a short seasonal tale.
a-little-pilgrim-in-the-unseen: Margaret Oliphant writes a little pilgrim in the unseen, a wistful vision of the next world. The pages sprang from thoughts that arise when the door of the unseen opens suddenly close by. They follow a gentle soul who never knew doubt into the new world. Oliphant offers a glimpse of its glory through a pilgrim's eyes.
a-little-pilgrim-stories-of-the-seen-and:
A Little Pilgrim, published in 1888 by Margaret Oliphant, gathers stories of the seen and the unseen. Oliphant frames the collection with a remarkable opening: a woman describes what it felt like to come to the very point of death after a long illness, and to return. There was no pain in it, she says, only a sense of sinking down through everything that should have held her.

From that threshold, the stories follow a little pilgrim into the world beyond death. Oliphant imagines the unseen country gently, as a place of rest, learning, and reunion rather than terror. The collection became one of her best-loved works, offering Victorian readers a tender vision of what might wait after dying.
a-miscellany-of-men:
G. K. Chesterton sorts his essays by types of men, as his contents page shows. Here are the suffragist, the poet and the cheese, and the man who thinks backwards. Here too are the mad official, the free man, the fool, and the miser. Each essay takes one figure and turns him over in Chesterton's hands until he looks new.

Chesterton writes about voters, priests, journalists, and Scotsmen with jokes that carry arguments about democracy, faith, and common sense. His method is paradox: defend the ordinary man against the experts, and find wisdom in old customs. The pieces first appeared as journalism, and they keep a newspaper's pace and sparkle.
a-mother-s-list-of-books-for-children: Gertrude Weld Arnold compiles a guide to children's reading arranged by the child's age rather than school grade, revising an earlier privately printed list for home use. The book groups fairy tales, rhymes, nature myths, legends, saints stories, and verses for boys and girls, with notes meant to help parents match each title to its reader. Published in Chicago in 1909, it favours titles chosen for home reading over classroom sets.
a-siren:
Thomas Adolphus Trollope's A Siren unfolds in six books around Ravenna at Carnival. Book one begins on Ash Wednesday morning, after the last night of Carnival. The diva has vanished, and the city wakes to scandal. Books two to four go back four months to tell how the trouble began.

Paolina Foscarelli, the siren singer, arrives with an impresario's report and a great love to be taught. The Marchese Lamberto di Castelmare, his uncle, a cardinal, and a contessa circle her voice. Book five, Who Did the Deed?, turns the novel into a murder inquiry, with a post-mortem and a prison visit. The friar's testimony and the trial close the case. Thomas Adolphus, Anthony's elder brother, lived in Italy and wrote its modern life. His Ravenna of priests, attorneys, and opera is drawn from residence, not tourism.
a-study-of-the-textile-art-in-its-relati: William Henry Holmes studies the textile art in its relation to the development of form and ornament, in this paper from the Bureau of Ethnology's sixth annual report. The contents move from form and colour in textile art through relations of form to ornament into a geometric system grown within the art. Relief phenomena, reticulated work, superconstructive and adventitious features, and geometry imposed on adopted elements show how weaving shapes decoration.
advice-to-a-mother-on-the-management-of-:
Pye Henry Chavasse, a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons, addresses mothers directly. His preface boasts of a thirteenth edition. The twelfth, of twenty thousand copies, had sold out in under three years. Translations into French, German, Polish, and Tamil followed. The contents divide the child's life into three parts: infancy, childhood, and boyhood and girlhood.

Each part covers washing, clothing, diet, exercise, sleep, and the nursery, then dentition, vaccination, ailments, and the treatment on the moment of pressing illnesses and accidents. Chavasse writes in a question-and-answer, conversational manner meant to calm a young mother at midnight. The manual was the child-care authority of its age, and it now reads as a full record of Victorian nursery practice.
aladdin-o-brien:
Gouverneur Morris opens Aladdin O'Brien with Poe's Annabel Lee and a forbidden river. Aladdin entices Margaret from Sunday-school to a skiff he barely knows how to row. He whistles through his front teeth and blows grapevine smoke through his nose. To be with him, the narrator says, was a delicious lesson in corruption.

The river nearly drowns them both, and Margaret's scarf becomes the book's token. Aladdin grows into a charming, reckless young man of politics and newspapers. Washington draws the grown pair into its intrigues, where his luck and nerve keep rescuing him. Morris writes a picaresque of American charm: a boy with a lamp-like gift for escaping scrapes. Margaret's steady love measures the man against the child. The novel's lightness is deliberate, a fairy tale of the republic's capital.
alec-forbes-of-howglen: George MacDonald tells the story of Alec Forbes of Howglen, a Scottish lad whose growth is shaped by school, friendship, and faith. The novel follows Alec from boyhood into manhood among the folk of a northern parish, with MacDonald's blend of realism and spiritual reflection. It remains one of the author's best-loved Scottish novels, warm in its portrait of community life.
arnim-die-majoratsherren:
Property passed rigidly from heir to heir becomes a curse in Arnim's Die Majoratsherren, given here in German. The Lords of the Entailed Estate turns a dry legal institution, the entail, into the engine of a dark family drama. Inheritance and family pride grind the characters between them like millstones.

Arnim blends realism with the uncanny in his characteristic way, letting old houses and older papers gather menace. Portraits, wills, and decaying rooms carry the family's buried guilt. The novella asks what wealth does to love when law forbids it to move freely. German Romanticism rarely aimed its strangeness at so concrete a target. The result reads like a ghost story with a lawyer in it.
arnim-isabella-von-agypten:
Gypsy wanderers and settled townsfolk collide in Achim von Arnim's novella Isabella von Aegypten, presented in German. Isabella, a young gypsy leader, crosses into a richly imagined past of emperors and camps. Love strains against the boundary between her people and the settled world that fears them.

Arnim helped collect the folk songs of Des Knaben Wunderhorn, and that folk learning saturates his fiction. Antiquarian detail and Romantic invention braid together here into something strange and beautiful. The novella asks who belongs and who must wander, questions its century pressed hard. Its heroine carries both pride and sorrow in equal measure. Few German tales of the period feel so lush and so sad at once.
b09-hutten-obscure-men:
Epistolae Obscurorum Virorum, Letters of Obscure Men, appeared in Latin in 1515 as a joke with teeth. Crotus Rubeanus began the mock letters, and Ulrich von Hutten wrote much of the crushing second part of 1517. The letters pretend to come from dim scholastic monks writing to a master at Cologne.

In bad Latin and worse logic, the fake monks expose their own folly on every page. The satire struck the Cologne scholars who had hounded the humanist Reuchlin and his Hebrew studies. Learned Europe laughed, and the old school of theology never shook off the scorn. The work stands as the great humanist satire on the eve of the Reformation.
bashful-fifteen:
L. T. Meade published this school story with Cassell of New York in 1892. Meade, the most prolific girls' writer of her day, opens with curiosity and a new girl, then crowns a queen of the school. Ribbons and roses, the breaking in of a wild colt, and captivity set the early terms: a boarding school where reputations are made and unmade by small acts.

Irish Bridget, homesick at fifteen, frets over a posted letter and the postal order inside it, begging Janet not to mock the people she loves — Pat and Norah at home. Janet raises her delicate brows in well-acted astonishment. Meade writes the schoolgirl world in earnest: loyalty, snobbery, and kindness fought out in whispers, with bashfulness itself as the heroine's cross and cure.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-07-great:
John Lord gives the seventh Beacon Lights volume to great women, opening with Héloïse under the single heading Love. Her contents read as a romance outline. Extraordinary gifts, Abélard's genius and early triumphs, and mad infatuation lead to scandal. A secret marriage, its discovery, and separate convents close the tale. Lord retells the letters and her unconquered love without flinching.

Queens, saints, and court ladies follow in the same biographical manner. One duchess, whose story these pages tell, keeps her offices and palace apartments after favour cools. She is still addressed as a great person while envy gathers round her. Lord judges his heroines by character and influence, in the gallant, sermonising tone of the Victorian lecture hall, where a woman's life proved a civilisation's tone.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-09-europ:
John Lord's ninth Beacon Lights volume turns to the statesmen of Europe. Mirabeau opens it as the great voice of the French Revolution. The contents follow the fall of the old order step by step. Ruined finances, the Assembly of Notables, and the States-General come first. Then the Third Estate seizes power, the Bastille falls, and Mirabeau shows a strange wish to save the crown. Talleyrand and the seizure of Church lands close his tale.

Lord dwells on Talleyrand in a later talk. Cast out of the Church for his lack of faith, the bishop turned diplomat cared little for the ban. In London he charmed the highest circles with the shine of his talk and the bite of his wit. The Jacobins mistrusted him on his return, and he fled to England. Lord judges each statesman as an actor in a vast drama of revolt.
behind-the-arras-a-book-of-the-unseen:
Bliss Carman published this book of poems with Lamson, Wolffe of Boston in 1895, with designs by T. B. Meteyard. Its title names the theme: the unseen behind the arras of daily life. Contents move through The Moondial, The Face in the Stream, The Cruise of the Galleon, The Red Wolf, The Lodger, The Night Express, and Exit Anima, the soul's departure.

The lyrics keep one foot in the field and one in the spirit world. Apple blossom, orioles, and poppies do the seeing in one spring poem. Field-wise creatures — crickets and swallows — are called Brahmins of the universal grass, holier than the tiger-lilies they pierce past. Carman, Canada's lyric laureate of the nineties, writes nature as a veil: beautiful in itself, and always about to lift on something behind it.
bimbi-stories-for-children:
Bimbi, stories for children by Ouida, the pen name of Louise de la Ramee, gathers five tales written with a painter's eye for place. The longest and best known, The Nurnberg Stove, opens in Hall, a little town in Austria's Upper Inn valley. Ouida describes its green meadows, glacier fed river, latticed shop panes, and grand Gothic church before she ever introduces August, the boy who knows no other world.

August's treasure is a great porcelain stove, and the tale follows his fight to keep it when hard times press his family. Around it the collection sets The Ambitious Rose Tree, Lampblack, The Child of Urbino, and Findelkind, stories of plants, artists, and lost children across Italy and Germany. Ouida wrote for adults chiefly, but her children's tales keep her signature style: rich scenery, tender feeling, and beauty treated as a serious matter.
biographies-of-working-men:
Grant Allen's Biographies of Working Men, published in 1884, tells seven lives of men who rose from labour. Thomas Telford, the stonemason who became a great engineer, opens the volume. Allen begins with Telford's birth in a shepherd's cottage in Eskdale in 1757. His widowed mother raised him on her own ten fingers.

George Stephenson the engine-man and John Gibson the sculptor follow. William Herschel, once a bandsman, reached the stars as an astronomer. Jean François Millet the painter and James Garfield the canal boy turned president carry the theme abroad. Thomas Edward, a shoemaker naturalist, closes the set. Allen drew on earlier lives by Samuel Smiles and others. The book preaches energy and perseverance to working readers, Victorian self-help at its most earnest.
bonnie-prince-charlie-a-tale-of-fontenoy:
G. A. Henty's Bonnie Prince Charlie tells the Jacobite rising through the battles of Fontenoy and Culloden. The tale opens on a dull September evening in 1728, when Bailie Anderson's household sits down to supper above the shop, apprentices eyeing the food while grace drags on.

A knock at the door breaks the meal, and the old servant must peer through the grille before opening, since these are not times to admit a stranger lightly. From that domestic opening Henty builds toward the Young Pretender's cause, Highland campaigns and the disaster of Culloden. Young readers of historical adventure will find Henty's usual blend of domestic detail and battlefield action.
books-and-bookmen:
Andrew Lang's Books and Bookmen, printed by Longmans in 1887, opens with a verse dedication asking whether ladies can care for gossip of texts and bindings old. Chapters follow on Elzevir editions, curiosities of parish registers, the Rowfant library, Japanese bogie-books, and ghosts in the library. Literary forgeries and bibliomania in France get long treatments.

Lang retells how the Shakespeare Society was taken in by young William Henry Ireland's sham documents, with Boswell kneeling to kiss the relics. A bookman's purgatory and lady book-lovers round out the miscellany. The volume defined the amiable amateur tradition in English book collecting: learned, funny, and more interested in readers than in prices.
britannica-1911-aalen: Aalen is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry sets the town in Württemberg, on the Kocher river at the foot of the Swabian Alps, east of Stuttgart, with rails to Ulm and Cannstatt. Its people are counted at ten thousand. Woollen and linen goods, ribbon looms, and tanneries employ the town, with large iron works near by. A statue of the poet Christian Schubart is noted. Aalen held free imperial city rank from 1360 until Württemberg took it in 1802.
britannica-1911-abdomen:
Abdomen receives a medical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word, from Latin abdere, to hide, or from adeps, fat, names the belly region holding most digestive organs. Anatomy points onward to other articles; surgery takes the space here.

Exploratory laparotomy, opening the belly to find the fault by finger and hand, leads the argument. Holmes's line rules the case: you cannot tell a table's wood without lifting the cloth. Delay, the entry charges, once spoiled case after case as drug trials failed in medical wards. Prompt transfer to surgeons changed results day by day. Public trust grew as surgeons proved no reckless operators. Each organ's surgery sits with its anatomy elsewhere in the set, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-abraham-men: Abraham-men is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the name as a nickname for vagrants who infested Tudor England. The phrase stands as old as 1561. Such beggars pretended to be patients discharged from the Abraham ward at Bedlam. True discharged Bedlamites could roam and beg, wearing a badge. Gross abuse of that humane privilege bred the slang phrase to sham Abraham, the entry closes, fixing a bit of Tudor street language and the fraud that coined it.
britannica-1911-adam-of-bremen:
Adam of Bremen was a historian and geographer. He was probably born in Upper Saxony before 1045. Archbishop Adalbert likely invited him to Bremen. He arrived there about 1067. By 1069 he was a cathedral canon. He also mastered the cathedral school. A visit took him to Denmark's king Sweyn. After Adalbert died, Adam began his history. He finished the Historia about 1075.

Scope makes the work a primary authority. It covers the Hamburg-Bremen diocese fully. All North German and Baltic lands enter it. Scandinavian colonies appear as far as America. Vinland receives its earliest mention here. Russia, Kiev, and the Wends all feature. Trade at Jumne, Birka, and Novgorod is described. Adam gathered records and oral reports alike.
britannica-1911-aiken:
Aiken, a city in South Carolina, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county-seat of Aiken county, seventeen miles east-north-east of Augusta, Georgia. Its population grew from 2,362 in 1890 to 3,911 in 1910. Railways and an electric line to Augusta serve the city, set about five hundred feet above sea level.

Fashionable winter visitors, chiefly Northerners, made Aiken's name. It sits in the state's famous sand-hill and pine-forest region, where dry, even temperatures and pine-scented air drew people seeking health and pleasure. The climate was said to help those with lung disease especially. Fine hotels, club houses, and cottages served the season, with golf, fox-hunting, polo, tennis, and shooting for sport. Cotton mills, lumber mills, and schools, including the Schofield Normal and Industrial School, round out the entry's picture.
britannica-1911-alhazen:
A boast about the Nile nearly wrecked Alhazen, the Arabian scholar of the eleventh century named Abu Ali Al-Hasan Ibn Alhasan. Born at Basra, he died at Cairo in 1038. He is not the Alhazen of a century before, who turned Ptolemy's Almagest into Arabic. This one had bragged he could build a machine to tame the floods, and the caliph Hakim called him to Egypt to do it.

The plan could not work, and fear of the caliph's wrath drove him to play the madman until Hakim died in 1021. His true field was optics, where no great finder had come since Ptolemy. Alhazen told why sun and moon look bigger near the skyline. He taught that sight does not come from rays shot from the eye. He also cracked the mirror puzzle: where on a curved mirror a ray from one point bounces to reach a second point.
britannica-1911-alien:
Who counts as a British subject, and who stays an alien? British law of the constitution takes up that question under a word drawn from the Latin alienus. An alien lacks the standing of a subject; in plain terms, a foreigner who forms ties with a state yet still owes loyalty to a ruler abroad. Much of the entry sorts out who falls on each side.

Birth inside British lands makes a subject, English law holds. A noted case in James I's reign ruled that Scots born before the crowns joined were aliens in England. Those born later were subjects, since loyalty runs to the king's own person. A child born overseas could claim the same standing through a British father or grandfather. The Naturalization Act of 1870 then swept away many bars, letting aliens own land and goods and pass them on as subjects could.
britannica-1911-almaden:
Mercury made Almadén famous. The Spanish town, also called Almadén del Azogue, sits in rough country in Ciudad Real province, west-south-west of its capital, and counted 7,375 people in 1900. Rome knew it as Sisapon, and Romans and Moors alike dug its mines.

The ore grows richer as shafts sink, and for ages the mines matched Idria's in South Austria as the world's most valued. That rank held until California's New Almaden deposits grew fast in the 1850s. Convict labour long did the digging, the underground air being foul; miners won freedom from military service after two years. Lead and sulphur also come from the ground nearby.
britannica-1911-bailen:
