Bailén is a town of southern Spain in the province of Jaén, twenty-one miles north of Jaén city, with 7,420 people in 1900. It is probably the ancient Baecula, where Scipio the elder twice beat the Carthaginians, in 209 and 206 B.C.

Near it, too, was fought the great battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Castile's Alphonso VIII crushed the Moors there. The chroniclers claimed 200,000 Moorish dead against twenty-five Christians. The entry dismisses that estimate as absurd. The town's lasting fame is the capitulation of Bailén in July 1808. The French general Dupont surrendered 17,000 men to the Spaniards there. Hard fighting ran for several days before it. It was the first severe blow France suffered in the Peninsular War.
britannica-1911-baillet-adrien:
Baillet, Adrien (1649-1706), was a French scholar and critic born at Neuville near Beauvais in Picardy, whose poor parents could afford only the village school. Friars at a nearby convent taught him Latin and brought him to the bishop of Beauvais's notice, winning him a full education at the seminary.

Ordained in 1676, Baillet became librarian in 1680 to Lamoignon, the Paris parlement's advocate-general, and catalogued that library in thirty-five handwritten volumes. The rest of his life was unbroken labour, five hours a day allowed for rest. His Judgments of the Learned on authors' chief works is his most celebrated book; his Life of Descartes mines sound sources, and his Lives of the Saints, critical on miracles, caused scandal. Praising Jansenists in the Judgments earned him the Jesuits' hatred.
britannica-1911-barmen:
Barmen is a town of Germany, in the Prussian Rhine province, in the district of Düsseldorf. Its growth was rapid: 19,030 people in 1816, 116,144 in 1890, and 156,148 in 1905. It lies just east of Elberfeld, with which it virtually forms one town, and stretches some four miles along the narrow valley of the river Wupper.

Twenty bridges cross the Wupper inside the town, and a suspended trolley line runs above the riverbed the whole length to Elberfeld. High wooded hills surround the streets. The 1911 Britannica entry lists nine Evangelical and two Roman Catholic churches, and a modern town hall. It also lists a Hall of Fame with statues of two emperors, a theatre, a picture gallery, and an ethnographical museum.
britannica-1911-batten:
Batten is a word with two distinct lives, set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. As a noun it is a form of baton, used in joinery for a board not more than seven inches broad or three thick. Such boards strengthen laths and other woodwork. On ship, a batten is a strip nailed to a mast to stop rubbing, or fixed over a tarpaulin on a hatchway to keep water out.

As a verb, batten has a different root. It is found in words of several Teutonic tongues meaning profit or gain, and it is kin to the English better and boot. To batten is to improve in condition, above all in the case of animals by feeding. From that sense it also means to feed greedily. In a figure, it means to thrive at another's cost.
britannica-1911-bautzen:
Bautzen, in Wendish Budissin, is a town of Saxony, Germany, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on a height above the right bank of the Spree, thirty-two miles east-north-east of Dresden, and is the capital of Saxon Upper Lusatia. Its people grew from 21,515 in 1890 to 29,412 in 1905. Walls ring the town, and old ramparts beyond them have been turned into walks. The cathedral of St Peter, from the 1400s, is shared: Protestants and Catholics both use it, split by an iron screen.

Scars and trade share the entry. The town was already standing when Henry the Fowler conquered Lusatia in 928, and it grew rich in part on pilgrims to a relic of St Peter. It suffered in the Hussite wars and worse in the Thirty Years' War. A battle of 1813 bears its name. Its trades run from woollens to leather, paper, and cigars.
britannica-1911-ben:
Ben, from an Old English word meaning “within,” is the inner room in the Scots phrase “a but and a ben.” Such a house has only one outer door, so the inner room is reached through the outer one. The outer room is the but, from a word meaning “without.”

Put together, “a but and a ben” first meant a living room and a sleeping room under one roof. From there the phrase widened to mean the whole dwelling, a cottage as such. The entry is a short word note, tracing how two plain room names grew into a fixed Scots expression for a small home.
britannica-1911-berchtesgaden:
Berchtesgaden is a town of Germany set high on the south-eastern edge of Bavaria, 1,700 feet above the sea. It lies on the southern slope of the Untersberg, six miles from Reichenhall by rail, and counted 10,046 people in 1900. Beauty of setting is its first claim on the visitor.

Rock-salt mines, worked as early as 1174, made the town’s living for centuries. Toys and small goods of wood, horn and ivory are its other famous products. Three old churches stand in the town, the early Gothic abbey church with its Romanesque cloister chief among them. The district was once its own church principality, founded in 1100 and secularised in 1803.
britannica-1911-bergen:
Bergen is a city and seaport of Norway, a county by itself on the west coast at about the latitude of the Shetlands. It counted 72,179 people in 1900. The town lies at the head of the broad Byfjord, partly on the rocky Nordnaes point between the Vaagen harbour and the Puddefjord.

Rain is Bergen’s weather mark: seventy-four inches a year on average, feeding lush growth on the steep hills. Timber ships and fishing smacks crowd the harbour, and Strandgaden, the main street, runs along it to the market square. King Olaf Kyrre founded the town, then called Björgvin, about 1070–1075. It is the birthplace of Holberg, Welhaven, the painter Dahl and Ole Bull, and now ranks first among Norwegian ship-owning ports.
britannica-1911-bertrand-henri-gratien:
Henri Gratien Bertrand (1773–1844), a French general, was born at Châteauroux. He had just finished his studies when the Revolution broke out. He joined the army as a volunteer. In Egypt Napoleon made him colonel in 1798, then brigadier-general. After Austerlitz he became Napoleon's aide-de-camp. From then on his life stayed bound to the emperor's. Napoleon trusted him fully and made him grand marshal of the court in 1813.

The 1911 Britannica entry marks his key services in brief. He directed the bridge building for the Danube crossing at Wagram in 1809. His action after Leipzig in 1813 saved the army from full destruction. He followed Napoleon to Elba, then to Waterloo, then to St Helena. In 1840 he was chosen to bring Napoleon's remains back to France. His fidelity made his name popular in France.
britannica-1911-bingen:
Bingen is a German town in the grand-duchy of Hesse-Darmstadt, 15 miles north-west of Mainz. It stands on the left bank of the Rhine, facing Rüdesheim. The Nahe stream joins the Rhine at the town. A stone bridge of Roman origin crosses the Nahe near its mouth. The 1905 population was 9,950. Above the town stands the ruined castle of Klopp, on a fortress site of Drusus.

Higher still sits the chapel of St Roch, rebuilt in 1895 after a fire. Thousands of pilgrims gather there each August, the 1911 Britannica entry says. The town trades in wine, grain, and cattle. New quays handle a transit trade in coal and iron. Downstream lies the Bingerloch whirlpool. On a mid-stream rock rises the Mäuseturm, where legend says mice ate Bishop Hatto in 969.
britannica-1911-bitumen:
Bitumen was the Roman name for the natural hydrocarbons, since classical Latin had no word petroleum. In its widest sense it covers the whole range of those substances. Natural gas stands at the light end of the family. Liquid petroleum grades follow, and solid asphalt closes the scale. Alberta-like solids such as albertite, gilsonite, elaterite, and ozokerite all fall under the name. The middle stuff, between asphalt and thin crude, is often called maltha.

The 1911 Britannica article groups the trade kinds under gas, petroleum, and asphalt. It sends readers to those heads for full treatment of each. Bible references to slime in Genesis are read as bitumen in the Vulgate. Herodotus is quoted on its early uses as well. The closing theory holds that solid kinds form as liquid petroleum escapes upward. Air and evaporation then thicken it in fissures and surface strata. Boverton Redwood signs the survey.
britannica-1911-blaikie-william-garden:
William Garden Blaikie (1820–1899) was a Scottish Free Church minister, editor, and social reformer. Born in Aberdeen, he studied at Marischal College and then under Thomas Chalmers at Edinburgh. He was among the 474 ministers who signed the deed of demission and left their livings at the Disruption.

He served the Free Church at Pilrig, between Edinburgh and Leith, from 1844 to 1868, and pushed better housing for working people. His book Better Days for Working People sold 60,000 copies, and model buildings rose at Pilrig through his work. He edited church magazines for years, raised £14,000 for the Waldensian churches, and wrote lives of Livingstone and Chalmers.
britannica-1911-blaubeuren:
Blaubeuren is a small town in Württemberg, Germany, 12 miles west of Ulm and joined to it by rail. It held 3114 people in 1900. The town sits 1600 feet up in a deep, wild valley of the Swabian Alps, partly ringed by old walls, and has two hospitals.

Its abbey church is the chief sight. Built in late Gothic style between 1465 and 1496, the choir holds fine carved stalls of the 1400s and a high altar with a triptych of 1496. Only the choir is still used for Protestant worship, while the nave serves as a school hall. The Benedictine abbey itself was founded in 1095 and, after the Reformation, became a school and then a Protestant training college for clergy.
britannica-1911-boieldieu-francois-adrie:
François Adrien Boieldieu (1775–1834) was a French composer of comic opera, famed for La Dame blanche. Born at Rouen, a cathedral organist's harsh pupil, he had two operas staged in his home city in 1795 and left for Paris the same year. Grand opera ruled there, and he lived at first by playing piano.

Work as accompanist to the singer Garat spread his songs through Paris drawing rooms, and stage success followed, with Le Calife de Bagdad in 1800. Fleeing a troubled marriage, he spent years at St Petersburg writing operas for the emperor. Back home he gave Jean de Paris in 1812, took a Conservatoire chair in 1817, and crowned his career with La Dame blanche in 1825, its libretto drawn in part from Scott.
britannica-1911-botzen:
Botzen, also Bozen or Bolzano, is a town in Austrian Tirol where the Talfer meets the Eisak, a little above its junction with the Adige. It stands 869 feet up on the Brenner railway, 58 miles south of the pass and 35 miles north of Trent. In 1900 it held 13,632 people, mainly German-speaking Catholics, though the Italian share was growing.

The entry calls it a Teutonic town in Italian surroundings and the busiest trading town of German Tirol. Its crossroads site, where the Brenner route from Germany meets the Swiss road down the upper Adige, brought a great transit trade and four large fairs a year. Its Gothic parish church of the 1300s and 1400s is praised, and a statue of 1889 honours the singer Walther von der Vogelweide, said to have been born nearby. Local wine is noted as early as the 600s.
britannica-1911-brixen:
Brixen, in Italian Bressanone, is a small city in the Austrian province of Tirol and chief town of its administrative district, with 5767 people in 1900. It sits in the Eisack valley where the Rienz joins that stream, on the Brenner railway 34 miles south-east of the pass and 24 miles north-east of Botzen.

Church rule gives the city its look: it is still a bishop's see, with an 18th-century cathedral, episcopal palace and seminary, twelve churches and five monasteries. The see was founded late in the 8th century at Saben above Klausen and moved to Brixen in 992. In 1027 the emperor Conrad II gave its bishops wide temporal powers, lost only to Austria in 1803. Walls rose in 1030, the first outbreak of the great peasants' revolt flared here in 1525, and the fortress of Franzensfeste guards the Brenner road nearby.
britannica-1911-brocken:
Brocken is a mountain of Germany in Prussian Saxony, the highest point of the Harz range at 3733 feet. A huge, bare, granite-strewn dome, it is the greatest height in north Germany and commands sweeping views in every direction. On clear days Magdeburg and the Elbe, the towers of Leipzig and the Thuringian forest can all be picked out from the top.

A mountain railway of 12 miles climbs from Dreiannen-Hohne, and two carriage roads come up from the Bodetal and Ilsenburg. Legend clings to the peak: long after Christianity reached the region it stayed a place of heathen worship. On Walpurgis night, the first of May, rites held there fed the belief that the devil and witches held their orgies on the summit. Country folk still hold it haunted that night, and Goethe fixed the fame in the Brocken scene of Faust.
britannica-1911-bryant-william-cullen:
William Cullen Bryant (1794–1878) was an American poet and journalist. This 1911 Britannica biography gives his life at length. He was born at Cummington, Massachusetts, on 3 November 1794. His father was a country physician. Bryant had little formal schooling. He entered Williams College at sixteen. He left without a degree when family money ran short.

The article follows his twin careers in verse and journalism. His Poems appeared in 1821 and again in 1832. Later volumes include The Fountain and Thirty Poems. He also made blank-verse translations of Homer. His Iliad came out in 1870 and his Odyssey in 1871. The Poetical Works followed in 1876. The entry ranks him among the master poets of America. It calls him, in history, the first of them. His verse praises the divine mind seen in earth and sky.
britannica-1911-calf-the-golden:
The golden calf was an image made by the Israelites in the desert. This 1911 Britannica article examines the story and its background. Moses had climbed the Mount of Yahweh to receive the Law. His long absence alarmed the people below. They clamoured for gods to lead them on. Aaron took their jewellery and made a molten calf from it. A festival was held around it.

Moses came down and stayed the full wrath of Yahweh. Still, 3000 men fell to the Levites' swords. The article then asks where calf worship came from. It rules out the Egyptian Apis, which was a living bull. Image worship was common among the Canaanites, it notes. Early Israel itself used images in worship without shame. Later writers, shaped by the Deuteronomic reform, condemned all such cults. The article notes that Elijah and Elisha never attacked the calf shrines.
britannica-1911-carmarthen:
Carmarthen is a town of Wales, county town of Carmarthenshire. Its Welsh name is Caerfyrddin. It stands on the right bank of the river Towy. The river is tidal and navigable for small craft there. Its population in 1901 was 10,025. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town and its role. Railways of two companies serve Carmarthen from several directions.

Works in the town make woollens and ropes. Tanneries also operate in Carmarthen. Its chief importance is as a market town, though. It serves a large and fertile district around it. The Saturday market is well attended each week. It shows scenes of modern Welsh agricultural life. The town holds the gaol for three Welsh counties. The lunatic asylum for the same three counties stands there too. The article then gives Carmarthen's long history as a borough.
britannica-1911-cherchen:
Cherchen is a town of East Turkestan at the north foot of the Altyn-tagh, a range of the Kuen-lun, at 4,100 feet. The town spreads along channels drawn from the left side of the Cherchen-darya river. Its people numbered about 2,000 in 1900. The entry gives its place as 85 degrees 35 minutes east, on a river that starts in the Arka-tagh range.

Most of the entry follows the Cherchen-darya itself. The river flows north to the desert below Cherchen, then turns north-east through a wide bed lined with dense reeds. It ends by joining the Tarim at the lake of Kara-buran, after a course put at 500 to 600 miles. Falls, a broad delta, winter freezing and a basin of 6,000 to 7,000 square miles are all noted.
britannica-1911-churching-of-women:
Churching of Women is the Christian ceremony of thanksgiving by mothers shortly after the birth of their children. It no doubt began in the Mosaic rule on purification in Leviticus, the entry says. In ancient times the ceremony was usual but not binding in England, while in the Greek and Roman Catholic Churches today it is imperative. No ancient form of service survives, and the English prayer book form dates only from the middle ages.

Custom set the fortieth day after confinement as the usual date, matching the presentment of Mary and the child Jesus at the Temple. A woman was thought unlucky if she left home before being churched, and services were sometimes said in private houses. Special churching seats, veils and churching cloths appear in parish records. Lighted tapers, offerings and rules on where the woman should kneel fill the detail of custom.
britannica-1911-churchwarden:
Churchwarden, in England, is the guardian or keeper of a church and the representative of the body of the parish. The name comes from the original duty of custody of the fabric and furniture of the church, fixed on parishioners in the 14th century. Churchwardens are always lay persons, yet in law they act as quasi-corporations, able to hold goods and bring actions for them. Resident householders are chiefly eligible, with some classes exempt or barred.

Choice is set by the 89th canon, by joint consent of minister and parishioners where possible, and otherwise one each. Local customs vary widely, from township choices in the north to vestry or manor appointments. Appointment usually falls in Easter week, after which each warden swears to execute the office faithfully. Duties cover service needs, offertory, order, seating, goods, repair of church and churchyard and presentment of offences.
britannica-1911-cohen: Cohen is a Jewish family name. It comes from the Hebrew word for priest. The name points to descent from the ancient Hebrew priests. Many families that claim such descent do not bear the name, though. Other forms of the name are Cohn, Cowen and Kahn. The entry is very short and gives no more than that core claim and those variant forms. It closes with a reference to the Jewish Encyclopedia for fuller treatment.
britannica-1911-covent-garden:
Covent Garden was once an open space north of the Strand in London. It now holds the chief flower, fruit and vegetable market of the capital. The ground was at first the convent garden of the abbey of Saint Peter at Westminster. That old use gave the place its name. No trace of the garden itself stays in the entry's tale.

In the first half of the 1600s Inigo Jones laid the site out as a square. A piazza ran along two of its sides. By 1656 the square was turning into a market for the same goods sold there now. A theatre has stood on the site since 1733. Covent Garden Theatre, built in 1858, is the chief seat of grand opera in London. Fire took its earlier houses in 1809 and in 1856. The entry is short and keeps to ground, square, market and stage.
britannica-1911-crossen:
The hosted text opens partway through its account of Crossen, in the middle of a sentence about the town's churches. What survives lists a modern school, a technical school for vine and fruit growing, and a dairy school. Manufactories of copper and brass ware and of cloth are named. The country round the town lives by fruit and grape growing. A brisk shipping trade, mainly in wine, fruit, and fish, is also recorded.

The closing history says Crossen was founded in 1005 and mattered in the middle ages as a crossing place on the Oder. It gained civic rights in 1232. For a time it was capital of a Silesian duchy. On the death of Barbara of Brandenburg, widow of the last duke, it passed to Brandenburg in 1482. In May 1886 a whirlwind devastated the town.
britannica-1911-cullen:
Cullen is a royal, municipal, and police burgh of Banffshire in Scotland, with 1,936 people in 1901. It stands on Cullen Bay, west of Banff and north-west of Aberdeen by rail. The Deskford Burn cuts it into Seatown, the older part, and Newtown, dating only from 1822. St Mary's church, a cross-shaped building, was founded by Robert Bruce, whose second wife died at Cullen. Rope and sail making, boat-building, brewing, and fishing employ the town.

The harbour, built between 1817 and 1834, counts among the best on that coast though wholly artificial. Cullen House, a seat of the earl of Seafield, stands a mile south and holds fine works of art. Ruins of Findlater Castle crown the cliffs two miles east. The entry closes with Portsoy, a thriving fishing town five miles east. Portsoy adds fish-curing, a distillery, and quarries of pink granite and marble to the district's trades.
britannica-1911-culloden:
Culloden is a bleak tract of moorland in Inverness-shire, Scotland, part of the north-east of Drummossie Muir. It lies about six miles east of Inverness by road. Its fame is the battle of 16 April 1746, by which the fate of the house of Stuart was decided. Highlanders more often call it the battle of Drummossie. About 1,000 clansmen lie in its trenches. Memorial stones of 1881 name the clans at the head of each trench.

A cairn twenty feet high marks the chief scene of the fight. The Cumberland Stone, a huge boulder, shows where the English commander stood. A mile north stands Culloden House, once the seat of Duncan Forbes of the Court of Session. The Culloden Papers, documents from 1625 to 1748, were found there in 1812 and published in 1815. South of the field, the plain of Clava holds stone circles, cairns, and other remains from before history.
britannica-1911-darien:
Darien is a district covering the eastern part of the isthmus that joins Central and South America, lying mainly within Panama. Rodrigo Bastidas reconnoitred it in the first year of the sixteenth century, and Santa Maria la Antigua was its first settlement. In 1513 Balboa stood on a peak in Darien and saw the Pacific below him, and the narrow neck long seemed to promise a passage between the two oceans.

The first serious trade attempt was Scotland's. A company chartered in 1695, advised by William Paterson, planted a colony called New Caledonia in 1698 with 1200 settlers. Want, sickness and anarchy emptied it within a year, and a second expedition ended besieged by Spaniards and forced to capitulate. Only a handful of the settlers ever reached home.
britannica-1911-emden:
Emden is a maritime town of Germany in the Prussian province of Hanover, near the mouth of the Ems, 49 miles north-west from Oldenburg by rail. Its population was 20,754 in 1905. The Ems once flowed beneath its walls but is now two miles away, joined to the town by a broad, deep canal. That canal splits into an inner dock harbour and an outer free port.

Canals cross the town and link it with most towns of East Friesland, whose trading capital it is. The entry notes its gabled medieval houses, giving it the look of an old Dutch rather than a German town. The Great Church, a large Gothic building finished in 1455, holds the tomb of Enno II, count of East Friesland. Emden trades in farm produce, live-stock, timber, coal, tea, and wine, and its deep-sea fishing fleet numbered 67 vessels in 1902.
britannica-1911-emmendingen:
Emmendingen is a town of Germany in the grand-duchy of Baden, close to the Black Forest, on the river Elz and the main railway from Mannheim to Constance. Its population is given as 6200. The town has a Protestant church with a fine spire and a Roman Catholic church. It also has a handsome town-hall and an old castle, now a hospital, once the home of the counts of Hochberg.

Spinning mills and tanneries work in Emmendingen, and its factories make photographic instruments, paper, machinery, and cigars. A large trade in timber and cattle is also carried on. The entry recalls Johann Georg Schlosser, husband of Goethe's sister Cornelia, who served here as bailiff for some years. Emmendingen was once the seat of the counts of Hochberg, a side branch of the margraves of Baden. It gained market rights in 1418 and town status, with walls, in 1590.
britannica-1911-ettlingen:
Ettlingen is a German town in Baden on the Alb, on the Mannheim–Basel railway south of Karlsruhe. Its 1905 population was 8,040. Old walls and ditches still ring it, giving a medieval, picturesque air. Buildings include an old princely residence with grounds, one Evangelical and two Roman Catholic churches, and a former monastery. Roman remains survive, notably a Neptune sculpture built into the town-hall wall. Paper-making, spinning, weaving and machine building lead its trades.

Wine and fruit growing also support a good deal of trade. The first notice of Ettlingen dates from the 8th century. It became a town in 1227, when Frederick II gave it to the margrave of Baden. The French pillaged it in 1689. Near the town, Moreau beat the archduke Charles on 9 and 10 July 1796. The entry is a compact gazetteer notice of the town's fabric and past.
britannica-1911-flamen:
A flamen was a Roman sacrificial priest. His name is taken from flare, to blow up the altar fire. Flamens served under the pontifex maximus, each consecrated to one god. The highest were the flamen Dialis, Martialis and Quirinalis, always chosen from the patricians. Their founding is credited to Numa. When the number rose from three to fifteen, those three were called maiores. The other twelve, lesser priests of lesser gods, were called minores and drawn from the plebs.

Flamens held office for life, yet neglect or an ill omen could force resignation. Their dress included the apex, a white conical cap, the laena mantle and a laurel wreath. The entry details the gear of the flamen Dialis, priest of Jupiter. It lists his white cap with olive branch and woollen thread, his heavy mantle woven by his wife, the sacrificial knife and a rod.
britannica-1911-fox-sir-stephen:
Sir Stephen Fox (1627-1716), English statesman, was born on 27 March 1627. He was the son of William Fox of Farley in Wiltshire, a yeoman farmer. At fifteen he got a place in the household of the earl of Northumberland. He then served the earl's brother, Lord Percy, and was with the royalist army at the battle of Worcester as Percy's deputy at the ordnance board. When Charles II fled to the continent, Fox went with the exiled court into its hardest years.

On Clarendon's advice, Fox was made manager of the royal household in exile. Clarendon praised his languages, clerkship, honesty and discretion. His skill in handling the tiny finances of the wandering court won him trust and promotion, and he ran several important missions. The entry follows the farmer's son who kept a king's purse in exile and rose high after the Restoration.
britannica-1911-fu-kien:
Fu-kien, formerly Min, is a south-eastern province of China, bounded by Cheh-kiang, Kwang-tung, and Kiang-si, with the sea to the east. It covers 53,480 square miles and holds an estimated 20,000,000 people. The capital is Fuchow Fu, and the province is cut into eleven prefectures. Ranges of the Nan-shan cross it from north-east to south-west.

The main river is the Min, formed by three streams joining near Yen-pʽing Fu and reaching the sea some 30 miles below Fuchow. Its upper course is narrow and full of rapids, fit only for small native boats. The soil is rich, the hills green and terraced, and the lead product is tea, the best being Bohea from the Wu-e Mountains. Open ports are Fuchow and Amoy, both opened in 1842, and Funing, opened in 1898. Salt, sugar, timber, and paper also figure in the trade.
britannica-1911-fussen: Füssen is a Bavarian town in Germany at the foot of the Alps on the Lech, 2500 feet above the sea, with some 4000 people. It has six Roman Catholic churches, a Franciscan monastery and a castle on a rocky height. Rope-making is an important industry of the town. The castle is remembered for the peace signed there on the 22nd of April 1745 between Maximilian III Joseph of Bavaria and Maria Theresa. Hohenschwangau castle stands two miles south-east, and Neuschwanstein, built by Louis II, a little to the north.
britannica-1911-girard-stephen:
Stephen Girard (1750-1831) was an American financier and philanthropist, founder of Girard College in Philadelphia. The 1911 Britannica entry has him born near Bordeaux on 20 May 1750, a sea captain's son with little schooling, who lost the sight of his right eye at eight. He traded to New Orleans and the West Indies before settling at Philadelphia in 1776.

His fleet grew, its ships named for French authors: Rousseau, Voltaire, Montesquieu. In 1810 he used about a million dollars held with the Barings to buy depreciated Bank of the United States stock, a move that steadied American credit in Europe. When the bank's charter lapsed he bought its building and opened the Bank of Stephen Girard in 1812. The entry closes with his great bequest: Girard College, a school for orphans run by trustees, with training partly industrial and partly preparing boys for college.
britannica-1911-golden:
Golden is a city in Colorado, county-seat of Jefferson county, on Clear Creek about 14 miles west by north of Denver. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 2,152 people in 1900 and 2,477 in 1910. It stands about 5,700 feet above the sea, and serves as a residential suburb of Denver.

Castle Rock rises 600 feet above the city, and Lookout Mountain, a natural park of 3,400 acres, lies to the west. In Golden stands the Colorado State School of Mines, opened in 1874, teaching mining and metallurgical engineering. Pottery, firebrick and tile come from local clays, and coal, copper and gold are found nearby. The first settlement was a gold camp of 1859, named for Tom Golden, a pioneer prospector. Golden was capital of Colorado Territory in 1862, though the offices sat there only in 1866-1867.
britannica-1911-goppingen:
Goppingen is a town of Germany, in the kingdom of Wurttemberg, on the right bank of the Fils, 22 miles east-south-east of Stuttgart. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 20,870 people in 1905. Its castle, built by Duke Christopher in the 16th century partly from Hohenstaufen stones, now houses public offices.

The town has two Evangelical churches, a Roman Catholic church, a synagogue, and classical and modern schools. Its manufactures are large: linen and woollen cloth, leather, glue, paper and toys, with machine shops and tanneries. Three miles north stand the ruins of Hohenstaufen castle. Goppingen belonged first to the Hohenstaufen house, passed to Wurttemberg in 1270, was walled in 1129, and was almost wholly rebuilt after a fire in 1782.
britannica-1911-gottingen:
Gottingen is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Hanover, in the broad, fertile valley of the Leine, 67 miles south of Hanover. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its population as 34,030 in 1905, up from 17,057 in 1875. The Leine canal parts the old town from the new, and tree-planted ramparts ring it as a promenade.

The town's fame is its university, the Georgia Augusta, founded by George II in 1734 and opened in 1737. It rose fast to a leading place, with 1,547 students in 1823. The entry notes the churches of St John and St James, the 14th-century town hall, and thriving trades: publishing, cloth, and mathematical and scientific instruments. The long article then gives the university's history in full, through its political troubles and famous teachers.
britannica-1911-greifenhagen:
Greifenhagen is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Pomerania, on the Reglitz, 12 miles south-south-west of Stettin by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 6,473 people in 1905. Its prosperity depends chiefly on agriculture, the entry says, and it has a considerable trade in cattle.

Felt making and saw mills are its other industries. The town was built in 1230 and raised to town rank and fortified about 1250. Its wars fill the rest of the notice. In the Thirty Years' War both imperialists and Swedes took it. In 1675 the Brandenburgers captured it, and in 1679 it came finally into their possession. The whole entry is a compact gazetteer paragraph: river, distance, population, the cattle trade, and a four-century outline of sieges.
britannica-1911-greisen:
Greisen, in the 1911 Britannica, is a rock made from granite by change. The hosted text opens part-way into the article, in the account of that change, so the entry's beginning does not survive in this record. What remains explains the process as pneumatolytic: vapours freed by cooling granite magma worked on the rock, probably while it was still hot.

The same change, white mica, quartz and tourmaline growing together, appears in sedimentary rocks around granite masses. Greisen stands close to schorl rock in make-up and origin, the entry says. Both often carry small shares of tin oxide, cassiterite, and are worked as tin ores. They occur in Cornwall, Saxony, Tasmania and other tin districts, though many greisens hold no tin. A table of analyses closes the piece. It shows fluorine and boron entering, and the alkalies falling, as Cornish granite became greisen.
britannica-1911-gretna-green:
Gretna Green is a village in the south-east of Dumfriesshire, Scotland, about nine miles north-north-west of Carlisle, near the river Sark, the border with England. The 1911 Britannica entry explains its notoriety. As the nearest village on the Scottish side, it was the resort of eloping couples who lacked their parents' consent.

Until 1754, clandestine marriages were commonly made in London's Fleet prison. Lord Hardwicke's act ended that, and couples crossed the border, where a simple declaration before witnesses sufficed. At Gretna the blacksmith usually performed the ceremony, though the toll-keeper or anyone else might. Fees ran from half a guinea upward, and as many as two hundred couples a year married at the toll-house. The traffic ended in practice in 1856, when the law required three weeks' residence in Scotland first.
britannica-1911-hallowe-en:
Hallowe'en, or All Hallows Eve, falls on 31 October. It is the vigil of Hallowmas, or All Saints' Day. Its ceremonies long predate Christianity. Two traits marked the ancient festival. People lit bonfires on that night. They also believed ghosts and witches wandered then. The Druids held their autumn festival near 1 November. They lit fires for the Sun-god in harvest thanksgiving.

Druid belief gave the night its darker side. Saman, lord of death, summoned wicked souls that evening. Those souls had spent the year in animal bodies. Ireland still knew the night as the Vigil of Saman. Roman Pomona customs added nuts and apples. Apple-ducking and nut-roasting became standard sports. Highland fires survived in Scotland and Wales into recent years. Stones in the embers foretold who would die within the year. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hallowe'en entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-havet-julien:
Julien Havet (1853–1893) was a French historian. He was born at Vitry-sur-Seine on 4 April 1853. Ernest Havet was his father. He showed remarkable aptitude for learning early. Pure rhetoric, though, held an aversion for him. The École des Chartes trained his critical faculty. He took first place entering and leaving that school. Historical method became his ruling passion there.

His thesis on the Norman Islands' guardians appeared in 1876. It rested wholly on original documents in London and the islands. Later research barely touched its conclusions. He then attacked Fustel de Coulanges' system on Frankish law. The Gallo-Romans, he showed, were conquered, not absorbed as equals. The Vrain Lucas forgeries drew him to questions of authenticity. Many short monographs ranged across varied subjects. His friends published his Mélanges in 1895.
britannica-1911-hawarden:
Hawarden is a market-town of Flintshire, North Wales. People pronounce its name Harden. Its Welsh name is Penarlâg. Chester lies six miles to the east. Its population in 1901 was 5,372. It stands on a height with an extensive prospect. Coal surrounds it, and clay beds lie near. Coarse earthenware and draining tiles are manufactured. Fire-clay bricks are another local product.

Hawarden castle stands in a fine wooded park. The present house was built in 1752 and Gothicised in 1814. An older castle of the same name stands nearby. William the Conqueror gave that castle to Hugh Lupus. Dafydd of Wales took it in 1282. Parliamentarians destroyed it in the Civil War. It passed from the Glynne family to W. E. Gladstone by marriage. St Deiniol church was restored in 1857 and 1878.
britannica-1911-hawes-stephen:
Stephen Hawes (fl. 1502–1521) was an English poet. He was probably a Suffolk native born about 1474. Oxford educated him, and he travelled widely. His accomplishments won him a court place on his return. By 1502 he was groom of the chamber to Henry VII. Poetry was his most excellent vein. He could repeat most English poets by heart. Lydgate was the master he acknowledged.

His capital work is The Passetyme of Pleasure. Wynkyn de Worde printed it in 1509. Its hero, Graunde Amour, seeks La Bel Pucel. Fame and her greyhounds, Grace and Governance, guide him. The poem allegorises man's life in seven-lined stanzas. Its sections borrow the machinery of romance. The knight's education through the seven sciences structures it. Martianus Capella's Marriage of Mercury and Philology underlies the design. Hawes died before 1530.
britannica-1911-hawker-robert-stephen:
Robert Stephen Hawker (1803–1875) was an English antiquary and poet. He was born at Stoke Damerel, Devonshire, on 3 December 1803. His father later became vicar of Stratton in Cornwall. Liskeard and Cheltenham grammar schools educated Robert. He matriculated at Pembroke College, Oxford, in 1823. The Newdigate prize for poetry came in 1827. In 1834 he became vicar of Morwenstow in Cornwall.

His parishioners were smugglers, wreckers and dissenters of many hues. He was a high churchman who ruled with a high hand. Yet his people loved him greatly. Stories of his eccentric sayings multiplied. The Quest of the Sangraal is his best poem. His Cornish Ballads gave the world the Trelawny refrain. He died at Plymouth on 15 August. Reception into the Roman Catholic Church preceded his death. That step aroused bitter newspaper controversy.
britannica-1911-hawtrey-edward-craven:
Edward Craven Hawtrey (1789–1862) was an English educationalist. He was born at Burnham on 7 May 1789. His father was the parish vicar. Eton and King's College, Cambridge, educated him. In 1814 he became an assistant master at Eton. Dr Keate was headmaster at that time. In 1834 Hawtrey himself became headmaster of Eton. His administration proved a vigorous one.

New buildings rose under him, including the school library. A sanatorium was built and the chapel restored. He closed the Old Christopher Inn. He suppressed the Montem custom of street begging. He founded the prize for English essay himself. The prince consort's language prizes were supposedly his suggestion. In 1852 he became provost of Eton. London called him the English Mezzofanti for his languages. He died on 27 January 1862.
britannica-1911-heathen:
Heathen is a term for people outside the Jewish and Christian faiths. It originally included Mahommedans as well. Modern usage usually restricts it to polytheistic races. That restriction now excludes Mahommedans. The word's derivation has been much debated. It is common to all Germanic languages. German Heide and Dutch heiden are its cognates. A Gothic word haiþi, meaning heath, is the usual source.

Ulfilas' Gothic Bible calls the Syrophoenician woman haiþno. The Vulgate there has gentilis. Heathen would thus mean people of the heath. That matches Latin paganus, people of the village district. Old worship lingered longest in country places. Bugge suggested an Armenian source instead, from the Greek ethnē. Gentilis in Latin meant tribesman, then foreigner. Church usage fixed it on non-Christian nations. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the heathen entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-helvetius-claude-adrien:
Claude Adrien Helvétius (1715–1771) was a French philosopher and littérateur. He was born in Paris in January 1715. His family of physicians bore the name Schweitzer originally. His grandfather introduced ipecacuanha to medicine. His father was first physician to Queen Marie Leczinska. Claude trained for finance but wrote verses in spare hours. At twenty-three the queen made him farmer-general. That post was worth 100,000 crowns a year.

Wealth let him enjoy life to the utmost. Ageing, he dreamed of more lasting distinction. Voltaire the poet and Montesquieu the philosopher spurred him. His poem Le Bonheur appeared after his death. His famous book De l'esprit came in 1758. It aimed to rival Montesquieu's Esprit des lois. It drew immediate attention and formidable opposition. He had already retired to a country estate. There he relieved the poor and encouraged agriculture and industry.
britannica-1911-hen:
Hen is a female bird, especially the female of the common fowl. Old English hæn is the feminine of hana, the male bird. German Hahn and Henne show the same correlation. Dutch haan and hen, Swedish hane and hönne, match too. The old English male name has disappeared entirely. Cock replaced it in ordinary speech. That word is probably onomatopoeic in origin. Its base kuk- or kik- also appears in chicken.

French coq and medieval Latin coccus carry the same base. The whole entry is a few lines of word history. Definition first, then Teutonic cognates, then the cock problem. Nothing about poultry keeping or breeds appears. It is one of the briefest entries in its band. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hen entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hildburghausen:
Hildburghausen is a town of Germany, in the duchy of Saxe-Meiningen, in a wide valley on the river Werra, 19 m. S.E. of Meiningen. Its population was 7,456 in 1905. Its chief buildings are a ducal palace of 1685–1695, now barracks, the old town hall, two Evangelical churches, a Roman Catholic church and a theatre.

A technical college occupies the rooms where Meyer's Bibliographisches Institut worked from 1828 until it left for Leipzig in 1874. Local trades include linen and cloth, toys, buttons, optical instruments, farm machines and condensed milk. In the 13th century the place belonged to the counts of Henneberg, then passed to Thuringia and Saxony. In 1683 it became the capital of a small principality, united to Saxe-Meiningen in 1826.
britannica-1911-hilden: Hilden is a town in the Prussian Rhine province, on the river Itter, 9 m. S.E. of Düsseldorf by rail. Its population was 13,946 in 1905. It has an Evangelical and a Roman Catholic church and a monument to the emperor William I. Its manufactures include silks, velvets and carpets, calico-printing, machinery and brick-making. The entry is a short gazetteer notice giving the town's place, size, churches and trades in a few lines.
britannica-1911-hohenstaufen:
Hohenstaufen takes its name from a village and ruined castle in Swabia, in the kingdom of Württemberg. The castle gave its name to a celebrated Swabian family. Its members were emperors or German kings from 1138 to 1208, and again from 1214 to 1254. The earliest known ancestor was Frederick, count of Büren (d. 1094), whose son built the castle and took its name.

That son, Frederick I, stood firm for the emperor Henry IV. Henry rewarded him with the dukedom of Swabia in 1079 and with his daughter Agnes in marriage. Yet Swabia was his only after twenty years of struggle. His son Frederick II, the One-eyed, held south-west Germany for Henry V with his brother Conrad. After failing to win the throne in 1125, Frederick submitted at Bamberg but kept his dukedom. In 1138 Conrad of Hohenstaufen was elected German king, followed in 1152 by Frederick Barbarossa.
britannica-1911-hooft-pieter-cornelissen:
Pieter Cornelissen Hooft (1581–1647) was a Dutch poet and historian, born at Amsterdam on the 16th of March 1581. His father was a leading citizen of Holland and for a time burgomaster of Amsterdam. At seventeen Hooft joined the chamber of rhetoric In Liefde bloeiende. Before it he produced his tragedy Achilles and Polyxena, printed only in 1614.

In June 1598 he left Holland for Paris, then went on to Venice, Florence and Rome, and in 1600 to Naples. He studied the best Italian writing deeply as he travelled. From Italy he sent home a fine letter in verse on his hopes for Dutch poetry. He came back through Germany after three and a half years away. The life follows the honours and works that made him the central figure of Dutch letters in his age.
britannica-1911-kempen:
Kempen is a town in the Prussian Rhine Province, 40 miles north of Cologne by the railway to Zevenaar. Its people numbered 6319 in 1900. It has a monument to Thomas à Kempis, who was born there. Its industries are of fair size and count silk weaving, glass making, and the making of electrical plant.

Kempen belonged in the middle ages to the archbishopric of Cologne and gained civic rights in 1294. It is remembered as the scene of a victory won on the 17th of January 1642 by the French and Hessians over the Imperialists. The entry is a short town note: a birthplace of a famed devotional writer, a set of trades, a medieval grant of rights, and one battle of the Thirty Years' War.
britannica-1911-knickerbocker-harmen-jan:
Harmen Jansen Knickerbocker (c. 1650–c. 1720) was a Dutch colonist of New Netherland, born at Wyhe in Overyssel, Holland. Before 1683 he settled near what is now Albany, New York. In 1704 he bought, through Harme Gansevoort, one-fourth of the land in Dutchess county near Red Hook that had been patented to Peter Schuyler in 1688. Schuyler later deeded lots in that share to Knickerbocker's seven children.

The family line runs on at the Schaghticoke estate, down to Harmen Knickerbocker (1779–1855), a lawyer who sat in Congress in 1809–1811 and in the New York Assembly in 1816. His courtly welcome at his manor earned him the name "the prince of Schaghticoke." Washington Irving borrowed his name for Diedrich Knickerbocker's History of New York (1809), and from that book the name Knickerbockers passed into wide use.
britannica-1911-krumen:
The Krumen, also called Kroomen, Krooboys, Krus or Croos, are a people of the west coast of Africa. Their villages run along the coast of Liberia from below Monrovia nearly to Cape Palmas. Their name was once wrongly derived from the English word "crew,". It more likely comes from Kraoh, the old name of one of their tribes. With kindred peoples such as the Grebo and Basa they number some 40,000.

The Krus proper live between the Sino river and Cape Palmas, in five chief villages. They are noted as skilled seamen and bold fishermen, a stout and strong-built race. They are described as honest, brave and proud, so set on freedom that they would starve rather than be taken, and they never traded in slaves. Their small commonwealths have hereditary chiefs who speak for them to strangers, while real rule rests with the elders.
britannica-1911-langton-stephen:
Stephen Langton (died 1228), cardinal and archbishop of Canterbury, won fame first as a scholar at Paris. English by birth, he rose there as a leading teacher of church learning, wrote large commentaries, and is linked with the splitting of the Bible into chapters. Friendship with Lothar of Segni, later Pope Innocent III, shaped all that followed.

Innocent made him a cardinal in 1206, then pushed his name when the Canterbury election fell into dispute. Set aside rival votes were followed by a fresh choice at Rome, and Langton was consecrated on 17 June 1207. King John shut out the Canterbury monks in anger. An interdict on England in 1208 and the king's own ban in 1209 followed, and only a threat of French invasion forced John to make peace.
brood-of-the-witch-queen:
Sax Rohmer wrote a tale of sorcery built round Antony Ferrara, in an edition of the 1918 novel. A note at the front sets the aim. Ferrara's strange deeds show forms of sorcery as old records claim they were worked. Egypt of old and Europe of the middle ages both feed that lore. No power laid to him tops what those records claim, the note holds.

Egypt gives the tale its gods, masks, and old books. Chapter heads in the twin print name the Ring of Thoth, the Mask of Set, and the Book of Thoth. Dr. Cairn stands against Ferrara in that print's cast. Beasts and rites crowd the path: beetles, bats, spiders, and a thug's cord. Standard Ebooks built this copy from a Project Gutenberg text and old scans. Its makers give their work to all, free of rights claims.
brothers-of-pity-and-other-tales-of-beas:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote a set of tales of beasts and men for young readers. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge put out the book at London. Most tales first ran in Aunt Judy's Magazine. A note gives the book to the author's sister, Horatia Katharine Frances Gatty.

Two tales grew from Fedor Flinzer's pictures: Father Hedgehog and his Neighbours, and Toots and Boots. Toots was a real cat, the preface grants. In late life he dined at the Royal Engineers' Mess at Aldershot as a guest of rank. The Hens of Hencastle is not Ewing's own work. It is a free English form of a German tale by Victor Blüthgen, turned by Major Yeatman-Biggs. Kindness to beasts, and the pity of the title, bind the set as one.
business-hints-for-men-and-women:
Business Hints for Men and Women, by A R Calhoun, is a practical manual for farmers and small property holders who must handle their own paperwork. Calhoun opens with common sense farming. Wealth, land, labor, and money come first. The farmer is a producer and seller. He needs business methods as much as a plow. From the farm he moves to the desk.

Whole chapters teach documents a countryman actually signs. Deeds and abstracts of title come first, then forms of deeds and mortgages, payments, assignments, and the equity of redemption, the borrower's right to recover his land. Wills get a chapter of kinds, limits, and executive duties. Letter writing closes the early course, with forms for business letters and letters of introduction. The book belongs to the era when a farm was a firm, and its owner was expected to be his own lawyer at the kitchen table.
c-f-meyer-das-leiden-eines-knaben:
A gentle boy suffers under the cruelty of the adult world in C. F. Meyer's Das Leiden eines Knaben, given here in German. The Sufferings of a Boy tells its sad story with restraint and deep sympathy. School discipline, a harsh father figure, and a child's helplessness close around the young hero.

Meyer, himself a late bloomer who knew suffering from inside, writes with unforgettable tenderness. Nothing is exaggerated, which makes the boy's fate harder to bear. The novella ranks among literature's most heartbreaking portraits of childhood wronged. Its quiet protest against needless severity has not lost force. Readers often finish it in one sitting and sit silent afterward.
canada-for-gentlemen:
James Seton Cockburn's Canada for Gentlemen prints the letters of a young emigrant, sent home to his family circle and published by his father. The elder Cockburn explains that friends were so eager to read the manuscript letters that printing them saved the originals from wearing out.

The letters describe the real difficulties of young emigrants, a subject the emigration agencies said little about, and their lessons are often more valuable than tales of uniform success. Fictitious names replace those of friends, and the father hopes the price of the book may even buy the writer his winter furs. Readers interested in emigration, or in Canada as newcomers actually found it, will find these letters frank and useful.
carmen:
Prosper Mérimée told Carmen as a tale inside a tale, in Lady Mary Loyd's translation. His narrator, an archaeologist hunting a Roman battlefield in Andalusia in 1830, falls in with the smuggler Don José and hears his confession. José, a Basque soldier, let a gypsy cigarette girl named Carmen escape arrest, joined her smugglers, and slid from love into jealous murder among the mountains.

Mérimée keeps the telling dry and swift, letting Carmen's freedom and José's obsession collide without excuse or sermon. The story later fed Bizet's opera, which softened what Mérimée left hard. Read here in its original form, Carmen is a cool, fatal little masterpiece about a woman who would rather die than be owned.
castren-ethnologische-vorlesungen:
Castrén's Ethnological Lectures on the Altaic Peoples appeared in German in 1857. The lectures give the great Finn's summing of his life's work. Turks, Mongols, and Tungus peoples stand in one wide frame.

Castrén compares their tongues, faiths, and ways from his own travel notes. He died young after reshaping the whole field he founded here. The talks became a founding text of Ural-Altaic studies for Europe. Students across the north took their first map of the field from him. His calm, vast scheme still earns respect from scholars across the north today. The lectures turn hard travel into ordered, lasting knowledge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aachen:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Aachen describes the city known in French as Aix-la-Chapelle and in Latin as Aquae Grani. Aachen lies in a Prussian valley among wooded heights, on the Wurm stream, and owes its origin to health-giving springs already known to the Romans.

Charlemagne chose Aachen as his favourite residence, adorning it with an imperial palace and chapel where he wished to be buried. Relics gathered by Charlemagne and Otto the Third drew medieval shrine pilgrimages from across Europe, and thirty-seven German emperors were crowned there between 813 and 1531. Later religious strife, bans of the empire and Protestant risings troubled the city, yet its chapel and pilgrimage tradition endured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Saint-Ouen describes a Benedictine house at Rouen reaching to Merovingian times. Its foundation is credited variously to Clothair the First and to St. Clothilda, without sufficient evidence to settle the question.

First dedicated to St. Peter, the house took St. Ouen's name after the Archbishop of Rouen, dead in 678, was buried there. Its recorded history from 1000 holds nothing exceptional, and in 1660 it joined the Congregation of St. Maur, numbering twenty-four at its suppression in 1794. The abbey's chief interest lies in its glorious church, larger and lovelier than Rouen Cathedral, begun in 1318 by Abbot Jean Roussel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-wald:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Waldsassen, meaning settlement in the woods, describes a famed Cistercian house on the Wondreb in the Upper Palatinate, near Bohemia's border. Gerwich von Wolmundstein, a Benedictine monk of Sigeberg, built it between 1128 and 1132 with his former abbot Kuno's leave.

The first monks came from Volkenrod in Thuringia, of Morimond's line, and the first abbot was elected in 1133. Waldsassen soon ranked among the most famed and strong houses of the age, founding Sedlitz and Ossegg in Bohemia and Walderbach near Regensburg. Several of its thirty-seven abbots before the Reformation were famed for holiness and learning, though wars, famines, taxes and attacks later brought swings of good times and decay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aberdeen:
Aberdeen is a Scottish see founded in 1063 at Mortlach by Blessed Beyn. Its first firm record is a bull of Adrian IV from 1157, confirming its churches and lands to Bishop Edward. The granite cathedral went up in 1272-1277. Bishop Thomas Spence's Franciscan house dates to 1480, and Bishop Elphinstone's King's College at Old Aberdeen to 1505. The see moved to Old Aberdeen about 1125 and stayed there until 1577, served by twenty-nine bishops.

From 1653 prefects-apostolic governed Scotland's Catholics, followed by vicars-apostolic. In 1878 Leo XIII restored the Scottish hierarchy, and John MacDonald became first bishop of the restored see. Aberdeen became one of four suffragan sees under St. Andrews and Edinburgh. The entry also notes Fort Augustus, raised to an abbey directly subject to Rome in 1882.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-contzen:
Adam Contzen was an economist and exegete born in 1573, or 1575 by Sommervogel, at Montjoie in Julich. He died at Munich on 19 June 1635. He joined the Jesuits at Trier in 1595 and taught philosophy at Wurzburg in 1606. He moved to Mainz in 1610, holding Holy Scripture's chair for over ten years. He helped organize the University of Molsheim in Alsace, serving as chancellor in 1622 and 1623.

Contzen was a learned, versatile writer on controversy, political economy, and scripture. He defended Bellarmine against Pareus of Heidelberg. When Pareus sought to unite Calvinists and Lutherans against Catholics, Contzen showed the project's impracticality in De Pace Germaniae of 1616. In 1623 he published commentaries on the Gospels and Pauline epistles, plus a political novel on an Abyssinian king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-breme:
Adam of Bremen was an eleventh-century German historian and geographer, whose birth and death dates are unknown. His Gesta Hammaburgensis Ecclesiae Pontificum covers the Hamburg see and northern Christian missions from 788 to 1072. Northern regions before the thirteenth century are known chiefly through it. In his preface he signs himself only by the initial A.

Helmold's Slavic Chronicle identifies A as Adam, author of the Hamburg church history. That he came from Saxony, more precisely Meissen, is mere conjecture from dialect traces in the work. He reached Bremen in 1068 at Archbishop Adalbert's invitation, was made cathedral canon and director of schools, and signed an official document on 11 June 1069. Soon after arriving he journeyed to King Svend Estridson of Denmark, famed for knowledge of northern history and geography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agen:
Agen, ancient Aginnum, is a French diocese comprising the Lot and Garonne department. It has been successively suffragan to Bordeaux under the old regime, to Toulouse from 1802 to 1822, and to Bordeaux since 1822. Legends no older than the ninth century about the hermit St. Caprasius, martyred alongside St. Fides under Dacianus, and the story of Vincentius, written about 520, give no foundation for traditions making these saints Agen's early bishops.

History's first known bishop, St. Phoebadius, was St. Hilary's friend and published a treatise against the Arians in 357 and figured at the Council of Rimini in 359. Later bishops include Wilhelmus II, sent by Urban IV to St. Louis in 1262, Bertrand de Goth, uncle of Clement V, Cardinal Jean de Lorraine, the preacher Jules Mascaron, and de Bonnac, first to refuse the constitutional oath in 1792. The church of St. Caprasius, a fine Romance building, is now the cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-aac:
Albert of Aachen, also called Albertus Aquensis, was a chronicler of the First Crusade, now usually thought to have been a canon of Aachen. His Chronicle of Jerusalem on the Holy War, in twelve books covering 1095 to 1121, survives in early printed collections of crusade histories. Whether he belonged instead to the church of Aix-en-Provence remains doubtful, the entry notes, following Wattenbach.

The entry judges his narrative harshly on method: it has little order, less critical skill, inexact chronology, and often mangled place names. Yet it values the work as the writing of a deeply religious man with a poet's heart. He saw Christian knighthood as the salvation of Christendom. In that light, it says, the severe criticism of von Sybel loses much of its point.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-nam:
Seven men named Alexander appear in Scripture. Alexander the Great, King of Macedon from 336 to 323 B.C., is mentioned in 1 Maccabees and is thought to figure in Daniel's visions. Alexander Balas, eleventh King of Syria from 150 to 145 B.C., won his throne with promises to Jonathan, followed a pro-Jewish policy, and was beaten by his father-in-law Ptolemy Philometor. Alexander, son of Simon of Cyrene, is named by St. Mark as a son of the man who carried the cross after Jesus.

Another Alexander sat on Peter and John's trial court, and some identify him with Alexander Lysimachus, brother of Philo. A further Alexander, Jew or Jewish Christian, tried to defend St. Paul, and some identify him with Simon's son. The last two are an Ephesian Christian who fell away with Hymenaeus and a coppersmith who did St. Paul evil. Some take them to be the same man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonse-magn:
Alphonse Magnien, clergy educator, was born at Bleymard in 1837 and died in 1902. A classics student at Chirac and philosophy and theology student at Orléans, he showed brilliant talents and character. He joined Orléans on Dupanloup's appeal. In the seminary a Sulpician vocation grew in him, postponed by the bishop. For two years after ordination he taught at La Chapelle St-Mesmin. He then taught sciences at Nantes and theology and Scripture at Rodez.

In fall 1869 he began Baltimore work, known to American priests. At St. Mary's he taught philosophy, later Scripture and dogma. He grasped a question's vital part instinctively, resting only on truth. After Dubreul's death in 1878, Magnien became superior. For a quarter century he shaped American clergy formation. Upright, frank, manly, a true priest devoted to the Church, he was most at home on the rostrum. Speaking almost daily on spiritual topics, he never tired hearers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-screen:
The altar screen is embroidered needlework, cloth of gold, or tapestry, as wide as the altar and sometimes extending along its sides. It hangs above a high altar attached to the wall or within three feet of it. It bears images of Our Lord, the Blessed Virgin, or saints, unless such images are already painted on the wall.

A permanent screen has a base as long as table and steps, a panel framing picture, bas-relief, or statue, and a cornice of frieze and pediment topped by a cross. Metal served in the eleventh century, stone in the thirteenth, wood from the fourteenth. Folding doors sometimes covered the picture except on grand festivals. Its nave-facing side is the retable, its reverse the counter-retable. Enriched with niches, statues, and buttresses, it becomes a reredos, sometimes spanning the church's breadth nearly to the ceiling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amen:
Amen is one of few Hebrew words imported unchanged into the Church's liturgy, for its exceptionally sacred example, as Augustine put it. Trent's Catechism notes how frequent it was in Our Saviour's mouth, Matthew attributing it to him twenty-eight times and John twenty-six in doubled form. It derives from Hebrew aman, to strengthen or confirm.

In Scripture it works almost always as an adverb, adopting another's words as one's own, as Jeremiah answering Hananias in chapter 28, verse 6. Synagogue use as the people's answer to aloud prayer passed to Apostolic-age Christians. A third use closes discourses or chapters with a doxology ending in Amen, now a mere formula. Two special cases earn separate treatment: the people's Amen closing the great Prayer of Consecration, and the Amen after Communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnold-jansse:
Arnold Janssen, founder and first head of the Society of the Divine Word, was born at Goch in the Rhine Province on 5 November 1837. He died at Steyl in Holland on 15 January 1909. From a very young age he showed an inclination for priesthood. After classical studies at Gaesdonck college, philosophy at Münster academy, and theology at Bonn and Münster, he was ordained on 15 August 1861.

He spent years in pastoral work and teaching Christian doctrine, becoming chaplain and head at the Ursuline convent of Kempen in 1873. As diocesan head of the Apostleship of Prayer he laboured to spread that association, and in that role felt called to found a missionary base for Germany. The result was Steyl's Mission House of St. Michael, opened 8 September 1875, from which the Society of the Divine Word grew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baden:
Baden was a Grand Duchy in the southwest of the German Empire, bounded by Switzerland, Alsace, and Bavaria. It covered 5,821 square miles, and its 1905 census counted 2,010,728 people. Catholics numbered 1,198,511, Evangelicals 762,826, and Jews 25,893, among other faiths. At the Christian era its land formed the tithe lands, guarded by a wall against German tribes.

After Emperor Probus died in 282, the Alemanni seized the southern tithe lands. Frankish victories in 496 and 536 made them masters of the region. Pepin the Short ended tribal dukedoms in 748 and set Frankish imperial order in place. Frankish power brought Christianity: Columbanus and Gall worked the south about 610, Pirminius followed a century later. Trudpert labored in the Breisgau, Kilian in the northeast, and Mainz evangelized the Rhine valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-ernst-v:
Baron Ernst von Feuchtersleben was an Austrian poet, philosopher, and physician, born at Vienna in 1806, who died in 1849. After the Theresian Academy he studied medicine from 1825 and took his doctorate in 1833. In 1844 he began free lectures on psychiatry at Vienna, became faculty dean in 1845, and vice-director of medico-chirurgical studies in 1847. In July 1848 he became under-secretary for public instruction, but resigned, discouraged by reform's difficulties.

His Zur Diätetik der Seele of 1838 brought him great popularity and ran to a forty-sixth edition by 1896. His 1845 textbook of medical psychology appeared in English as Principles of Medical Psychology in 1847. As a poet he is best known for the song Es ist bestimmt in Gottes Rat, set to music by Mendelssohn. His complete non-medical works were edited by Friedrich Hebbel in seven volumes from 1851 to 1853.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-guillau:
Baron Guillaume Dupuytren was a French anatomist and surgeon, born at Pierre-Buffière in 1777, who died at Paris in 1835. His poor parents sent him to the Collège de la Marche on charity. By competitive examination he became anatomy's prosecutor at Paris's new medical school at eighteen. In 1803 he became assistant surgeon at the Hôtel-Dieu, and by 1815 its head surgeon and professor of clinical surgery.

Indefatigable, he built one of the largest surgical practices of all time and amassed a great fortune. He battled a consumptive tendency all his life, and it finally carried him off. His will endowed the anatomy chair at the medical school and founded a home for physicians in distress. The palm contraction crippling the fingers still bears his name, and his chief writings treat the artificial anus and gunshot wounds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-von-mun:
Baron von Münch-Bellinghausen, writing as Friedrich Halm, was an Austrian dramatist born at Cracow in 1806, who died at Vienna in 1871. Schooled at Melk and Vienna in philosophy and law, he began an official career in 1826. His teacher Enk von der Burg urged his Griseldis on the Hofburg theatre, and its 1835 success fixed his reputation. He rose to Government councillor in 1840 and keeper of the Court Library in 1844, a post Grillparzer had sought in vain.

His best-known plays are Griseldis, The Son of the Wilderness (1842), and The Gladiator of Ravenna (1857). Griseldis tests a faithful wife's loyalty to triumph, while Son of the Wilderness sets womanly love against barbarian strength. He also wrote lyrics, stories, and the narrative poem Charfreitag, and superintended the court theatres from 1867 to 1870. His complete works appeared at Vienna in eight volumes, with four more posthumously.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-van-:
Benedict van Haeften, a Benedictine writer and provost of Afflighem, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Utrecht in 1588, he died at Spa in 1648 while seeking his health. After study at Louvain, he entered Afflighem in 1609, took vows in 1611, and was ordained priest in 1613.

He became prior in 1616 and provost, or head, of the monastery in 1618, guiding it through a dispute over joining a stricter congregation. Under his prudent rule the house flourished in spirit and in goods. His chief book, a twelve-volume study of the Rule of St. Benedict, appeared at Antwerp in 1644, with six shorter devotional works beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bohemian-bret:
The Bohemian Brethren, also called Moravian Brethren or Unitas Fratrum, put lived faith before creeds and took Scripture as their only rule of faith. Founded in Bohemia in 1457 and renewed by Count Zinzendorf in 1722, the body still lived when the entry was written. Personal faith in the crucified Saviour grounds its fellowship, while debate over doctrines like the Trinity is shunned.

Its history runs from Wyclif through Hus, whose burning at Constance in 1415 outraged Bohemia. The entry follows the old Unitas Fratrum to 1722, then the renewed brotherhood under Zinzendorf. Later sections cover the Brethren in England, the Moravian Church in America, and the body's present condition, with baptism and the Lord's Supper as its only sacraments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bremen:
Bremen, once an archdiocese on the lower Weser and Elbe, began with Saint Willehad, consecrated bishop in 787 after Charlemagne's Saxon conquest. He chose Bremen, first named in 782, and built a cathedral dedicated in 789. The diocese itself rose only under his successor Willerich, and after Leuderich's death in 845, Mainz joined Bremen to Hamburg's archdiocese under Saint Anschar.

Hamburg's Viking ruin in 845 pushed the see toward Bremen, though the title moved formally only in 1223. Nicholas I confirmed the union in 864 against Cologne's protests, and Formosus freed Bremen from Cologne in 892. Rembert and Adalgar, Benedictines from Corvey, advanced the northern missions, Hungarians burned city and diocese under Hoger, and Unni died at Birka in 936 on a Scandinavian mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brixen:
Brixen, a prince-bishopric of Austria suffragan to Salzburg, covers most of northern Tyrol and all Vorarlberg across 6,705 square miles with over 440,000 people. It continues the see of Saben, where Christianity reached a Roman customs post by the third century and Ingenuin stands as first proven bishop about 580. Bajuvari and Lombards took the faith early, though Puster Valley Slavs held paganism until the eighth century.

Bishop Rihpert or Albuin moved the seat to Brixen in the late tenth century, Hartwig raised it to a city, and emperors showered it with land. Frederick I made its bishop a prince of the empire in 1179, which helps explain why Brixen's bishops backed emperors against popes, notably at the 1080 pseudo-synod deposing Gregory VII. Later bishops fiefed away much land to Tyrol's counts, shrinking their own temporal power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cap-haitien:
Cap-Haïtien is a Haitian diocese erected by Pius IX in October 1861 within the province of Port-au-Prince. It covers the northern department of the island republic. In 1906 it counted some 650,000 Catholics, more than a quarter of Haiti's people. The land forms the western third of Santo Domingo, the second largest of the Greater Antilles.

Its history runs from Columbus's second voyage in 1493, when Dominicans came to the island. Jesuit and Franciscan parish work followed, with a large Jesuit hospital. Later bishops built schools for boys and girls and a diocesan seminary. The entry closes with the diocese's religious and educational state, including Masonic lodges that once drew members when clergy were scarce. They now gather only a few times a year for festivals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catechumen:
A catechumen was a person in the early Church who had not yet been baptized but was preparing for initiation. The word comes from the Greek verb for being instructed, and it appears in Galatians, Corinthians, Luke, and Acts. Since accepting Christianity meant believing a body of doctrine and keeping the divine law, converts needed some teaching first, simple and short in apostolic times.

As churches became organized, the preparation grew longer and more formal. The article explains that the danger of apostasy, or even betrayal during persecution, led to special precautions around admission. It traces how a short instruction for Jews and pagans developed into a regulated period of probation before the sacred mysteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-le-go:
A life of Charles Le Gobien, the French Jesuit who founded the celebrated Lettres édifiantes et curieuses, a vast collection of missionary letters. Born at St-Malo in 1671, he entered the Society of Jesus. As procurator of the French mission to China, he worked to stir educated readers to support the spread of Christianity in East Asia. His own writings took up the progress of religion in China and the fierce dispute over Chinese rites, the ceremonies honouring Confucius and the dead.

In 1702 he issued letters from Jesuit missionaries in China and the East Indies, the seed of a collection that grew to thirty-six volumes by 1776, with later reissues and abridgements. It remains a key source for the history of Catholic missions, preserving first-hand reports from distant stations. Le Gobien also wrote a history of the newly converted Mariana Islands before his early death in Paris in 1708.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-plowd:
An entry on the Tudor lawyer Edmund Plowden, whose legal writings and courtroom wit made him famous. Humphrey Plowden's son, of Plowden Hall, Shropshire, he was educated at Cambridge without taking a degree. Called to the Middle Temple in 1538, he was praised by Camden as the greatest lawyer of his age. He also qualified as a surgeon and physician in 1552.

Under Mary he sat in Parliament and served on the Council of the Marches of Wales. His Catholic faith blocked promotion under Elizabeth, who is said to have offered him the lord chancellorship if he joined the Anglican Church. Defending a man charged with hearing Mass, he won an acquittal by showing the service had been staged by a lay informer, crying, in effect, no priest, no Mass. The episode gave rise to the proverb, the case is altered, quoth Plowden. His Commentaries appeared in 1571.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-churching-of-:
An entry on the churching of women, the Church's blessing of mothers recovered from childbirth. Only a Catholic woman who bore a child in lawful wedlock may receive it. It is a pious custom from the early ages, not a precept. As soon as she can leave home, the mother presents herself in church to thank God for a happy delivery and to gain grace for raising her child Christianly.

The prayers bless the mother alone, so the child need not come, though many places dedicate the child to God as well. The blessing is given even if the child was stillborn or died unbaptised. Churching is not strictly parochial, yet a parish priest asked to give it must do so. It must be given where Mass is celebrated, since the rite is a pilgrimage of thanksgiving to the church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-frasse:
Claude Frassen, a Scotist theologian of the Friars Minor, was born near Peronne in 1620 and died at Paris on 26 February 1711. He entered the Franciscans at Peronne at seventeen, finished his studies at Paris, and stayed as professor of philosophy and theology for thirty years. In 1662 he became a Sorbonne doctor and definitor general, elected in 1682, attending general chapters at Toledo and Rome. Louis the Fourteenth held him in high esteem.

Frassen died at ninety-one, after seventy-four years in religion. His best-known work, Scotus Academicus, ranks among the most important presentations of Duns Scotus's theology. Few interpreters of Scotus match his blend of simple style, clear method, and Scotistic subtlety, with quotations from the Fathers and statements of controverted questions. Its first volume lists heresies from Christian beginnings to the 1400s. The Rome edition of 1900 to 1902 runs to twelve volumes from his notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-of-:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry traces children's Communion through ancient practice and present discipline. Early Christians often gave infants Communion right after baptism. Saint Cyprian notes the practice. In the East it ran nearly universal and lingers in places still. In the West it stayed narrower, kept to baptism and dangerous illness. It may have sprung from a mistaken idea that the Eucharist was absolutely needed for salvation, drawn from John chapter six.

Present law was settled by the Fourth Lateran Council and later confirmed. A keener religious sense is asked for Communion than for confession. Pastors bear the weighty duty of preparing children for First Communion. Morrisroe lists the norms: pascal time, the parish church as a rule, lasting impression on the child, and a solemn Mass with boys and girls attired and seated apart. A short address may precede the distribution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-von-bo:
Barnabas Dieringer's entry follows Conrad von Bolanden, pen name of Joseph Bischoff, German novelist born at Niedergeilbach in 1828, son of a rich merchant. He attended Blieskastel's Latin school and Speyer's seminary, then Munich University for theology in 1849. Ordained in 1852, he served as cathedral assistant pastor. Two years later he became pastor at Kirchheim Bolanden, source of his pen name, then at Börrstadt and Berghausen.

During these years he wrote A Wedding Trip, Queen Bertha, Historical Tales of Frederick II, and Gustav Adolf. In 1870 he resigned his parish for literary work alone, living in retirement at Speyer. Later novels include Canossa, Trowel or Cross, Night of Saint Bartholomew, Savonarola, Crusades, Wambold, Charlemagne, and Otto the Great. Written for the people, brilliant and simple, they defend the Catholic standpoint with original sources. Day's questions draw severe, unjust criticism, yet the works found wide readers and translations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelis-enge:
George Williamson's entry treats Cornelis Engelbrechtsen, also Engelberts and Engelbrecht, now usually Engelbrechtsz. The Dutch painter, born at Leyden in 1468 and died there in 1533, may be Cornelis de Hollandere, of Antwerp's Guild of Saint Luke in 1492. He is said to have been Holland's first oil painter, and a profound student of Jan Van Eyck.

His principal paintings were executed in Leyden. The city still holds his large Crucifixion, its wings showing the Sacrifice of Abraham and the Brazen Serpent, and a Pietà with six scenes from Christ's life. A Madonna and Child hangs in London's National Gallery, a Crucifixion in Munich, and two double pictures at Antwerp. Most of his religious works perished in Holland's sixteenth-century iconoclastic movement. His sons were Cornelis, called Kunst, 1493 to 1544, and Luke, called Kok. Luke came to England under Henry VIII, and a signed picture of his sits at Penshurst.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-ammen:
A biographical entry follows Daniel Ammen, an American naval officer and author born in Ohio in 1820 and dead at Washington in 1898.
