Appointed midshipman in 1834, he studied briefly at West Point under his brother Jacob, later a Union general, and rose to lieutenant in 1849 and rear admiral in 1877. In the Civil War he served on blockade duty with Admiral Dupont's fleet.

Ashore, he led the Bureau of Yards and Docks and then the Bureau of Navigation until retirement in 1878. He designed the ram Katahdin and the Ammen balsa life raft. He championed a Nicaraguan canal, serving on the 1872 commission that backed that route and as delegate to the 1879 Paris congress. In retirement he farmed at Ammendale, where his generosity built Saint Joseph's church, and wrote naval memoirs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dresden:
Dresden, capital of the Kingdom of Saxony and home of its royal family, lies on both banks of the Elbe, crossed there by five bridges and ringed by pleasant heights. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry counts, with suburbs, over five hundred thousand people in December 1905. Most were Evangelical Lutherans, with some forty-four thousand Catholics, three thousand Jews, and a small Reformed body.

Dresden housed the vicar apostolic for Saxony, the Catholic consistory, and the vicarial court. In 1907 it counted twenty-four clergy, six Catholic parish churches, a garrison church shared with Protestants, and schools and charities. The entry closes with Dresden histories and journals for readers who want the city's Catholic story in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-plowde:
Edmund Plowden was an English Jesuit of the age of suppression and restoration, born in 1743 and dead in France in 1821. Schooled at Saint Omer, he joined the Society in 1759 and was ordained at Rome in 1770. When the Society was suppressed in 1773 he was minister of the English College at Bruges, and the local government kept him locked up for months after the college closed.

Freed, he taught at Liege, served as chaplain at Lulworth, and preached at the consecration of Bishop Carroll in 1790. He helped run Stonyhurst College from its start in 1794, became the first master of novices when the Society returned in England, and was made provincial in 1817. Dying on the road home from Rome, he was buried with full military honours by mistake, since townsfolk took him for an army general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-arden:
Edward Arden was a Warwickshire Catholic gentleman put to death in 1583, in a case the entry calls a plain miscarriage of justice. Head of a family prominent in the county for six centuries, he had been high sheriff in 1575. His father was a second cousin of Mary Arden, the mother of Shakespeare. Arden kept a priest, Father Hugh Hall, at Park Hall disguised as a gardener.

His son-in-law John Somerville, angered by the wrongs of Mary Queen of Scots, spoke threats against Queen Elizabeth. Seized and racked, Somerville named Arden in a plot to kill the queen. Tried at Guildhall in London on 16 December 1583, Arden was convicted largely on Hall's word and hanged at Smithfield two weeks later, still protesting that his only crime was his faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-haward:
Edward Hawarden, also spelled Harden, was an English theologian and controversialist born in Lancashire in 1662 and dead in London in 1735. His family kept private chapels through persecution and often appears on recusant rolls. After a brilliant course at Douai he taught classics and philosophy there, was ordained in 1686, and took the chair of divinity.

In 1688 he spent two months teaching divinity at Magdalen College, Oxford, which James II meant to make a Catholic seat of learning, but the revolution sent him back to Douai. Charges that he spread Jansenism were cleared by Rome. From 1707 he worked on missions at Gilligate and Aldcliffe, then in London as a writer of controversy, winning Oxford's thanks for defending the Trinity against Samuel Clarke in 1719.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-patric:
Edward Patrick Allen was the fifth Bishop of Mobile, Alabama, born at Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1853. He took his college course at Mount Saint Mary's in Emmitsburg, Maryland, graduating in 1878, and stayed on there for theology. Ordained priest in December 1881, he taught at Mount Saint Mary's, then served as assistant at the Boston cathedral and at Framingham.

In 1884 he returned to Mount Saint Mary's as its president, a post he held until he was named Bishop of Mobile. He was consecrated at Baltimore in May 1897, and Georgetown University had given him a doctorate in divinity in 1889. The entry is a short record of steady academic and pastoral service rising, step by step, to the head of a southern diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-father-damien:
Father Damien was a Belgian missionary priest who served the lepers of Molokai. Born in 1840, he joined the Fathers of the Sacred Heart at Louvain. Sent to Hawaii in 1864, he built chapels with his own hands. In 1873 he volunteered as resident priest of the Molokai leper settlement.

Six hundred lepers lived there when he arrived, with almost no medical care. Damien dressed ulcers, raised cottages, dug graves, and made coffins. After twelve years he found the disease in himself, yet kept working. He died in 1889, his name later cleared of slander by Stevenson and others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frances-allen:
Frances Allen, born at Sunderland, Vermont, on 13 November 1784 and dead at Montreal on 10 September 1819, was the first New England-born woman to become a nun. Her father was Ethan Allen, the Revolutionary soldier and pioneer of Vermont, an atheist, and her stepfather also kept religion out of her mind as far as he could. Yet her keen, inquiring intellect drew her toward Catholic belief, and at twenty-one she asked to travel to Montreal, supposedly to learn French.

There she became a pupil of the Sisters of the Congregation of Notre Dame in 1807. A sister's simple request that she place flowers on an altar and adore the Real Presence began her deeper conversion. She entered religious life despite a background that made such a step seem least likely. The entry presents her short life as a striking case of conviction formed against family and circumstance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-plowd:
Francis Plowden, born in Shropshire on 8 June 1749 and dead at Paris on 4 January 1819, was a Catholic lawyer and historian of the penal-law age. Son of William Plowden of Plowden Hall, he was educated at St. Omer and entered the Jesuit novitiate at Watten in 1766. He was teaching at Bruges when the Society was suppressed, which freed him from his first vows since he was not yet in holy orders. He married Dorothea Phillips, entered the Middle Temple, and practised as a conveyancer, the only legal work then open to Catholics.

 Quarrels with the Lord Chancellor, improvidence, and extreme views ended his practice, and he turned to writing. His Historical Review of the State of Ireland, written for the government in 1803, condemned too outspokenly for their taste and drew sharp replies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-philip-:
Franz Philip Kaulen, born at Dusseldorf on 20 March 1827 and died at Bonn on 11 July 1907, was a German scriptural scholar who gave his life to the Bible. Schooled at Dusseldorf, he studied theology at Bonn from 1846 to 1849 and was ordained at Cologne on 3 September 1850. He served missions in Cologne diocese and became lecturer at Bonn's theological school in 1859. He took a doctorate at Wurzburg in 1862 for a commentary on Jonah and won the Old Testament chair at Bonn in 1863. He became extraordinary and ordinary professor of theology in 1880 and 1882.

 His works include a Manchu grammar of 1875, a study of the confusion of languages at Babel, and above all his editorship of Herder's great Church Lexicon. He contributed many articles to it. In its 1882 preface he set the programme his work followed: depth of learning with church correctness and clear, intelligible presentation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-xaver-f:
Franz Xaver Freiherr von Wulfen, born at Belgrade on 5 November 1728 and died at Klagenfurt on 17 March 1805, was an Austrian Jesuit botanist and pioneer explorer of the Eastern Alps. Son of Lieutenant Field-Marshal Christian Friedrich von Wulfen, he finished studies at Kaschau and joined the Jesuits in 1745. He lived as student and teacher, chiefly of mathematics and physics, at Vienna, Graz, Neusohl, Gorz, Laibach, and from 1764 Klagenfurt, remaining there after the Jesuits' suppression.

From his twenty-second year he gave himself with keen zeal to botany. His unusual talent, exact observation and description, and tireless research over fifty years make him a leading botanist of the post-Linnaean age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-ber:
Friedrich Maassen, a professor of law born at Wismar in 1823, became a leading historian of canon law. After studying at Jena, Berlin, Kiel, and Rostock, he practiced as an advocate and took his degree in 1851. A convert to the Catholic faith soon after, he left public office hopes behind and turned to teaching at Bonn. His 1853 book on the Roman primacy won him swift scholarly fame.

Count Thun called him to Pesth in 1855, and chairs at Innsbruck, Graz, and Vienna followed. His great history of canon law sources reached only one volume, published at Graz in 1870. His articles, his Pseudoisidor studies, and his edition of Merovingian councils for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica filled the gap. He also denounced the Prussian Kulturkampf in ringing prose.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-von:
Friedrich von Hausen, one of the earliest German minnesingers, sang of love in forms borrowed from France and died on crusade. His name first appears in a Mainz document of 1171, and his dialect points to the middle Rhine, though several towns claim his birth. He served at Italian courts, met Frederick Barbarossa, and rode with the emperor's crusade of 1189.

Hausen fell with his horse at Philomelium in May 1190 while chasing the enemy, and the whole army mourned him. With Veldeke he brought the Romance strain into German love song, shaping verses on a French ten-syllable line with dactylic beat. His rhymes stay rough at times, and his songs prize wordplay and artifice over plain feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fuenfkirchen:
Fünfkirchen, now Pécs in Hungary, is a diocese whose roots reach an early Christian burial chamber of the fourth century. Named for its five churches, it became a bishopric under King Stephen I in 1009, with the Frankish Benedictine Bonipert as first bishop. His successor Maurus raised a cathedral on the old church of Saint Peter and stands as Hungary's first church writer.

The see's fortunes swung with history: its school rose to a university in 1367, then faded after the Turkish victory of 1526. Turks held the city from 1543 and turned the cathedral into a mosque until 1687. Later bishops held synods, founded a lyceum, and restored the cathedral. By the article's count the diocese held 178 parishes, German, Magyar, and mixed alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-allen:
George Allen, an educator born at Milton, Vermont, in 1808, taught ancient languages at two universities before becoming a Catholic. He graduated from the University of Vermont in 1827 and was admitted to the bar in 1831. Turning to theology, he served as rector of an Episcopal church at Saint Albans, Vermont, from 1834 to 1837.

In 1837 Allen became professor of ancient languages at Delaware College in Newark. In 1845 he took the same chair at Philadelphia's university, later as professor of Greek. He entered the Catholic Church in 1847, midway through his Philadelphia career. He died at Worcester, Massachusetts, in May 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerhard-of-zu:
Gerhard of Zutphen, a mystical writer born in 1367, stood among the first Brothers of the Common Life. Founded by Gerard Groote and Florentius Radewyns at Deventer, the community prized plain living and high thinking, and Gerhard surpassed it in absorption in sacred science and oblivion of earthly things. As librarian, his strong grasp of moral theology and canon law helped the brothers meet prejudice against their way of life.

His best-known works, Homo Quidam and Beatus Vir, are almost identical, preserved in de la Bigne's Patristic Library. Two treatises on prayer and Scripture reading in the mother tongue are also ascribed to him. Controversialists like Ullmann have used his zeal for vernacular Scripture to tie the Brothers to the German Reformers, but his own arguments, as quoted, give that claim almost no foundation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerlac-peters:
Gerlac Peterssen, a contemplative born at Deventer in 1377 or 1378, lived the Brethren of the Common Life's quiet craft. He gave his days to calligraphy, copying manuscripts, teaching, and prayer, keeping company with Rucksack, Radon, Kale, Gerard of Zutphen, the à Kempis brothers, and Vos of Hayden. When Radon founded Windesheim's monastery of regular canons in 1386, Gerlac followed and stayed until 1403 as a simple clerk, his only post that of sexton.

Called another Kempis, Gerlac left his brethren for his cell, saying somebody waited for him there. Critics have credited Kempis with Gerlac's words and theories, and the Imitation is said to reproduce his ascetic spirit. Thomas à Kempis even copied into his 1441 Imitation Gerlac's Soliloquies passage accepting hell forever for God's greater glory, an interpolation soon deleted. The two men's ascetic theories differ numerously and deeply.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gnesen-posen:
Gnesen-Posen is an archdiocese in the Kingdom of Prussia, joining the dioceses of Gnesen and Posen, separate until 1821, under one archbishop, with the bishopric of Culm in its province. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces both sees from their tenth-century foundations.

Posen was founded in 968 under Duke Miecyslaw, baptized through his wife Dubravka, with Jordan as first bishop, suffragan to Magdeburg. Gnesen rose around the shrine of Saint Adalbert, martyred by the heathen Prussians. Otto III made it an archbishopric on his pilgrimage in 1000, creating Cracow, Breslau, and Kolberg as its suffragans. Since the twelfth century Posen has been undisputedly a suffragan of Gnesen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godfrey-hensc:
Godfrey Henschen, also called Henskens, was a Jesuit hagiographer born at Venray in Limburg on 21 June 1601, who died at Antwerp on 11 September 1681. Son of a cloth merchant, he studied at the Jesuit college of Bois-le-Duc and entered the novitiate at Mechlin in 1619. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the collaborator who gave the Acta Sanctorum its definitive form.

Ordained priest in 1634 and sent to Antwerp the next year, he joined Father Bollandus on the first volumes of the Acta Sanctorum. His commentary on the Acts of Saint Amand suggested the course to follow and shaped the scientific work. He collaborated on seventeen volumes, January through the first six of May. He journeyed with Papebroch through Italy, France, and Germany from 1660 to 1662, and served as first librarian of the Bollandist museum at Antwerp.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gottfried-hag:
Gottfried Hagen was town clerk of Cologne and author of the Cologne Reimchronik, or rhymed chronicle, who died in 1299. He held many influential posts and took an active part in his native city's public life. He served as pastor of Saint Martin the Lesser and dean of Saint George's chapter. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls his chronicle a pamphlet for municipal liberty, not a neutral record.

Written at earliest in 1270 with a supplement in 1271, the chronicle runs to some three thousand couplets. It opens with legend and recounts Cologne's conflicts with Archbishops Conrad and Engelbert II and the feuds of patricians and guilds from 1252 to 1271. Fairly accurate in facts but a thorough partisan of the Overstolzen patricians, Hagen opposed the Weisen, the guilds, and the archbishops. Yet he always treated bishops and the Holy See with respect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heaven:
Heaven, the abode of God and the blessed, is treated here under seven heads, from its names and place to its eternity and the nature of its happiness. Scripture calls it by many titles: kingdom of heaven, house of the Father, heavenly Jerusalem, paradise, crown of life, and great reward. The entry traces the word itself from Anglo-Saxon and Gothic roots meaning a covering or a home.

Theologians generally hold heaven a real place beyond the earth's limits. There the blessed dwell together, though free to move, and where at the world's end the transformed earth joins their home. Its existence is argued from reason as well as revelation. Its bliss lies chiefly in possessing God through the beatific vision, and its joy admits no sin, no end, and no unmet longing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-blys:
Jesuit controversialist Heinrich Blyssen, born at Cologne or Bonn in 1526, was sent by St. Ignatius himself with eleven companions to Bohemia to face Luther's and Hus's disciples. Only twenty-five, he debated with honour, became professor of theology and Hebrew at Prague in 1556, and published theses on choice of foods and fasting in 1559.

Rector at Prague from 1561 and at Graz from 1570, he kept up Sunday polemical lectures for clergy and laity. He answered Jacob Heerbrand's attack on his doctrine of the Church in 1577. His chief work, on receiving the Eucharist under one or both kinds, appeared at Ingolstadt in 1585, the year before his death at Graz as provincial of Austria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-von-:
Cologne Carthusian Heinrich von Dissen, born at Osnabrück in 1415, spent a laborious life in one monastery reading, copying, and writing. After philosophy and theology at Cologne, taught by Heinrich von Gorinchem, he took solemn vows in the Carthusian house there in January 1437. He stayed until his death in 1484, serving as subprior from 1457.

His Latin works, none ever printed so far as the entry knows, cover commentaries on the Psalms, Apocalypse, Sunday and feast Gospels, Athanasian Creed. Lord's Prayer, with sermons, homilies, and treatises on priestly dignity, the wiles of heretics, the whole Missal, the antiphonary, the Song of Songs, and the thirteen mansions. Copying books for the monastery library filled the hours his writing left.

Meissen lyric poet Heinrich von Meissen, called Frauenlob or woman's praise, marks the passage from Minnesong to Mastersong in German verse. Born at Meissen about the mid-thirteenth century and dead at Mainz in 1318, he wandered Germany praising princes from Bohemia and Carinthia to Denmark. He settled at Mainz in 1311 and is said to have founded the first Mastersingers' school there.

Tradition says women bore him to his grave and his Mainz tomb was restored in 1842. His nickname is traced to a contest where he ranked Frau above Weib, though he bore it young. His many lyrics on theology, morals, love, and gnomic wisdom praise women and marriage. Learned allusion and far-fetched metaphor make them formal and often obscure, at their best in the gnomic Spruch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-holden:
Henry Holden, an English priest born in 1596, studied at Douai and Paris and became a doctor of divinity and professor at the Sorbonne. He served as penitentiary at Saint-Nicolas du Chardonnet and as the Archbishop of Paris's grand vicar. Bishop Richard Smith's flight from England in 1631 sent Holden to Rome. He represented the secular clergy against those who thought a bishop in England inadvisable, and worked to avert the dissolution of the chapter. On Smith's death in 1655 he defended his friend Thomas White, alias Blackloe, beginning the Blackloist controversy, though he persuaded White to retract condemned teaching.

Holden's Divinae Fidei Analysis of 1652 sparked a long controversy with Anglican divines, and he also wrote on usury and annotated the New Testament. Late in life the Blue Nuns of Paris drew his keen interest, and he became their superior in 1661.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-of-noer:
Henry of Noerdlingen, a fourteenth-century Bavarian secular priest, is known almost entirely from his letters and the Ebners' writings between 1332 and 1351. He advised Margaretha Ebner, the mystic of Medingen, and linked the Gottesfreunde. He wrote to Tauler, Christina Ebner, Suso, and Rulman Merswin, translated Mechthild of Magdeburg into High German, and urged mystics to record their visions.

After three years at Nördlingen, Henry went into voluntary exile at Avignon in 1335 during the dispute between pope and emperor. For abiding by the interdict, he fled through Augsburg and Constance to Basle in 1339. There crowds filled his confessional and pulpit. Leaving Basle in 1347, he preached through Alsace during the Black Death and returned home in 1350, shortly before Margaretha's death. After 1352 he vanishes from the record. His fifty-eight surviving letters form the first true letter collection in German literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-cohen:
Born in Hamburg in 1820 to a Jewish merchant family, Hermann Cohen became a musician, studied under Liszt in Paris, and then turned sharply toward the Catholic faith. After his baptism in 1847 he took the Carmelite name Augustin-Marie of the Blessed Sacrament and was ordained priest in 1851. He won notice as a fiery preacher, and his own change of faith gave his sermons a stir that drew large crowds.

Cohen helped found Carmelite houses at Bagnères-de-Bigorre, Lyons, Tarasteix near Lourdes, and London, and he spread the practice of night adoration before the Blessed Sacrament. Later preaching tours took him through Germany and France, and war drove him to Switzerland. He died of smallpox in 1871 while running a hospital ward at Spandau, after a life that moved from concert rooms to cloisters and sick wards.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-of-mi:
Hermann of Minden was a thirteenth-century Dominican who led the order's German province through one of its stormiest periods. Born near Minden to the noble Scynne family, he became papal penitentiary and chaplain, served as vice-provincial, and held the provincial office from 1286 to 1290. He attended the German national council at Würzburg in 1287.

Secular clergy and towns fought hard against the young order, and quarrels with Warburg, Strasburg, Ratisbon, and Zofingen marked his term. The entry credits his energy and tact with keeping the order growing in Germany despite that pressure. His writings were few but pointed: a short treatise on the church interdict, a lost work on trials within the order, and letters prized by historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hilarius-of-s:
Hilarius of Sexten, born Christian Gatterer in the Tyrol valley of Sexten in 1839, was a Capuchin moral theologian who died in 1900. His Brixen studies done, he joined the Capuchin Franciscans in 1858 and was ordained in 1862. He taught moral theology at Meran from 1872, and clergy far beyond his own convent consulted him on hard cases, prizing his gift for applying principles to real facts.

At the order general's command he published his Compendium of Moral Theology at Meran in 1889, later adding treatises on the sacraments and on censures, plus many articles for the Linz quarterly. His somewhat original treatment won wide sales in Germany and Austria though not universal approval. He also held offices as lector, guardian, definitor, and minister-provincial, always ready to preach and hear confessions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-green:
Hugh Green was an English martyr, born about 1584 and martyred on 19 August 1642. His Protestant parents sent him to Peterhouse, Cambridge, where he graduated in 1605, but conversion led him into Douai College in 1610. He left in 1612 to test a Capuchin vocation, but poor health or some other cause ended it, and he became chaplain at Chideock Castle, home of Lady Arundell.

In March 1641, hoping to placate the Puritan Parliament, Charles I proclaimed all priests banished from England, and Green resolved to obey. News reached him late, so when he embarked, the month of grace had just run out. Arrested, tried, and condemned in August, he moved fellow captives by his constancy: women sentenced with him sought his absolution before death. A disguised Jesuit then absolved Green himself before his noble confession of faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hyacinthe-lou:
Hyacinthe-Louis de Quélen was archbishop of Paris, born there in 1778 and dead there in 1839. Educated at the Collège de Navarre and under private tutors, he was ordained in 1807, served as vicar-general of St. Brieuc, then as secretary to Cardinal Fesch. Under the Restoration he became spiritual director of Paris schools, vicar-general of Paris, and coadjutor to Cardinal Talleyrand-Périgord, succeeding him in 1821.

Royal favour from Louis XVIII and Charles X never made him subservient. As a peer he opposed converting the national debt for the middle classes' sake, praised the disgraced Chateaubriand at his Academy reception, and demanded in vain an amnesty for exiled Convention members. The 1828 ordinance disbanding Jesuits and limiting clergy recruitment issued against his advice, and he disapproved the July ordinances of 1830.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ian-theodor-b:
Jan Theodor Beelen was a Dutch exegete and orientalist, born at Amsterdam in 1807 and dead at Louvain in 1884. After a brilliant course at Rome crowned by a doctorate in theology, he became professor of Sacred Scripture and oriental languages at Louvain's reorganized Catholic University in 1836. He held that chair until 1876, resigning it to his pupil T. J. Lamy.

Among his biblical works, his commentary on Romans is especially esteemed. He also wrote a dissertation arguing that Scripture's literal sense is not always multiple. He wrote commentaries on Philippians and Acts with Greek and Latin texts, and a grammar of New Testament Greek. He set out Dutch rules for a new translation of the New Testament, then made his own three-volume translation, plus a volume of epistles and gospels for the church year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-konigsh:
Chronicler Jacob Twinger von Königshofen was born at Königshofen near Strasburg in 1346. He died at Strasburg on 27 December 1420. Few details of his life survive. He became a priest in 1382. For a time he held the parish of Drusenheim. In 1394 he became notary apostolic. In 1395 he became a canon of St Thomas at Strasburg. There he kept the archives, stock-books, and registers.

From youth he pursued history with special zeal. A Latin chronicle from before his priesthood survives. It holds extracts from many authors and reads as a mere collection. Yet it was an excellent preparation for his later work. His German chronicle became a major source for Alsatian history. The entry presents an archivist whose gathering habit preserved a region's past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-van-hoo:
Theologian and controversialist Jacob van Hoogstraten was born about 1460 at Hoogstraten, Belgium. He died at Cologne on 24 January 1527. He studied classics and theology with the Dominicans at Louvain. In 1485 he was among the first there to earn a Master of Arts. He then entered the Dominican order. He was ordained priest in 1496. He continued theology studies at Cologne university.

In 1498 the Ferrara general chapter named him theology professor at Cologne's Dominican college. In 1500 he became prior at Antwerp. After his term he returned to Cologne. In February 1504 he earned his doctorate in theology. At Pavia in 1507 he became regent of studies and university theology professor. His vast learning made him a leading defender of scholastic theology. The entry follows a Dominican scholar into the Reformation debates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaen:
Jaén is a diocese in southern Spain, its city capital of the province of the same name. The city sits in northeastern Andalusia on Monte Jabalcuz's lower northeastern slope, about 1,800 feet above sea level. In 1900 its population was 26,434. From 1013 to 1090 the city, the Romans' Aurgi, was capital of the independent Moorish kingdom of Djayyan. St Ferdinand III of Castile and León reconquered it from the Moors in April 1246.

Local tradition names St Euphrasius as first bishop, counted among the seventy disciples. He is said to have been sent to southern Spain with St Torquatus and five other apostolic pupils by Peter and Paul. He settled at Iliturgis, now Andújar, where tradition says he suffered martyrdom in the year 68. The entry pairs a mountain city's Moorish and Christian past with its bishop list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Terrien, a French Jesuit theologian born in 1832 and dead near Paris in 1903, taught dogmatic theology for most of his life. He entered the Society at Angers in 1854, taught philosophy for two years. He then taught dogma for twenty-two years at Laval and Saint Helier, and later at the Catholic Institute of Paris.

Terrien published little at first beyond a Latin treatise for private use and manuscript works in the positive style of Franzelin. A neo-Thomist study of 1894 marked a turn, and he then wrote popular French works on devotion to the Sacred Heart and on grace as adopted sonship. Those books carried deep theology to ordinary readers.

Jean-Baptiste Van Eycken, a Belgian painter born at Brussels in 1809 and dead at Schaerbeek in 1853, left trade for art after his father's death in 1829. He joined the Belgian Academy in 1830, won a major prize in 1835, and became professor of drawing and painting four years later.

A trip to Italy in 1838 sharpened his eye, and his Divine Pity, shown in 1839, won a gold medal in France. For La Chapelle church he painted Captive Christians, Saint Boniface, and fourteen scenes of Christ's Passion, earning the Order of Leopold. His Abundance, copied for England's prince consort, remains his best-known picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-joseph-t:
Jean-Joseph Thonissen, a Belgian law professor and minister born at Hasselt in 1817 and dead at Louvain in 1891. He began in the magistracy and provincial administration while writing on penal law. Dismissed by a Liberal ministry, Louvain gave him the criminal law chair in 1848, and in 1863 he entered parliament.

Thonissen won fame in penal law but ranged across history and social science, taking the 1886 national prize for social science. He commented on the penal code, pushed reform of criminal procedure as minister, and planned a vast history of criminal law. He completed parts on Brahmin India, Egypt, Judea with a Pentateuch penal code, Athens, and the Franks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-ernest:
Johann Ernest Hanxleden, a Jesuit missionary in India born at Ostercappeln in 1681 and dead in Malabar in 1732. He volunteered for India as a young student and made his novitiate on the road. Leaving Augsburg in December 1699 with Fathers Weber and Mayer, he crossed Italy, Turkey, Syria, Armenia, and Persia to the Gulf, where his companions died at sea.

Landing alone in India in December 1700, Hanxleden laboured over thirty years on the Malabar coast, dying as professor in the Saint Thomas Christians' seminary. With Heinrich Roth he pioneered European Sanskrit study, first to write a Sanskrit grammar and first to compile a Malabar-Sanskrit-Portuguese lexicon. Paulinus carried his grammar manuscript to Rome, hailing him his day's finest Sanskrit scholar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-jacob-:
Johann Jacob Christoffel von Grimmelshausen, the seventeenth century's greatest German novelist, was born near Gelnhausen about 1625 amid the Thirty Years War and died in 1676. Carried off as a boy by marauding troopers, he lived a soldier's life until war's end in 1648, and from 1667 served Strasbourg's bishop as bailiff at Renchen.

Little is known of Grimmelshausen from 1648 to 1667, though his books show wide travel, and he moved from Protestant youth to Catholic death, as Renchen's parish record attests. His picaresque Simplicissimus of 1669, modelled on Spanish rogue tales, tells a hero's war fortunes. Coarse episodes, unfailing humour, and deep religious spirit mark it, followed by Trutzsimplex, Springinsfeld, and Bird's Nest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-jansse:
Johann Janssen, a German historian born at Xanten in 1829 and died at Frankfurt in 1891. He was schooled at home, apprenticed briefly to a coppersmith from 1842 to 1844 without aptitude, and graduated from Recklinghausen gymnasium in 1849. He studied theology and history at Münster, Louvain, Bonn, and Berlin.

Janssen took a Bonn philosophy doctorate in 1853 on Wibald, abbot of Stablo and Corvey, lectured at Münster academy in 1854. That September he took Frankfurt gymnasium's history chair for Catholic pupils, holding it until death. Spare hours went to research in many learned volumes and archive visits, including months in Italy and Rome in the mid-1860s among Vatican papers on the German past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-allen:
John Allen was Archbishop of Dublin, canonist, and Chancellor of Ireland in the stormy years of Henry VIII's break with Rome. Born in 1476, he studied at Oxford and Cambridge, spent years in Italy on business for Archbishop Warham, and was ordained in 1499. He became Cardinal Wolsey's supple commissary in suppressing minor monasteries, work that drew complaints to the king.

Rewarded with Dublin in 1528 and the Irish chancellorship, he aided Wolsey's legatine business, including the collusive suit meant to annul Henry's marriage to Katharine without her knowledge. He wrote on the pallium and on guardianship customs, and ordered two great registers of his see, the Black Book and the Green Repertory, still preserved at Dublin. He was murdered in 1534, a victim of the political violence of the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bellende:
John Bellenden was a Scottish poet and translator who brought Boece's history of Scotland into the Scots tongue. Born at Haddington or Berwick late in the fifteenth century, he studied at St. Andrews, took a doctorate in divinity at the Sorbonne in Paris, and returned carrying Hector Boece's Historia Scotorum, winning great favor at the court of James V.

The king set him to translate the Historia into the Scots vernacular. That work, with his poems of the period, took about three years. The king also commissioned a translation of Livy, never before attempted in English. Made Archdeacon of Moray, he opposed Protestantism vigorously under the next reign. He fled to escape persecution and died at Rome about 1587. He may be the same man who served as secretary to the Earl of Angus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-dryden:
John Dryden was the English poet, dramatist, and critic who dominated the Restoration stage and shaped the heroic couplet. Born in Northamptonshire in 1631 to a Parliamentary family, he was a king's scholar at Westminster. He entered Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1650. He mourned Cromwell in his Heroic Stanzas of 1658 before welcoming Charles II with Astraea Redux in 1660.

His Essay on Dramatic Poesy appeared in 1668. His plays, from The Wild Gallant of 1662 through The Indian Emperor and The Maiden Queen, mixed Spanish models with his own developing theory, set out in famous prefaces. Elected to the Royal Society in 1662 and married to Lady Elizabeth Howard in 1663, he became the age's leading man of letters. The entry traces a career that moved from Cromwellian elegy to royalist celebration without ever losing its command of verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josef-wilhelm:
Josef Wilhelm Karl Kleutgen was a German Jesuit theologian and philosopher who led the nineteenth-century revival of Scholastic thought. Born at Dortmund in 1811, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1834, taught in Switzerland and Rome, and became a consultor of the Congregation of the Index. His mastery of Thomas Aquinas earned him the nickname Thomas returned to life.

Kleutgen wrote the Theology and Philosophy of Former Times against modern German thinkers. He drafted the first version of Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Aeterni Patris on Scholasticism and helped prepare the Vatican Council's constitution on faith. A false 1879 charge of complicity in a poisoning was formally denied by the Inquisition's own notary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-galien:
Joseph Galien was a French Dominican who taught theology and dreamed of sailing the air. Born at Saint-Paulien in 1699, he joined the order at Le Puy, taught philosophy at Bordeaux from 1726, and held chairs of theology and philosophy at Avignon. In 1751 he gave up teaching to study weather and physics full time.

His 1755 booklet on hail argued that airships could float in the hail belt, where air is far lighter than water. To carry a whole army to Africa, he planned a giant cube of waxed canvas and leather, each edge about six thousand five hundred feet. The scheme was fanciful, but it stands as an early, reasoned sketch of aerial navigation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-jose-egu:
Juan José Eguiara y Eguren was a Mexican scholar who defended American learning against European scorn. Born in Mexico late in the seventeenth century, he studied at San Ildefonso College and became rector of Mexico University. His learning spanned theology, canon law, philosophy, mathematics, and letters, with a gift for oratory.

Stung by Dean Martí's 1735 dismissal of New World writers, Eguiara began his Biblioteca Mexicana, a Latin roll of learned Americans. The first volume, letters A through C, appeared in 1755, with biographies to J left in manuscript. He refused the bishopric of Yucatán to keep writing. His sermons, eulogies, and fourteen volumes of theology followed. He died in 1763.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kalands-breth:
The Kalands Brethren were religious and charitable associations of priests and laypeople, thickest in northern and central Germany. They grew from monthly clergy meetings held on the first day of the month, the Kalendae, which gave them their name. After the thirteenth century those meetings hardened into organized societies of priests and laity, men and women alike. Statutes governed their reunions, their directors, their services, their funds, and their charitable spending.

A dean headed each association and a treasurer handled its revenues, while bishops assigned them churches or altars for worship. Prayers and Masses for dead members were a special care. The oldest known confraternity, at Ottberg near Höxter, is documented in 1226. The brotherhoods flourished in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, then decayed as banquets at their meetings degenerated into revels. The Reformation dissolved most of them, and only the Münster association is known to survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-august-l:
Karl August Lossen was a German petrologist and geologist, born at Kreuznach in 1841 and dead at Berlin in 1893. After practical work as a mining engineer, he studied at Berlin and Halle, graduating in 1866. He joined the Prussian geological survey, and his petrographic studies of the Harz Mountains lasted until his death. He taught petrology at the Berlin mining academy from 1870 and became professor in 1882.

Over a hundred treatises, mostly in the German Geological Society's journal from 1867 to 1891, carried his results. Harz survey maps followed from 1877, with his exhaustive work on Berlin's soil. His papers on contact and dynamometamorphosis made him the authority London's 1888 congress asked to address on crystallized slate. The mineral lossenite, from Laurion, bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-von-haim:
Karl von Haimhausen, a German missionary of noble Bavarian family, was born at Munich in 1692 and died in Chile in 1767. He entered the Society of Jesus and went to Chile as a missionary in 1724. He taught theology and served for years as rector of Santiago's Collegium Maximum. As provincial procurator, master of novices, and instructor, he won such esteem that Spanish bishops and the viceroy chose him as confessor.

He finished Santiago's college church, built a novitiate and two retreat houses, and served the colony's industry. Spain's American gold and silver had ruined home industry, and colonial crafts decayed in turn. Their revival owed much to German and Dutch missionaries, and Haimhausen founded an arts-and-crafts school at Calera, staffing it from Germany. Its bell-founders, watchmakers, goldsmiths, organ-builders, and furniture makers produced work Chile had never seen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ligamen:
Ligamen, Latin for bond, is the existing marriage tie barring a second marriage in canon law. Since marriage is monogamous and indissoluble, one still joined in valid marriage cannot contract another.

Protestantism does not take this stand, as Luther's action in Landgrave Philip of Hesse's double marriage shows. Hence one already married must prove the first tie no longer stands before marrying again. Since only death regularly dissolves marriage, proof of that death must precede the second marriage. The proof required is an official death certificate, from the parish priest or other authorized ecclesiastic, by the proper civil official, hospital directors, or military commanding officer. A secular judge's decision backed by a death certificate cannot by itself settle the question for church authorities. Death may be shown by two credible witnesses on oath, by one witness above suspicion, or by hearsay from unsuspected sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lockleven:
Lochleven is a lake in Kinross-shire, Scotland, whose island of St. Serf, eighty acres wide, sheltered monks for some seven centuries. tradition credits Brude, king of the Picts, with granting the island to the Culdees about 840, perhaps within St. Serf's own lifetime.

Later kings and bishops confirmed the gift, and in the tenth century the Culdees handed the island to the bishop for food and clothing. David I gave it to St. Andrews canons about 1145, and it stayed a cell of St. Andrews until the Reformation. Its famed prior Andrew Wyntoun likely wrote his chronicle of Scotland there, and only chapel fragments now remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludwig-van-be:
Ludwig van Beethoven was the German composer, born at Bonn probably on 16 December 1770 and dead at Vienna on 26 March 1827. His father sang tenor in the Cologne elector's chapel, where his Dutch grandfather had led the music, so the boy grew up inside music.

A stern father drilled him on violin from five, and teachers Pfeiffer, Van den Eeden, and Neefe trained him on piano, organ, and composition. By thirteen he had published six sonatas, later disowned, and by fifteen he was assistant court organist. Vienna in 1792 brought study with Haydn, then Albrechtsberger, and the deafness, symphonies, and quartets that made him the age's towering voice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-jose:
Cologne theologian Matthias Joseph Scheeben (1835-1888) was a mystic whose mind dwelt on grace, the union of God and man in Christ, the beatific vision, and God's all-pervading presence. He studied at Rome's Gregorian University from 1852 to 1859 and was ordained in 1858. He taught dogmatic theology at Cologne's seminary from 1860 to 1875, awing pupils with long, abstruse sentences that shed scant light.

His books open with three treatises on grace, including Die Herrlichkeiten der gottlichen Gnade of 1863. His chief work, the Handbuch der katholischen Dogmatik of 1873-87, stayed unfinished at his death. It was later completed in German by Atzberger and Englished as A Manual of Catholic Theology. He also defended the Vatican Council against Dollinger and the Old Catholics, and founded Cologne's Pastoralblatt in 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-meissen:
Meissen, a former see of north-east Germany, grew from a castle King Henry I built about 928 to shield German settlers among the Wends. To secure Christian missions, Otto I proposed at the Roman Synod of 962 a new archdiocese at Magdeburg. John XII agreed, and at Ravenna in 967 three suffragans were planned: Meissen, Merseburg, and Zeitz. The founding year is unknown, since the oldest records are forgeries, but Otto's endowment of 971 is genuine.

The first bishop, Burchard, who died in 969, founded a monastery that grew into a chapter of canons in the eleventh century. By 1346 the diocese ran from the Erzgebirge south to the Neisse and Queis mouths, east to the Oder, and north to the middle Spree. It held five provostries, four archdeaconries, and two deaneries, from Meissen and Riesa to Bautzen and Niederlausitz. Poorly endowed at first, it later gained large estates under Otto III and Henry II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-o-log:
Michael O'Loghlen was born at Ennis, County Clare, in 1789 and died in 1846. He learned at Ennis Academy and Trinity College, Dublin, and qualified for the Irish Bar in 1811. Sheer talent made him a dazzling pleader. His first real triumph came as O'Connell's stand-in on the day of O'Connell's duel with D'Esterre in 1815.

From 1820 to 1830 case after case came his way through O'Connell. In 1834 O'Connell's backing carried him into office as solicitor general for Ireland, the first Catholic in that post since James II. He sat as M.P. for Dungarvan. When Perrin rose to the Bench in 1835, O'Loghlen became attorney general. Twelve months later he took Sir William Cusack Smith's place as baron of the exchequer, the first Catholic on the bench for nearly a century and a half. In 1837 he took the Irish mastership of the rolls, held it till death, and pushed through many legal reforms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michel-le-qui:
Michel Le Quien, French historian and theologian, was born at Boulogne-sur-Mer on 8 October 1661 and died at Paris on 12 March 1733. He learned at Plessis College, Paris, then at twenty joined the Dominicans at St-Germain and professed in 1682. At death he was librarian of the Rue St-Honore convent, a post held nearly all his life, helping learned men who sought light on theology and church antiquity.

Under Pere Marsollier he mastered classical tongues, Arabic, and Hebrew, at what seemed the cost of his French. His chief works: first, the Defense du texte hebreu et de la version vulgate of 1690, answering Pezron the Cistercian, who had built his chronology on the Septuagint alone. Pezron hit back, and Le Quien hit back again. Second, the Johannis Damasceni opera omnia of 1712, Greek text with Latin translation in two folio volumes, with dissertations, though a planned third volume never came.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minden:
Minden, a former Westphalian see on the Weser, is first heard of in 798, and in 803 the Treaty of Salz with the Saxons speaks of it as a see. Its first bishop, Erkambert, probably a Saxon, was appointed in 780 and died in 813. The third bishop, Dietrich I, fell in battle against the Northmen, and the fifth, Drogo, founded a convent at Mollenbeck.

The diocese grew until it stretched east across the Aller to Celle and west to the Hunte. But under Bishop Franz I of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttel, who embroiled the see in feuds and died of his excesses, the Reformation spread rapidly. His successor Franz II von Waldeck, a secret adherent of the new teachings, aided it privately. By the Peace of Westphalia the diocese was suppressed, its lands passing to Brandenburg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mrs-augustus-:
Mrs. Augustus Craven, born Pauline-Marie-Armande-Aglae Ferron de la Ferronnays in London on 12 April 1808, was a French Catholic author. She died in Paris on 1 April 1891. Her family had suffered emigration and lost estates in the Revolution. Her father, Comte Auguste-Marie de la Ferronnays, returned to France through devotion to the Duc de Berri. He served eight years as ambassador to Saint Petersburg, and became foreign minister to Charles X in 1827.

Pauline moved in brilliant Restoration society, and in Naples she met Augustus Craven, attache to the British legation. She married him in August 1834, days before he entered the Catholic Church. Diplomatic postings took them to Lisbon, Brussels and Stuttgart. Her later writing, above all the book Le Récit d'une soeur, drew on her family's sorrows and faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oettingen:
Oettingen, now Altötting in Upper Bavaria, grew from a Carolingian royal palace into a great pilgrimage town. King Karlmann founded a Benedictine monastery there in 876, Hungarians burned church and abbey in 910, and Duke Louis I rebuilt them in 1228 for twelve Augustinian canons.

The canons guarded the Liebfrauen chapel and its miraculous image of Our Lady, drawing some 300,000 pilgrims a year. Jesuits, Franciscans, Redemptorists, and Capuchins served the shrine in turn, and since the seventeenth century the hearts of Bavarian rulers have rested there. About 300,000 pilgrims come to the shrine annually, a figure the entry records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-of-blasi:
Otto of Blasien was a chronicler born about the middle of the twelfth century. He died on 23 July 1223 at Saint Blasien in the Black Forest. Nothing is known of his life's events, though he probably became abbot of the famed Benedictine house there in his later days. He is known as the writer who carried on the chronicles of Otto of Freising.

He shared his gift for a clear survey of events, and a lofty style modelled on the ancient classics. His annals run from 1146 to 1209, from Conrad III to the murder of Philip of Swabia. Writing at a distance from the facts, he stays objective, even while favouring the Hohenstaufen. After Otto IV won recognition as emperor, he writes of him just as evenly, yet the tale stops, with no clear cause, at his coronation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ottobeuren:
Ottobeuren, once a Benedictine abbey and now a priory, stands near Memmingen in the Bavarian Allgaeu. Blessed Toto founded it in 764 and dedicated it to Saint Alexander the martyr. Toto died about 815. Saint Ulrich held the abbacy in 972. Little else is known of its early years. Discipline sank in the eleventh century until Abbot Adalhalm brought the Hirsau reform in 1082.

Fire struck in 1153 and again in 1217, and by 1416 only six or eight monks remained, on revenues under 46 silver marks a year. Abbot Leonard Wiedemann revived the house from 1508, raising a printing shop and a common house of studies for Swabian Benedictines. Its most flourishing age followed. King Louis I of Bavaria re-established it as a priory in 1834. It took charge of the parish, a district school, and a trade school for poor boys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paten:
The paten is a small shallow dish of precious metal. It holds the bread offered to God at the Mass offertory, and receives the consecrated Host again after the Fraction. Paten comes from Latin patina or patena, after Greek patane, a flat open vessel like a plate or dish. Early patens gathered the faithful's bread offerings and shared the broken loaf's fragments, each communicant taking a portion in hand from the dish.

Duchesne argued from early Roman ordines that Rome used white linen bags instead. Church plate inventories in the Liber Pontificalis prove otherwise. They list silver ministerial dishes, some twenty or thirty pounds in weight, paired with ministerial chalices for the wine. Later pages trace the paten's shrinking to its modern small disc, its materials, blessing, and the rule that it match the chalice in metal and care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-cullen:
Paul Cullen was Cardinal Archbishop of Dublin, born at Prospect in County Kildare on 29 April 1803 and dead at Dublin on 24 October 1878. Schooled at Ballytore's Shackleton School, he entered Carlow College in 1816 and Rome's Propaganda College in 1820. Closing a distinguished course, he held a public disputation on 11 September 1828 in 224 theses from all theology and church history. Leo XII presided, ten cardinals attended, and the young Pecci, future Leo XIII, was present and deeply impressed.

Cullen mastered classical and Oriental tongues, and straight after ordination took Propaganda's chairs of Hebrew and Sacred Scripture, with charge of its famed press. Later pages follow his Roman years, his Dublin archbishopric, and his role at Vatican I. They cover his founding of schools, seminaries, and churches, and his sway over Irish Catholic life in a period of famine, emigration, and national stirrings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-joseph:
Pierre-Joseph van Beneden was a Belgian zoologist who taught at Louvain for nearly sixty years. He was born at Mechlin in 1809 and became curator of the Louvain natural history museum in 1831. Within five years he held Louvain's chairs of zoology and comparative anatomy. He opened new ground in the study of sea life and fossil whales.

His early work followed marine invertebrates, animals without backbones, at Ostend. In 1843 he built a seaside laboratory and aquarium there at his own cost. His prize-winning study of parasitic worms traced their tangled life histories. Later he turned to whales living and extinct, publishing with Paul Gervais a large illustrated survey of their bones.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-placidus-bock:
Placidus Böcken was a German Benedictine canonist, a scholar of church law, and vice-chancellor of the University of Salzburg. He was born at Munich in 1690 and professed at Saint Peter's Abbey in Salzburg in 1706. He was ordained in 1713, took doctorates in canon and civil law, and in 1721 succeeded Benedict Schmier as professor of canon law at Salzburg, where he taught for twenty years.

In 1729 he became vice-chancellor and served as councillor to four Salzburg archbishops. Friction with Archbishop Leopold led him to resign in 1741. His great Commentary on Universal Canon Law of 1735 to 1739 remains his chief work. It was reprinted at Paris in 1776. A 1740 sermon of his, claiming that honouring the saints is needed for salvation, stirred a sharp university quarrel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raffaello-mor:
Raffaello Morghen, Italian engraver, was born at Portici in 1768, though the entry notes 1761 as a rival year, and died at Florence on 8 April 1833. His father Filippo came from a family of German engravers, and his mother was the daughter of Liani, court painter. Taught first by his father and his uncle Jean, Raffaello had produced a plate before he turned twelve. At twenty he made seven plates picturing the carnival of 1778.

He then studied at Rome under Volpato, whose daughter he married. Moved by Raphael's pictures in the Vatican, Morghen engraved the Poetry and the Theology. In 1787 he finished Guido's Aurora, from the fresco in the Rospigliosi garden-house, a style that suited his art and age better than copying greater masters. A Naples visit in 1790 brought a court salary offer of six hundred ducats, the entry notes, and later plates after Poussin close the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ranulf-higden:
Ranulf Higden, Benedictine chronicler, died in 1364. This encyclopedia entry tells that he was a west-country man, professed as a monk at Saint Werburg's Abbey, Chester, in 1299. Beyond that date nothing is recorded of his personal life. He lives on through one great work, the Polychronicon, a universal history running down to his own times.

As the fullest history available in the fourteenth century, it won great popularity in that age and the next. Even its contemporary part, carrying the story to 1342, is of no remarkable value, the entry warns. John of Trevisa turned it into English in 1387, and Caxton printed that translation in 1482, with Wynkyn de Worde following in 1495. A later fifteenth-century translation fills nine Rolls Series volumes, whose introductions gather all that is known of Higden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regina-coeli-:
Regina Coeli opens the anthem of the Blessed Virgin. This encyclopedia entry sets its use: recitation is prescribed in the Roman Breviary from Compline of Holy Saturday until None of the Saturday after Pentecost. In choir the anthem is sung standing. It illustrates the anthem as a syntonic strophe, one depending on the accent of the word. The Latin runs: Regina coeli laetare, Alleluia, Quia quem meruisti portare, Alleluia, Resurrexit, Sicut dixit, Alleluia, Ora pro nobis Deum, Alleluia.

In the first two verses the accent falls on the second, fourth and seventh syllables, with quia counted as one syllable. In the last two verses it falls on the first and third syllables, and Alleluia serves as refrain. The anthem's author is unknown. The 1911 Vatican Antiphonary gives one melody form, and the lines' syllabic lengths make a faithful English verse translation hard, though composers have often set the anthem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-plowde:
Robert Plowden was an English Jesuit missioner who built up the Catholic community at Bristol. Charles Plowden's elder brother, born in 1740, he joined the Jesuits in 1756, with ordination following in 1763. After directing Carmelite nuns at Hoogstraet, he returned to England and served at Arlington in Devon from 1777 to 1787.

At Bristol he found Catholics with only a wretched room in a back alley for a chapel. His exertions raised St Joseph's Church with a presbytery and schools, and his work spread to Swansea and the South Wales district, of which he counts as principal founder. He stayed at Bristol nearly thirty years, beloved for frank character, disinterested labour, and bounty to the poor. Removed in 1815, he served as chaplain to the Fitzherberts at Swynnerton until 1820, then retired to Wappenbury, where he died in 1823. He also translated a French devotional work, The Elevation of the Soul to God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-pullen:
Robert Pullen was one of the first recorded masters of the Oxford schools, an English philosopher-theologian of the twelfth century. Nothing is known of his early life, though he was of English parentage. A conjecture placing his birth at Poole in Dorset has no evidence. Henry I is said to have offered him a bishopric, which he refused from devotion to philosophy.

He studied in England, then went to Paris during Stephen's troubled reign to study in peace, lecturing there before returning to teach at Oxford. He opened schools, taught without fees, supported scholars at his own cost, and fostered the growth of the Oxford schools. He was Archdeacon of Rochester by 1134, though long absence in Paris drew his bishop's complaint. St Bernard's letter excuses his detention in Paris for his sound doctrine. Doubts persist about identifying him with the cardinal of the same name. He died in 1147.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rogier-van-de:
Rogier van der Weyden was a Flemish painter of the fifteenth century, famed for religious pictures of dramatic force. Born at Tournai in 1399 or 1400 as De la Pasture, later Van der Weyden in Flemish, he came from a family settled there since 1260. Apprenticed to Robert Campin in 1427, he became a master and joined the Guild of St Luke in 1432. He served as painter to Brussels in 1435 until the office was abolished a year later.

Vasari wrongly called him a pupil of van Eyck; Flemish records prove Campin his master. His work is far more religious than van Eyck's, its figures dramatic, animated, and at times almost tragic. He lived at Brussels, well paid, with four children. He painted altarpieces for Miraflores, Scheut, Tournai, and Herinnes. His greatest works include the Seven Sacraments, the Adoration of the Magi, and the Prado triptych. He died at Brussels in 1464.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rouen:
Rouen is an archdiocese revived by the Concordat of 1802, with Bayeux, Evreux, and Seez as suffragans. Curtailed in 1802, it kept its archbishop's title of Primate of Normandy. Rouen, chief city under Constantine and later of Neustria, has been Normandy's capital since 912. Ninth- and tenth-century catalogues and the cathedral's Liber Eburneus to 1068 name St Mellon as first bishop. The Liber Niger of St Ouen and twelfth-century lists put a certain Nicasius before him.

The legend of Nicasius, based on Hilduin, makes him and his companions Quirinus and Scubiculus disciples of St Denis, martyred on the Epte's banks after coming from Rome. Under Bishop William the Good, 1079 to 1110, Nicasius was placed at the head of Rouen's episcopal lists. Saints succeeded St Mellon, including St Victricius, bishop about 380, who worked in England in 396 and pleaded for devotion to relics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruben-reuben:
Ruben is a biblical name designating a patriarch and a tribe of Israel. The patriarch Ruben, Jacob's eldest son by Lia, was born in Mesopotamia and named Ruben, see ye, a son, alluding to Lia's distress at Jacob's dislike of her. Ruben lost his birthright for an incest committed in Chanaan. At his suggestion his brothers threw Joseph into a pit instead of killing him, whence Ruben vainly hoped to rescue him.

When Jacob refused to let Benjamin go to Egypt, Ruben offered two of his sons as pledge for Benjamin's return. The tribe of Ruben lay east of Jordan, sharing with Gad the former land of the Amorite king Sehon. Its towns included Baalmaon, Bethphogor, Cariathaim, Dibon, Hesebon, Jassa, Medaba, and Sabama. In the wilderness the tribe counted over 40,000 men and marched with Gad and Simeon on Israel's south side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolph-von-l:
Rudolph von Langen, humanist and divine, was born at Everswinkel near Munster in 1438 or 1439 and died at Munster in 1519. In 1456 he entered Erfurt University, taking his B.A. in 1459 and M.A. in 1460. Before this he had been made canon of Munster cathedral and provost of the old cathedral. He went to Rome in 1466 over a bishop's election, bringing home many fresh ideas from Italy.

At Munster he anchored literary life, surrounded by like-minded men, with a library freely lent to others. Hermann von dem Busche was his pupil, gaining a love of classical literature. His own writing matters little: well read but lacking poetic talent. He wrote a lost poem on Jerusalem's destruction and a prose work published at Deventer about 1485. Poems printed at Munster in 1486 and a Rosarium in 1493 followed. His influence on others mattered far more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salminius-her:
Sozomen, one of the famous historians of the early Church, was born at Bethelia near Gaza in the last quarter of the fourth century and died probably in 447 or 448. What his epithet Salminius means cannot be settled, and any link with Salamis in Cyprus has no foundation. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with the family story he tells himself.

His grandfather became a Christian after seeing a miracle of Hilarion. Through years of persecution the household held firm, so Sozomen grew up in a Christian home and was schooled by local monks. Greek learning grounded him well, though a mention of Berytus wrongly suggested he studied law there. Settling at Constantinople, he wrote a church history prized for its use of documents and its calm, lawyer-like care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sankt-poelten:
Sankt Pölten, a diocese in Lower Austria, takes its name and origin from Fanum Sancti Hippolyti, a monastery founded in the ninth century for St Hippolytus. Its beginnings are obscure. Some hold that monks from Tegernsee in Bavaria founded a Benedictine abbey on the Traisen in 791. Charlemagne had just joined Avar lands to his empire, and Passau took the district as a mission field. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a frontier monastery.

In the ninth century Sankt Pölten marked the eastern edge of Christian civilisation, the only monastery east of the Enns. The house passed to secular canons in 985, and in 1080 the reformer Altmann of Passau replaced them with reformed Augustinian canons under Provost Engelbert. Passau's bishops prized the place as a prop of their eastern power, and the entry notes the 1284 synod held there by Bishop Gottfried.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxe-meininge:
Saxe-Meiningen, a Saxon-Thuringian duchy, covers 953 square miles with 278,792 people in 1910, including 4,870 Catholics, about two per cent, in 1905. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a small state through succession deals and a costly war choice.

The duchy arose in 1681 from succession agreements among the seven sons of Ernest the Pious of Saxe-Gotha. Later deals enlarged it, above all in 1826, when Saxe-Hildburghausen, 560 square miles with 70,000 people, was assigned to it. In the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, Duke Bernard II stood alone among Thuringian Saxon princes for Austria. Prussia occupied his land and transferred rule to his son George II, still reigning in 1911, whose heir Bernard married the Kaiser's sister Charlotte.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bridget-of:
St. Bridget of Sweden, also Birgitta, was the most celebrated saint of the Northern kingdoms, born about 1303. She died on 23 July 1373. This entry follows the daughter of Birger Persson, governor and provincial judge, or Lagman, of Uppland, and of Ingeborg Bengtsdotter. Her father was among the country's wealthiest landholders, and, like her mother, distinguished by deep piety. St. Ingrid, who died about twenty years before Bridget was born, was a near relative of the family.

Birger's daughter was carefully trained in religion, and from age seven showed signs of extraordinary religious impressions and illuminations. Her education — particularly an aunt who took her mother's place after her death about 1315 — gave her the unswerving strength of will that later distinguished her. In 1316, at thirteen, she was married to Ulf Gudmarsson, then eighteen, and the entry follows her from wife and mother to foundress and visionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-catherine-:
St. Catherine of Sweden was the fourth child of St. Bridget and her husband Ulf Gudmarsson, born in 1331 or 1332. She died on 24 March 1381. This entry follows a woman who at her death headed the convent of Wadstena, founded by her mother, hence her occasional name Catherine Vastanensis. At seven she was sent to the Riseberg abbess to be educated. Like her mother, she soon showed a desire for self-mortification and devotion.

At her father's command, when about thirteen or fourteen, she married Eggart von Kurnen, a noble of German descent. She at once persuaded her very religious husband to join her in a vow of chastity. Both lived in virginity, devoted to Christian perfection and active charity. Deep though her love for her husband was, Catherine accompanied her mother to Rome, where Bridget went in 1349, and the entry follows her there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fidelis-of:
Fidelis of Sigmaringen, Capuchin preacher murdered in 1622, had prayed from his novitiate for two favours: never to fall into mortal sin, and to die for the faith. Born in 1577 to the burgomaster of Sigmaringen, he studied at Freiburg, tutored Wilhelm von Stotzingen through France and Italy, then took his doctorate in law in 1611. Corrupt courts drove him from advocacy to priesthood and the Capuchins. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Sevis to 24 April 1622.

Sent to the Grisons with only crucifix, Bible, breviary, and rule, he preached in churches, streets, and even heretic conventicles. At Zizers his conferences won Rudolph de Salis and many others. Alarmed preachers painted his mission as Austrian politics, inflaming the people. In Lent 1622 his fervour peaked, and the mission he had prayed for ended in martyrdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-kevin-coem:
Kevin of Glendalough, whose name means fair-begotten, founded a monastery that became a city in the desert. Born about 498, son of Coemlog and Coemell, he was baptized by Cronan and educated by Petroc the Briton. From age twelve he studied under monks and embraced monastic life. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 3 June 618.

He founded Glendalough, the Valley of the Two Lakes, parent of several other houses. After visiting Columba, Comgall, and Cannich at Usneach, he reached Clonmacnoise three days after Cieran's death in 544. Once his own community stood firm, he withdrew alone for four years, returning only at his monks' earnest entreaty. Of Ireland's second order of saints, he was probably never bishop. His festival is kept throughout Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-manahen:
Manahen, foster-brother of Herod Antipas, helped send Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey. A member of Antioch's church, called syntrophos, household friend, in Greek, and collactaneus, foster-brother, in the Vulgate, he stood among Antioch's prophets and doctors. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places him at Acts 13:3, where, under the Holy Spirit, the church laid hands on Saul and Barnabas and sent them out.

Luke, himself an Antiochene by Eusebius's account, may have learned Herodian details from Manahen, one of the eyewitnesses and ministers of the word who delivered Luke's material on Antipas and his house. Manahen may have become Jesus' disciple alongside Joanna, wife of Chusa, Herod's steward. When Antipas sailed for Rome in 39 seeking Caligula's favour, he met instead condemnation to perpetual exile. The entry follows a court insider turned apostolic sender.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-mary-magda:
Mary Magdalen, named either for Magdala on the west shore of Galilee or for a Talmudic phrase, stands at the heart of a long identity debate. The Gospels name her among the women who served Jesus, and record seven devils cast out of her. They place her at the foot of the cross, and make her the first recorded witness of the Resurrection. Greek Fathers generally kept three figures apart, while most Latin writers merged them into one.

Working passage by passage through Luke and John, the entry weighs whether the sinner who anointed Jesus, Mary of Bethany, and Magdalen are the same woman. It argues that John points toward one person, while Luke alone gives no ground for merging them. Readers find a careful survey of Gospel evidence, patristic opinion, and modern criticism rather than a settled life story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nicholas-o:
Nicholas Owen, a Jesuit lay brother martyred in 1606, built the hiding places that sheltered priests across Elizabethan England. Probably a carpenter or builder, he entered the Society of Jesus before 1580 and served missionary fathers for eighteen years. Imprisoned after Edmund Campion's death for declaring that martyr innocent, he later helped Father Gerard escape from the Tower.

Arrested at Hindlip Hall while impersonating Father Garnett, he was taken to the Tower and racked to force disclosures of priest holes. He died under torture rather than betray anyone, and the government prized his capture precisely because his skill had hidden so many. The entry honours a craftsman whose secret carpentry kept a persecuted mission alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ouen:
Ouen, archbishop of Rouen, moved from the Frankish court to the cloister and then to reforming a great Norman see. Born at Sancy near Soissons about 609 to Gallo-Roman parents, he was schooled at St Medard and welcomed at the court of Clothaire II. Dagobert I made him referendary, or chancellor, and used his learning on missions and, it is believed, on compiling the Salic Law.

At court he befriended Eligius, and after Dagobert's death both men left secular service for theological study. Ouen founded the abbey of Rebais in 634, was ordained priest, and was then chosen archbishop of Rouen. He founded monasteries, reformed clergy, and preached through his diocese until his death at Clichy on 24 August 683.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-stephen:
Stephen, first king of Hungary, made his people Christian and his crown a symbol of the nation. Born at Gran in 975 to the chief Géza, he was baptised with his father by Adalbert of Prague in 985, exchanging his pagan name Vaik for Stephen. In 995 he married Gisela, sister of the future emperor Henry II, and succeeded his father in 997.

To firm his rule and Christianise Hungary, he sent Abbot Astricus to Rome. Sylvester II granted royal dignity, power to found sees, and a crown, with which Stephen was crowned at Gran on 17 August 1001. He founded a monastery at Jerusalem and pilgrim hospices at Rome, Ravenna, and Constantinople. His only son Emeric died in a boar hunt in 1031, and Stephen died on 15 August 1038.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-zita-s-hom:
St Zita's Home for Friendless Women, a New York shelter founded in 1890, took in any woman without application or inquiry into faith or past. Ellen O'Keefe, called Mother Zita, founded it at 158 East 24th Street. Born in County Limerick, she emigrated to New York in 1864 and trained as a nurse at the city hospital on Blackwell's Island.

There, pity for unfortunate women whose records barred them from employment gave her life's direction. With her own savings she started the home single-handed, later joined by Mary Finnegan and Katherine Dunne. Every applicant was received regardless of religion or previous character, with shelter and a chance to reform her life. Church authorities approved from the first, and growth forced a move to larger quarters. The entry traces a practical charity for women the world had written off.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sweden:
Sweden, largest of the three Scandinavian countries, fills the eastern half of the peninsula between 55 and 68 degrees north. Bounded by Norway, the Skagerrak, the Kattegat, Finland, and the Baltic, it counts Gotland and Öland too. It covers 172,876 square miles, of which 73,040 are forest, 15,000 water, and over 20,000 farm and grass land. Granite and gneiss form its soil, chalk appears in Gotland, and coal in Skåne.

Its lakes rank among Europe's largest after Russia's, with Wenern at 2,200 square miles, Wettern the most beautiful, and Mälar the most islanded and frequented. Swift rivers drive waterfalls like Trollhättan and hold some five million horsepower, canals link lakes to the sea, and the Göta Canal stands chief among them. The massive entry then covers history, church, and culture, closing with an extensive bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synods-of-rou:
Rouen's synods stretch from about 650 to 1830, and this entry follows them in order. The first, under Archbishop Saint-Ouen, left sixteen decrees, one against simony and the rest on liturgy and canon law, though a few writers place it in the later ninth century. Later archbishops and legates kept the series alive across the Middle Ages.

Mauger was deposed for loose morals at Lisieux in 1055, Maurilius drew up a creed against Berengarius the same year, and John of Bayeux pressed reform in 1072 and 1074. William proclaimed Clermont's decrees in 1096, legates enforced celibacy in 1119 and 1128, and the last provincial synod, under Bailleul in 1830, closed a run that also condemned Fénelon in 1699.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-terence-alber:
Terence Albert O'Brien was born at Limerick in 1600 and died there in 1651. He joined the Dominicans, taking the name Albert at Limerick, where his uncle was prior. In 1622 he studied at Toledo, returning after eight years to become twice prior at Limerick and once at Lorrha. In 1643 he became provincial of his order in Ireland. The Catholic Confederation's Supreme Council valued his services. At Rome he earned the degree of Master in Theology.

On his return he visited two Lisbon houses, where word came that Urban VIII might name him coadjutor at Emly. The Supreme Council named him in late 1645, on Rinuccini's recommendation. Named coadjutor with right of succession in March 1647, he was consecrated by Rinuccini eight months later. He backed the nuncio throughout, signing declarations against Inchiquin's truce in 1648 and Ormond in 1650. Urging besieged Limerick's resistance in 1651 cost him quarter, and he was executed the day after surrender.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-albright-: The Albright Brethren, known as the Evangelical Association, were a body of American Christians chiefly of German descent. The Rev. Jacob Albright, a Pennsylvania native born in 1759 and died in 1808, founded them in 1800. They are Arminian in doctrine and theology, and Methodist Episcopal in church government. They number 148,506 members, not counting children, with 1,864 ministers and 2,043 churches in the United States, Canada, and Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-garden-of:
Scripture's first garden, home of the first parents in Genesis chapter 2, is the subject here, under the popular name paradise. That word likely comes from Persian, where it meant a royal park or pleasure ground. It never appears in classical Latin or in Greek writers before Xenophon, and Hebrew writings use it only late, borrowed from Persian.

Asaph, keeper of the king's forest in Second Esdras, illustrates the royal-park sense. Septuagint translators adopted paradeisos for Eden's garden, and Christian tradition followed, turning a Persian park into the abode of innocence. Geography, the four rivers, the Fall, and later readings of paradise close a compact biblical study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-universit:
Scotland's northern university, one of three founded there in Catholic times, owes its birth to William Elphinstone, Bishop of Aberdeen from 1483 to 1514. Early in his episcopate a petition reached Rome in King James IV's name, probably framed by Elphinstone himself, pleading ignorance across his diocese and the kingdom's north. Papal bull of 24 February 1491, or 1495 by modern reckoning, erected the university.

Elphinstone, nine years a professor at Paris and Orléans, modelled the new house on Paris in form, organisation, and wide mental training. A royal charter of 1495 assigned church revenues to academic use and granted privileges of Paris, Saint Andrews, and Glasgow. Hector Boece, philosophy professor, and early colleges complete a concise foundation history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-jame:
Teacher of the poor Theodore James Ryken, known as Brother Francis Xavier, founded the Xaverian Brothers. Born at Elshout in North Brabant on 30 August 1797, he died at Bruges in 1871. His godly parents died while he was a child, and a pious uncle raised him. Love of good works marked his youth: catechist at nineteen, clerk at twenty-five to the convert Le Sage-ten-Broek for four years.

Nursing cholera cases at Groningen nearly killed him. Trips to Rome in 1826 and 1838 brought a medal from Leo XII and a talk with Gregory XVI. A short Trappist stay in 1827 ended when his confessor said God had other plans for him. Three years in America, 1831 to 1834, showed him that Catholic teachers were sorely needed, and he set out to train them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-bracke:
Thomas Bracken, poet, journalist and politician, was born in Ireland in 1843 and died at Dunedin, New Zealand, in 1898. Orphaned young, he emigrated to Victoria, Australia, at twelve, then went to Otago as a shearer in 1869. A small book of verse, Flights among the Flax, brought him notice and led to newspaper work in Dunedin.

He helped run the New Zealand Tablet, the Otago Guardian and the Morning Herald, and founded the Saturday Advertiser, which thrived only while he controlled it. Elected to Parliament for Dunedin in 1884 and again in 1886 as a Liberal, he wrote chiefly on local and colonial themes. His last collection, Musings in Maoriland, appeared in 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-godden:
Thomas Godden, whose true name was Tylden, was born at Addington, Kent, in 1624 and died in London in 1688. He studied at Queen's College, Oxford, and St. John's College, Cambridge, converted under the influence of John Sergeant, and went with him to the English College at Lisbon in 1642.
