Martha, a cry in the corridor, and a key to the garden follow. Dickon, a robin who showed the way, and Colin all appear. Magic and a curtain come near the end, with a final chapter in the garden.

Chapter one is titled There Is No One Left. Mary Lennox arrives to live with her uncle at Misselthwaite Manor. Everybody called her the most disagreeable-looking child ever seen, Burnett writes, and agrees it was true. Thin face, thin body, and thin light hair are her marks, with a sour expression over all. India, her birthplace, had yellowed her face and kept her always ill, the opening explains.
the-stories-mother-nature-told-her-child:
Jane Andrews, author of Seven Little Sisters, wrote these nature stories for children, issued in illustrated editions dated 1888 and 1894. A contents list promises many tales. They cover amber beads, Indian corn, and water-lilies. Sea-life, frost giants, and tadpoles follow. Golden-rod and asters close the list. The first story then begins with a question. Does the reader know Mother Nature? God has entrusted her with the care of all living things.

Andrews personifies nature as a storytelling mother whose children learn how the world works through her tales. Some tales give the talk of village trees. Others follow the carrying trade of winds and waters. One peeks into one of God's storehouses. Each turns simple natural facts into bedtime lessons.
the-story-hour-a-book-for-the-home-and-t: Kate Douglas Wiggin and Nora A. Smith compiled this story collection for the home and the kindergarten, opening with a Froebel motto on ears and hearts opening to the storyteller. Only the title page and contents are present here. The contents show an introduction and preface. The stories include The Oriole's Nest. Moufflou, adapted from Ouida, follows. The Babes in the Wood and a story of Christmas come next. The first Thanksgiving day appears too. George Washington tales in two parts close the list. The stories themselves do not appear.
the-surprising-adventures-of-baron-munch:
Rudolph Erich Raspe's Baron tells his marvellous travels in a volume whose 1895 edition carries a learned introduction on imaginary voyages. The introduction sorts imaginary voyages into types. The three great types were all created in England, it observes. Utopia serves the philosophical kind. Robinson Crusoe serves the edifying kind. Gulliver's Travels serves the satirical kind. Munchausen adds a fourth type. It is the wildly lying kind. It came at the end of the eighteenth century.

The Baron's notoriety is universal and his name proverbial, the introduction argues, though the learned condemned the work as worthless. It first appeared in London in 1785. The form was a slim pamphlet of forty-nine small pages. The Critical Review noticed it as a satire. It mocked bold parliamentary assertions. A second edition was printed at Oxford in 1786. It recommended the tales to country gentlemen. They could repeat them after a hunt.
the-survivors-of-the-chancellor-diary-of:
Jules Verne tells this shipwreck tale as the diary of J. R. Kazallon, a passenger on the Chancellor, and a companion record carries an editor's introduction to the same work. The diary opens at Charleston on September 27, 1869. At high tide the ship leaves the Battery quay. Captain Huntly commands her. She doubles Fort Sumter. By seven in the evening she stands free on the wide Atlantic.

Kazallon describes his ship proudly. She is a fine three-master of 900 tons, square-rigged. The Liverpool firm of Laird Brothers owns her. She is copper-sheathed and teak-decked. She is registered first class. She is making her third voyage between Charleston and Liverpool. He then explains that no direct steamship service ran between South Carolina and Great Britain, so travellers chose between New York and New Orleans sailings, but fate decided otherwise for him.
the-tale-of-balen:
Algernon Charles Swinburne retells the old wild tale of Balen in verse, published by Chatto and Windus in London in 1896. A dedication poem to his mother is dated March 24, 1896. He lays his hope, heart, and self before her in song. He hopes the remade tale will live through one springtide of strong April suns.

The poem itself then opens in hawthorn-time. The heart grows light there. The world turns sweet to ear and eye. Birds and glad thoughts take wing in the verse. Heather kindles toward the light. Whin burns like frankincense and flame. Swinburne's dense music sets the Arthurian story of Balen in a blaze of spring imagery.
the-tale-of-henrietta-hen: Henrietta Hen, by Arthur Scott Bailey, appeared in 1921 in his Slumber-Town Tales series, with drawings by Harry L. Smith. This record holds the title page and contents only, leaving Henrietta's story itself unread. Nine chapters are listed, beginning with her fine family and moving through wet feet, a swimmer, a capture by Mr. Crow, and a warning delivered to the rooster. A later chapter calls her haughty, so readers can guess at her proud character even without the pages that follow.
the-tale-of-tom-kitten:
Beatrix Potter's Tom Kitten was first published by Frederick Warne in 1907 and dedicated to all Pickles, especially those on her garden wall. Three little kittens, Mittens, Tom Kitten, and Moppet, tumble about the doorstep and play in the dust. Their mother, Mrs. Tabitha Twitchit, expects fine company to tea one day. She brings the kittens inside, to be washed and dressed before the guests arrive.

First she scrubs their faces, then she brushes their fur, dressing each kitten in clean clothes. Anyone who knows kittens can guess how long the good outfits last outdoors. Potter turns a mother's careful preparations into a comedy of dignity lost, and children enjoy watching tidy plans fall apart in the garden.
the-three-jovial-huntsmen:
Randolph Caldecott's Three Jovial Huntsmen, one of his celebrated picture books from Frederick Warne, sings of three huntsmen who go a-hunting with horns blowing. The verses run in broad dialect, with the refrain 'Look ye there!' after every discovery. One huntsman warns the others to mind their eyes and keep their noses right in the wind. Then the first thing they find is a tattered boggart in a field, and they leave it behind.

The joke builds as the three disagree over everything they meet: one calls the boggart a gentleman-farmer who has lost his way. Caldecott's pictures carry much of the comedy, with the huntsmen's solemn confidence mocked at every turn. It is a nursery favourite built from a folk song, valued for rhythm, dialect, and drawings that generations of children have pored over.
the-tree-of-heaven:
May Sinclair's Tree of Heaven, dated 1918, opens in its first part, called Peace, with Frances Harrison sitting in her garden. She rests under the tree her husband calls an ash, though the local people call it a tree of Heaven. The children keep her from dozing away the afternoon: Dorothy, Michael, and Nicholas are going to a party, and Nicky, for whom it is the first, is beside himself with excitement. Baby John, too young for parties, rides furiously on Mary-Nanna's knee to a singing game.

Frances describes the party for the third time: dancing, a Magic Lantern, a Funny Man, and Rosalind's cake with eight pink candles. Nine-year-old Dorothy laughs at Nicky, and his mother kisses him each time. Sinclair's family idyll, dated by its title Peace, stands knowingly on the edge of the war that will take these children.
the-two-noble-kinsmen: The Two Noble Kinsmen, credited on its title page to Mr. John Fletcher and Mr. William Shakspeare, is presented here through a contents list and the opening of its dramatis personae. The scenes run from Athens before a temple and Thebes's court, through prison rooms and forests, to the temples of Mars, Venus, and Diana and a block prepared for combat. The personae begin with Arcite and Palamon, cousins and nephews of Creon, King of Thebes. No line of their rivalry for Emilia appears here.
the-veiled-lady-and-other-men-and-women:
F. Hopkinson Smith heads his story collection with The Veiled Lady of Stamboul and adds ten more tales. A letter to readers admits the title may mislead, since the veiled houri is only one figure among many between the covers. One Venetian beauty, whose love affairs unsettled a quarter of the city, also appears.

Smith's letter ranges over the cast with affection: a motherly nurse, a plucky New England girl, a prim spinster comforted by a boarder, and rough sea-dogs kind to other dogs. Brave men make derricks of their arms, club swells chase adventure, and gay Bohemians taste everything. Story titles include Loretta of the Shipyards, A Coat of Red Lead, and Captain Joe and the Susie Ann.
the-ways-of-men:
Eliot Gregory, writing as An Idler, published The Ways of Men with Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1900. He dedicates the essays to Edith Wharton, quoting lines about her mild reproof and golden praise. Chapter one, Uncle Sam, begins with a governor at this century's birth who loved classical names.

That governor's ardour scattered Utica, Syracuse, and Ithaca across the map, raising trolley-car towns instead of historic pomp. He also christened a city Troy and its hill Mount Ida, little dreaming a youth on those slopes would give his name to the republic itself. Gregory then introduces two brothers, Ebenezer and Samuel, who walked from New York and set up a brickyard near Perry Street, Troy.
the-woman-who-toils-being-the-experience: Front matter alone is present for The Woman Who Toils, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1903. Mrs. John Van Vorst and Marie Van Vorst wrote it together. Its subtitle promises the experiences of two gentlewomen as factory girls. Photographs show one writer dressed for a pickle factory. The other is shown at work in a shoe factory. The sisters dedicate the book to Mark Twain.
topsy-turvy-land-arabia-pictured-for-chi: Samuel M. Zwemer and Amy E. Zwemer pictured Arabia for children in a book published by Fleming H. Revell in 1902, at New York, Chicago, and Toronto. They dedicated it at Bahrein, Arabia, to boys and girls helping to turn the world upside down. Contents begin by asking why Arabia is topsy-turvy land, on page fifteen. The dedication and opening contents are what is given in this record, giving the book's missionary purpose and child audience. The Zwemers' chapters on Arabian life themselves do not appear here.
treatise-on-parents-and-children: Bernard Shaw's Treatise on Parents and Children survives here as its full table of contents. The headings run from Trailing Clouds of Glory and The Child is Father to the Man to School, Taboo in Schools, and Children's Rights and Duties. Later headings cover children's happiness, earning a living, and the conflict of wills. The list ends with reforming society before reforming ourselves. Only the contents page is present here, so the essays themselves do not appear. Even the headings show Shaw attacking the schooling of his day.
troublesome-comforts-a-story-for-childre:
Geraldine Robertson Glasgow's Troublesome Comforts, a story for children from Thomas Nelson and Sons, opens in a stuffy third-class carriage at Liverpool Street Station. Mrs. Beauchamp looks wistfully at her husband on the platform. Behind her the carriage overflows with children, paper parcels, and packages held by straps.

The ticket collector cannot make the nurse's count come right: five halves, two wholes, a dog, and a bicycle. Susie, Dick, and Amy are named, the baby is in arms, and Tommy has vanished. He is under the seat, Dick announces, and crawls out covered in dust, quite unashamed. A seaside holiday begins in cheerful family chaos.
twelve-men:
Theodore Dreiser's Twelve Men, dated 1919, profiles a dozen men who marked his life. The contents name Peter, a doer of the word, his brother Paul, a country doctor, and Culhane the solid man. A mayor and his people, village feudists, and a man called the Mighty Rourke fill out the list.

The first portrait, Peter, opens with a claim about character. In any group, Dreiser writes, Peter stood out as deliciously and irrefutably different, an oasis in American intellectual dreariness. Dreiser met him at St. Louis in 1892, in the art department of the Globe-Democrat. Peter's spiritual freedom, facing nature unafraid, anchors the whole gallery of sketches.
val-d-arno-ten-lectures-on-the-tuscan-ar: John Ruskin's Val d'Arno offers ten lectures on the Tuscan art that came just before the Florentine year of victories. Pages present here hold the lecture list and a list of plates, so the lectures themselves are not shown. Titles move from Nicholas the Pisan and John the Pisan through heraldic subjects like Shield and Apron and Parted per Pale, to the Tyrrhene Sea and the Fleur de Lys. Plates promise Pisano's pulpit, the fountain of Perugia, the door of the Pisa baptistery, and scenes of St. John.
vendetta-a-story-of-one-forgotten: Marie Corelli, author of Ardath, Thelma, and A Romance of Two Worlds, wrote Vendetta, or A Story of One Forgotten. Pages present here give the title page and a contents list that names a preface and thirty-four numbered chapters with no titles given, so the story itself is not shown. Nothing in these pages names the forgotten one or the wrong that drives the revenge. Readers learn only the book's frame: a long novel in thirty-four chapters, built on a single buried life and the vengeance it seeks.
war-in-the-garden-of-eden: Kermit Roosevelt wrote War in the Garden of Eden about his service in Mesopotamia. The book came out at New York in 1919. He had served as a captain in the British forces, and then in the American field artillery. He dedicated the book to the memory of his father. Pages present here hold the title page, contents, and picture list only, so his narrative is not shown. Contents promise the Tigris front and patrols among the ruins of Babylon. Fights on the Kurdish and Persian fronts follow.
what-great-men-have-said-about-women:
E. Haldeman-Julius edited What Great Men Have Said About Women as number 77 in his Ten Cent Pocket Series. The little book came from Girard, Kansas. It gathers short quotes on women from famed male writers. Shakespeare leads the set, with lines drawn from several of his plays.

One quote praises a woman's eye as a teacher of beauty, from Love's Labour's Lost. Much Ado About Nothing adds a softer image of a life entering a man's thoughts. Other lines say kindness wins love more than looks do. Gifts, one verse warns, can move a woman's mind when words fail. Readers get a pocket set of old praise, wit, and bias.
when-we-dead-awaken:
Henrik Ibsen wrote When We Dead Awaken, his last play, in a version by William Archer. Archer's introduction tells how the play broke Ibsen's steady two-year rhythm. Fans expected a new work in 1898, but Christmas brought no word of one. Ibsen was past seventy, and the gap looked like a bad sign.

Archer met Ibsen at the new National Theatre in Christiania in September of the next year. Ibsen said he was at work on a new play, and planned to name it a dramatic epilogue. He wrote it in fever and haste, as if death stood behind him. The play came out just before Christmas 1899. An aging sculptor and a lost love face what their lives have cost.
ximenez-historias-origen:
Francisco Ximénez was a Dominican friar in Guatemala in the early 1700s. His Histories of the Origin of the Indians reached print in an 1857 edition. Carl Scherzer edited the old manuscript for its first wide release.

Inside stands Ximénez's Spanish version of the Popol Vuh itself. That text is the great creation epic of the Maya peoples. No European version of the epic had appeared before his work. His manuscript kept the story safe while conquest tried to erase it. The book that saved the Maya Bible still anchors study of it today. Without Ximénez, the epic might have vanished for good.
